concepts.name: The scientific method
concepts.why: Chemistry is a science based on observation and experimentation, and there is no single route from a question to an answer. What every route has in common is that it rests on experiments that can be repeated, so the path from question and observation to hypothesis, and from hypothesis through testing to law or theory, is the method the whole of the book argues by.
concepts.evidence: The section describes the path of discovery and defines the scientific method, Figure 1.4 draws it with its loops back to the hypothesis, and an exercise asks the reader to design a test for whether the outside temperature is below freezing without a thermometer.

concepts.name: Telling a hypothesis from a law and from a theory
concepts.why: These three words are used loosely outside science and precisely inside it. A hypothesis is a tentative explanation that guides the gathering of information, a law summarizes a vast number of observations and predicts, and a theory is a well-substantiated explanation that survived a large body of data. Reading a statement and knowing which of the three it is tells the reader how much weight it carries.
concepts.evidence: The section defines all three in turn and explains how a hypothesis may become a theory, and two exercises give six statements in all and ask the reader to classify each and explain the reasoning.

concepts.name: The macroscopic, microscopic, and symbolic domains
concepts.why: Chemists describe matter in three domains at once: the macroscopic, which can be seen and touched; the microscopic, which is mostly imagined; and the symbolic, the formulas and equations that stand for either. One of the challenges of learning chemistry is that the same symbol can stand for a thing in one domain or in the other, and one of the pleasures is explaining what can be observed by what must be imagined.
concepts.evidence: The section names and defines the three domains and works them through on water, Figure 1.5 shows an iceberg, the molecules in it and the formula H2O together, and four exercises underline items and ask which domain each belongs to and, for a symbol, which domain it stands for.

concepts.name: Matter
concepts.why: Matter is anything that occupies space and has mass, which is the working definition everything else in the book is stated about. It is worth stating carefully because a gas is as much matter as a solid is, even though it can be neither seen nor held.
concepts.evidence: The section opens by defining matter and argues that a gas is matter because a balloon inflates, and the summary states the definition again.

concepts.name: Solid, liquid, gas, and plasma
concepts.why: A solid is rigid and keeps its shape, a liquid flows and keeps its volume, and a gas takes both the shape and the volume of its container; a plasma is a gas carrying enough charged particles to behave unlike one. These are the states the book will move a substance between for the rest of the chapters, so the properties that tell them apart come first.
concepts.evidence: The section defines all four states, Figure 1.6 shows the three common ones in beakers and Figure 1.7 a plasma torch, and an exercise asks what properties distinguish solids from liquids, liquids from gases, and solids from gases.

concepts.name: Mass and weight are not the same
concepts.why: The mass of an object measures the amount of matter in it and does not change; weight is the force gravity exerts on it and changes with the gravity it sits in. An astronaut's mass is the same on the moon as on the earth while her weight is one sixth of it, so it is mass, not weight, that says how much matter is present.
concepts.evidence: The section defines mass and weight separately and works the astronaut through, and two exercises ask why mass rather than weight indicates the amount of matter, and why astronauts are called weightless but never massless.

concepts.name: The law of conservation of matter
concepts.why: There is no detectable change in the total quantity of matter when matter converts from one type to another or changes among the solid, liquid and gaseous states. It is the law every balanced equation and every mass calculation of the later chapters rests on, and the reason a mass that seems to vanish has gone somewhere that was not weighed.
concepts.evidence: The section states the law and illustrates it with brewing and with a lead-acid battery in Figure 1.8, and three exercises ask about a rusting nail, a loaf baked in an open oven, magnesium burning in air, a sealed flask of tin, and the masses in a fermentation.

concepts.name: Elements and compounds
concepts.why: A pure substance has a constant composition. An element cannot be broken down into anything simpler by a chemical change; a compound is made of two or more elements and can be broken down into them. The properties of combined elements are nothing like their properties uncombined, which is why sodium and chlorine make table salt.
concepts.evidence: The section defines pure substance, element and compound, shows mercury(II) oxide decomposing in Figure 1.9 and gives sodium chloride and sucrose as cases, and an exercise asks how an element differs from a compound and how the two are similar.

concepts.name: Homogeneous and heterogeneous mixtures
concepts.why: A mixture holds two or more kinds of matter in amounts that can vary and can be separated again by physical means. A heterogeneous mixture varies in composition from point to point, as salad dressing does; a homogeneous mixture, also called a solution, is the same throughout, as a sports drink is. The difference is what a sample taken from one place tells about the rest.
concepts.evidence: The section defines mixture, heterogeneous mixture, homogeneous mixture and solution, contrasts salad dressing with a sports drink in Figure 1.10, and two exercises ask how the two kinds of mixture differ and how a homogeneous mixture differs from a pure substance.

concepts.name: Classifying a sample of matter
concepts.why: Given a sample, the reader should be able to place it: constant composition or not, uniform or not, simplifiable by a chemical change or not. Two questions sort every sample into an element, a compound, a homogeneous mixture or a heterogeneous mixture, and the classification decides what can be done with the sample.
concepts.evidence: Figure 1.11 draws the decision as a flowchart, Table 1.1 lists the eleven elements that make up most of the earth's crust, and three exercises give more than sixteen substances between them and ask for the classification of each.

concepts.name: Atoms and molecules
concepts.why: An atom is the smallest particle of an element that keeps the properties of that element and can enter into a chemical combination; a molecule is two or more atoms joined by chemical bonds and moving about as a unit. Atoms are far too small and too light to imagine directly, and the whole microscopic domain of the book is built out of them.
concepts.evidence: The section defines atom and molecule, works through the size and mass of an atom, shows gold atoms in Figure 1.12, cotton down to its molecules in Figure 1.13 and seven molecules in Figure 1.14, and four exercises ask how an atom differs from a molecule, how a sulfur atom differs from a sulfur molecule, and how molecules of elements differ from molecules of compounds.

concepts.name: Physical properties
concepts.why: A physical property is a characteristic of matter that is not associated with a change in its chemical composition: density, color, hardness, melting and boiling point, electrical conductivity. Some can be observed without changing the matter at all, and others only while it is changing state, but in neither case does the substance become a different substance.
concepts.evidence: The section defines physical property and lists familiar examples, and an exercise asks the reader to classify six underlined properties of fluorine as chemical or physical, four of which are physical.

concepts.name: Chemical properties
concepts.why: A chemical property is the ability of a substance to change into another kind of matter, or its inability to do so. Flammability, toxicity, acidity and reactivity are chemical properties, and unlike a physical property, one cannot be observed without the substance in question becoming something else.
concepts.evidence: The section defines chemical property and contrasts iron, which rusts, with chromium, which does not, in Figure 1.19; nitroglycerin and neon make the same contrast, and the fluorine exercise asks for two chemical properties among its six.

concepts.name: Physical and chemical change
concepts.why: A physical change alters the state, form or properties of matter and leaves its chemical identity alone; a chemical change always produces one or more kinds of matter that were not there before. Wax melting and sugar dissolving are the first; rust forming and a match burning are the second, and the test is whether what is left is the same substance.
concepts.evidence: The section defines both changes, illustrates the physical with melting wax and condensing steam in Figure 1.18 and the chemical with copper in nitric acid, a burning match, cooking meat and a browning banana in Figure 1.20, and the section summary states the contrast again.

concepts.name: Classifying a change as physical or chemical
concepts.why: Deciding which of the two kinds of change has happened is a judgement the reader has to make about a described event, and the judgement comes down to one question: is the matter that is left the same kind of matter as the matter that was there before? A gas that expands has changed physically; a gas that has burned has not.
concepts.evidence: Three exercises give eleven changes between them, from condensing steam and melting gold to souring milk and an exploding firecracker, and two more ask about a volume of oxygen that changes with temperature and about hydrogen and oxygen combining to make water vapor.

concepts.name: Extensive and intensive properties
concepts.why: An extensive property depends on how much matter is present and is directly proportional to it; an intensive property does not. Mass and volume are extensive, temperature and density intensive, and the distinction matters because an intensive property identifies a substance while an extensive one only measures a sample of it.
concepts.evidence: The section defines both, contrasts a gallon and a cup of milk at the same temperature and a drop against a pot of hot oil, and three exercises ask the reader to explain the difference, to sort five properties, and to explain why density, the ratio of two extensive properties, is intensive.

concepts.name: The three parts of a measured quantity
concepts.why: Every measurement provides three kinds of information: a number, a unit that says what the number is compared against, and an uncertainty. The number and the unit are written down and the uncertainty is carried implicitly, and a quantity that is missing any of the three is at best confusing; a dose of one hundred without its unit can be a treatment or a lethal amount.
concepts.evidence: The section opens by naming the three parts, defines unit, argues the point with a soft-drink bottle, a hamburger and a prescription of phenobarbital, and the summary states that each measurement has an amount, a unit and an uncertainty.

concepts.name: Writing a measurement in scientific notation
concepts.why: A number in a measurement can be written in decimal form or in scientific notation, and for the very large and the very small the second is the only readable one. The mass of a mosquito is more usefully written as 2.5 x 10 to the minus 6 kilograms than as a string of zeros, and the notation will also be what settles how many digits of a measurement are meant.
concepts.evidence: The section introduces exponential notation with the takeoff weight of an airliner and the mass of a mosquito and points the reader at Appendix B for a review, the prefix table of Table 1.3 writes every prefix as a power of ten, and 1.5 asks for seven numbers in scientific notation with the correct significant figures.

concepts.name: The SI base units
concepts.why: Seven fundamental properties have units fixed by international agreement, and every other unit in the book is derived from them. Knowing that the meter, the kilogram, the second, the kelvin, the ampere, the mole and the candela are the base units is what makes a unit conversion a matter of bookkeeping rather than of memory.
concepts.evidence: Table 1.2 lists the seven base units with their symbols, the section then introduces the meter, the kilogram, the kelvin and the second one at a time with their definitions, and two exercises ask which SI base or derived unit is appropriate for fourteen measurements.

concepts.name: Using the SI prefixes
concepts.why: Fractions and multiples of an SI unit are always powers of ten, and each power has a prefix and a symbol. A kilometer is a thousand meters and a microliter is a millionth of a liter, so a reader who knows the prefixes can move a measurement up and down the scale without arithmetic.
concepts.evidence: Table 1.3 gives eleven prefixes from femto to tera with their factors and a worked example of each, and two exercises ask for the prefix that means a given factor and for the factor a given prefix symbol stands for.

concepts.name: Derived units
concepts.why: Many units are built out of the base units rather than agreed separately: a volume is a length cubed, and a density is a mass divided by a volume. Seeing a unit as the product and quotient of base units is what lets the reader check that a calculation has produced the kind of quantity it was meant to.
concepts.evidence: The section opens its treatment of derived units by saying that the base unit of length defines a unit of volume and that mass and length define a unit of density, and then derives the cubic meter, the liter and the gram per cubic centimeter in turn.

concepts.name: Volume and its units
concepts.why: Volume is the amount of space an object occupies, and its standard unit is the cubic meter, a cube one meter on an edge. The cubic decimeter is a liter and the cubic centimeter is a milliliter, so the units a chemist actually works in are nested inside the standard one by factors of a thousand.
concepts.evidence: The section defines volume, cubic meter, liter, cubic centimeter and milliliter, and Figure 1.25 nests the cubic meter, the liter and the milliliter inside one another and sets a cubic centimeter beside a dime.

concepts.name: Density
concepts.why: The density of a substance is the ratio of the mass of a sample to its volume, and it is the chapter's first derived quantity. It is intensive, so it identifies a substance rather than a sample: lead and gold are both dense, but a brick of gold and a brick of lead of the same size do not weigh the same, which is the whole of the section's opening story.
concepts.evidence: The section defines density, prints it as the section's one key equation, tabulates the densities of twenty-one common substances in Table 1.4, and Example 1.1 computes the density of a lead cube from its edge and its mass while an exercise identifies a piece of jewelry from its measured density.

concepts.name: Measuring a volume by displacement of water
concepts.why: A cube's volume can be calculated from its edge, but most objects are not cubes. Lowering an object into a partly filled graduated cylinder raises the water by exactly the object's volume, which turns an irregular shape into a subtraction and makes the density of anything that sinks measurable with a balance and a cylinder.
concepts.evidence: Example 1.2 works the method through on iron and on wood, reading a rise from 25.5 to 29.5 mL as a volume of 4.0 mL, its Check Your Learning applies it to a foam sample, three end-of-chapter exercises measure blocks the same way, and 1.5 uses the method again on a piece of rebar.

concepts.name: Exact and uncertain numbers
concepts.why: Counting is the only measurement free of uncertainty, and numbers fixed by definition are exact in the same way: a foot is exactly twelve inches and an inch exactly 2.54 centimeters. Every other quantity is uncertain to some extent, and knowing which numbers in a calculation are exact decides which of them can limit the answer.
concepts.evidence: The section defines exact number with the eggs in a carton and the defined conversions, and two exercises give twelve quantities between them and ask which can be determined exactly and which must be measured with some uncertainty.

concepts.name: Every measurement carries an uncertainty
concepts.why: A measurement is read as far as the instrument allows and then one digit further, and that last digit is an estimate. A scale with one milliliter divisions can be read to a tenth of a milliliter, and a balance that reads 6.72 grams is saying the mass lies between 6.71 and 6.73, so uncertainty is a property of the instrument and the reader together, not a mistake.
concepts.evidence: The section works through the meniscus of Figure 1.26, where the digits 2 and 1 are certain and the 6 is estimated, extends the same argument to a quarter weighed on two balances, and defines uncertainty.

concepts.name: Significant figures
concepts.why: All of the digits in a measurement, including the uncertain last one, are its significant figures, and their number is how a written quantity says how certain it is. A result is properly reported when its significant digits represent the certainty of the process that produced it, and no better.
concepts.evidence: The section defines significant figures and significant digits, notes that a measured zero is significant, and the summary states that a measured quantity's uncertainty is represented by the number of significant figures in its number.

concepts.name: Counting the significant figures in a number
concepts.why: The rule is to start at the first nonzero digit on the left and count every digit to its right, and the only difficulty is the zeros. A captive zero results from measurement and is always significant, a leading zero only locates the decimal point and never is, and a trailing zero to the left of the decimal point is ambiguous unless the number is written in scientific notation.
concepts.evidence: The section names leading, captive and trailing zeros on 3090 and 0.008020 and works through 1267 m, 55.0 g, 70.607 mL, 0.00832407 mL and the ambiguous 1300 g, and three exercises ask for the number of significant figures in twenty-two measurements.

concepts.name: Rounding a number to a given number of digits
concepts.why: A digit to be dropped that is less than five rounds down and one greater than five rounds up. When the dropped digit is a five with nothing but zeros after it, the retained digit is rounded to whichever value is even, which is a rule from statistics and is there to keep the rounding from leaning one way over many calculations.
concepts.evidence: The section states the three rounding rules and illustrates them on four numbers, Example 1.3 rounds four more with its Check Your Learning rounding four again, and two exercises round twelve numbers to two significant figures.

concepts.name: Carrying significant figures through a calculation
concepts.why: A result calculated from measurements is at least as uncertain as the measurements it came from, so the answer has to be rounded rather than copied off the calculator. A sum or difference is rounded to the decimal place of the least precise term, and a product or quotient to the number of significant figures of the least certain factor.
concepts.evidence: Examples 1.5.2, 1.5.3 and 1.5.4 work addition, subtraction, multiplication, division and a three-factor volume through with their Check Your Learning items, and two exercises set fourteen calculations and ask for each answer with the correct number of significant figures.

concepts.name: Accuracy and precision
concepts.why: Measurements are precise when repeating them gives very similar results and accurate when they fall close to the true or accepted value, and the two are independent. A dispenser can be precise and consistently wrong, or accurate on average and scattered, and only one that is both is working.
concepts.evidence: The section defines accuracy and precision, draws them on three archery targets in Figure 1.27, tabulates five fills from each of three cough-syrup dispensers in Table 1.5 and reads each one off, and two exercises judge four archers and three sets of repeated measurements.

concepts.name: Dimensional analysis
concepts.why: The units of quantities must be subjected to the same mathematical operations as their numbers. That one premise is what lets a reader divide a distance by a time and get a speed, and it is also what lets the reader check a calculation by looking only at the units, since a wrong arrangement of factors gives a unit nobody wanted.
concepts.evidence: The section derives a sprinter's speed and then rearranges the same relation for time, dividing the units at every step alongside the numbers, defines dimensional analysis and the factor-label method, and the summary names the strategy as what the whole section is about.

concepts.name: The unit conversion factor
concepts.why: A ratio of two equivalent quantities written in different units is equal to one, so multiplying by it changes a quantity's units without changing the quantity. Because the ratio can be written either way up, the reader chooses the arrangement that cancels the unit to be got rid of and leaves the one that is wanted.
concepts.evidence: The section derives the factor from 2.54 cm equal to 1 in., shows that the two forms of a factor are both available and that only one cancels correctly, tabulates twelve common factors in Table 1.6, and four exercises ask the reader to write factors as ratios from stated equivalences and from product labels.

concepts.name: Converting a quantity from one unit to another
concepts.why: Multiplying by one conversion factor after another, each oriented so that the unwanted unit cancels, converts a measurement through as many steps as it takes. It is the most-used skill of the chapter, and it works the same whether the conversion is between two metric units, between metric and customary units, or between units of an area or a volume.
concepts.evidence: Example 1.8 converts a frisbee's mass from grams to ounces and its Check Your Learning converts quarts to liters, and more than twenty exercises convert lengths, volumes, masses and speeds, including a red blood cell's diameter, a barrel of oil, a weight lifter's mass and the dimensions of a two-by-four.

concepts.name: Computing a quantity from measurements in mixed units
concepts.why: Beyond a simple conversion, the factor-label method solves a problem in which the quantity wanted is computed from two or more measured ones given in the wrong units. All the factors are arranged in one line so that the labels cancel and combine into the unit of the answer, and the arithmetic is done once at the end.
concepts.evidence: Examples 1.6.2 and 1.6.3 compute the density of antifreeze in grams per milliliter from a volume in quarts and a mass in pounds, and a fuel economy in miles per gallon and its cost from a distance in kilometers and a volume in liters, each set out both step by step and as a single line of factors; ten exercises compute densities, masses and volumes the same way.

concepts.name: Why temperature conversion is linear, not proportional
concepts.why: Most units of a property are directly proportional to one another and a single conversion factor moves between them. The Celsius and Fahrenheit scales do not share a zero, so the relation between them is a line with an intercept rather than a line through the origin, and converting between them takes both a slope and an offset.
concepts.evidence: The section sets the proportional case of feet and inches beside the temperature case, derives the slope from the two defining temperatures of water as nine Fahrenheit degrees to five Celsius degrees and the intercept as thirty-two, and explains that this is why temperature needs more than multiplication by a factor.

concepts.name: The Celsius, Fahrenheit, and kelvin scales
concepts.why: A temperature scale is fixed by choosing reference temperatures and dividing the space between them. Celsius puts the freezing and boiling of water at 0 and 100, Fahrenheit at 32 and 212, and kelvin is absolute: its zero is the lowest temperature that can theoretically be achieved, which is why its unit carries no degree symbol.
concepts.evidence: The section defines Fahrenheit and temperature, explains the origin of the absolute scale and the convention about the degree symbol, and Figure 1.28 sets the three thermometers side by side with the freezing and boiling temperatures of water marked on each.

concepts.name: Converting between Celsius and Fahrenheit
concepts.why: The Fahrenheit temperature is nine fifths of the Celsius temperature plus thirty-two, and the relation rearranges to give the Celsius temperature from the Fahrenheit one. Both forms are on the book's key equation list, and they are the conversion a reader meets outside the laboratory more often than any other.
concepts.evidence: The section derives both forms from the slope and intercept it computes, Example 1.11 converts body temperature from Celsius and Example 1.12 an oven setting from Fahrenheit, each with a Check Your Learning, and eight exercises convert temperatures from the boiling point of gold to the inside of a freezer.

concepts.name: Converting between Celsius and kelvin
concepts.why: A kelvin and a Celsius degree are the same size, so the two scales differ only by where their zeros sit: adding 273.15 to a Celsius temperature gives the kelvin temperature and subtracting it goes back. The 273.15 was determined experimentally and is not exact, which matters when the result is rounded.
concepts.evidence: The section derives both equations after noting that the two scales' reference temperatures differ by the same hundred, prints them among the section's key equations, and the two worked examples and their Check Your Learning items report a kelvin temperature alongside every Celsius and Fahrenheit one.

concepts.name: Dalton’s atomic theory
concepts.why: Dalton’s postulates say that matter is made of atoms, that the atoms of one element all have the same characteristic mass and differ from the atoms of every other element, that a compound holds atoms of two or more elements in a small, whole-number ratio, and that atoms are neither created nor destroyed in a chemical change but only rearranged. These postulates give a microscopic explanation of the macroscopic behavior of matter the reader has already met, including the conservation of matter, and every later picture of the atom starts from them.
concepts.evidence: The section lists the five postulates with Figures 2.2 to 2.4, and Example 2.1, its Check Your Learning and the first exercise ask whether a change drawn in colored spheres violates any of them.

concepts.name: The law of definite proportions
concepts.why: All samples of a pure compound contain the same elements in the same proportion by mass, which is what Dalton’s fourth postulate predicts if the numbers of atoms in a compound always stand in the same ratio. Note that the converse is not true: two samples with the same mass ratio are not necessarily the same substance.
concepts.evidence: Table 2.1 shows three samples of isooctane with the same carbon-to-hydrogen mass ratio of 5.33:1, and an exercise asks which postulate two samples of titanium dioxide of different composition would violate.

concepts.name: The law of multiple proportions
concepts.why: When two elements form more than one compound, a fixed mass of one element reacts with masses of the other in a ratio of small whole numbers. Taking the ratio of the two mass ratios is the step that reveals it, and atomic theory explains it at once, since one compound simply holds more atoms of one element per atom of the other.
concepts.evidence: The two copper chlorides of Figure 2.5 give a ratio of ratios of 2 to 1, and Example 2.2 and its Check Your Learning ask the reader to decide from mass data whether two compounds show definite or multiple proportions.

concepts.name: Thomson’s cathode rays and the electron
concepts.why: The beam in a cathode ray tube bends toward a positive charge and away from a negative one, is the same whatever metal the electrodes are made of, and has a charge-to-mass ratio showing its particles are far lighter than atoms. Thomson concluded that the particles are negatively charged subatomic constituents of all atoms, which is the first evidence that the atom is not indivisible.
concepts.evidence: The section argues from Figure 2.6 to Thomson’s conclusions, and an exercise asks how electrons and protons are alike and how they differ.

concepts.name: Millikan’s fundamental charge
concepts.why: The charge on every oil drop Millikan measured is a whole-number multiple of 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, so that value must be the charge of a single electron. Combined with Thomson’s charge-to-mass ratio, it gives the mass of the electron by a simple calculation.
concepts.evidence: Figure 2.7 tabulates the charges of five drops, and the section divides the electron’s charge by Thomson’s ratio to find its mass, 9.107 × 10⁻³¹ kg.

concepts.name: Rutherford’s nuclear atom
concepts.why: Most α particles pass straight through a gold foil, a few are deflected slightly and a very few bounce almost straight back. Rutherford reasoned that the atom must be mostly empty space with a small, heavy, positively charged nucleus at its center, which replaced both the plum pudding model and the Saturn-like model and is still the picture used today.
concepts.evidence: Figures 2.8 to 2.10 set the two earlier models beside the gold foil experiment and its explanation, and two exercises ask the reader to predict the paths of α particles fired at a plum pudding atom and at a Rutherford atom.

concepts.name: Protons, neutrons, and electrons
concepts.why: An atom is built from three kinds of subatomic particle: the negatively charged, very light electron outside the nucleus, and the positively charged proton and the uncharged neutron of nearly the same mass inside it. Everything the chapter says about atomic number, mass number, isotopes and ions is counted in these three particles.
concepts.evidence: The section introduces each particle with its discoverer, and exercises ask how protons and neutrons, and electrons and protons, are similar and how they differ; Table 2.2 in the next section gives their charges and masses.

concepts.name: Isotopes
concepts.why: Atoms of the same element can differ in mass while remaining chemically identical, because they have the same number of protons and different numbers of neutrons. The existence of isotopes is the reason Dalton’s second postulate had to be restated in terms of chemical properties rather than mass.
concepts.evidence: The section tells how Soddy recognized isotopes and how Chadwick’s neutron explained them, and an exercise asks which of Dalton’s ideas isotopes violate.

concepts.name: The atomic mass unit and the fundamental unit of charge
concepts.why: Atoms are so small that grams and coulombs are inconvenient, so their masses are given in atomic mass units, exactly one twelfth of the mass of a carbon-12 atom, and their charges in units of the charge of one electron. On these scales a proton and a neutron each weigh about 1 amu and carry charges of 1+ and 0, and an electron weighs about 0.00055 amu and carries 1−.
concepts.evidence: The section defines the unified atomic mass unit, the dalton and the elementary charge, and Table 2.2 lists the charge and mass of each subatomic particle in both kinds of unit.

concepts.name: Atomic number and mass number
concepts.why: The atomic number is the number of protons in the nucleus and is the defining trait of an element; the mass number is the total number of protons and neutrons. Their difference is the number of neutrons, and in a neutral atom the atomic number is also the number of electrons.
concepts.evidence: The section defines both numbers and writes A − Z as the number of neutrons, and several exercises ask for the numbers of protons, neutrons and electrons in given isotopes.

concepts.name: Ions, cations, and anions
concepts.why: When the numbers of protons and electrons in an atom are not equal, it carries a charge equal to the number of protons minus the number of electrons and is called an ion. An atom that gains electrons becomes a negatively charged anion, and one that loses electrons becomes a positively charged cation.
concepts.evidence: The section works the sodium cation and the oxide anion, and exercises ask for the symbol of an ion from its numbers of particles and charge.

concepts.name: Finding the numbers of protons, neutrons, and electrons in an atom or ion
concepts.why: Given an element’s atomic number, a mass number and a charge, the reader should be able to count the particles: the protons from the atomic number, the neutrons from the mass number less the atomic number, and the electrons from the protons less the charge. The same reasoning run backward gives the charge from the counts.
concepts.evidence: Example 2.3 counts the particles in an iodine anion, its Check Your Learning finds the charge of a platinum ion, and several exercises ask for the particles in isotopes used in medicine and in the diet.

concepts.name: Chemical symbols
concepts.why: A chemical symbol of one, two or three letters stands for an element or for one atom of it, whether the reader means a single atom or a jar full. Only the first letter is capitalized, which is why Co is cobalt and CO is carbon monoxide, and some symbols come from the element’s name in another language.
concepts.evidence: Figure 2.13 labels a jar of mercury Hg, Table 2.3 lists common elements and their symbols, and the section explains how new elements are named.

concepts.name: Writing and reading the symbol of an isotope or ion
concepts.why: The full symbol of an atom places the mass number as a left superscript, the atomic number as a left subscript (often omitted) and the charge as a right superscript on the element’s symbol. Reading and writing these symbols, and the equivalent names such as magnesium-24 or Mg-24, is how the book refers to a particular isotope or ion from here on.
concepts.evidence: Figure 2.14 labels the parts of the symbol, Table 2.4 gives the symbols of the isotopes of the first ten elements, and exercises ask the reader to write the symbol of an ion from its particles and charge.

concepts.name: Average atomic mass
concepts.why: The mass listed for an element in the periodic table is a weighted average over its naturally occurring isotopes, the sum of each isotope’s mass multiplied by its fractional abundance. That is why most atomic masses are not whole numbers, and it is important to understand that no single atom has the average mass: no boron atom weighs 10.8 amu.
concepts.evidence: The section computes the average mass of boron, Example 2.4 and its Check Your Learning compute the average masses of neon and magnesium, and exercises ask for the average masses of bromine and lithium.

concepts.name: Calculating isotopic abundances from an average mass
concepts.why: For an element with two isotopes, the fraction of one can be written as x and of the other as 1 − x, and the average mass equation then becomes one equation in one unknown. Solving it turns the average atomic mass back into the percent composition by isotope.
concepts.evidence: Example 2.5 finds the abundances of chlorine-35 and chlorine-37, its Check Your Learning those of the copper isotopes, and an exercise the boron abundances from Turkish and American ores.

concepts.name: Mass spectrometry
concepts.why: A mass spectrometer charges the atoms or molecules of a vaporized sample, deflects the ions through an electric or magnetic field by an amount that depends on their mass and charge, and records how many arrive at each mass-to-charge ratio. The height of each peak is proportional to the fraction of the ions at that ratio, so the spectrum reads off which isotopes are present and in what abundance.
concepts.evidence: Figure 2.15 shows the instrument and the mass spectrum of zirconium with five isotope peaks, and the chapter introduction uses the method to identify biomarkers in exhaled breath.

concepts.name: Molecular formulas
concepts.why: A molecular formula writes the symbols of the atoms in a molecule with subscripts giving how many of each there are. Many elements exist as molecules of their own, such as the diatomic H₂, O₂ and N₂ and the eight-atom S₈, and the formula of such an element differs from its symbol for that reason.
concepts.evidence: Figures 2.16 and 2.17 represent methane and sulfur, and exercises ask why the symbol of oxygen or of sulfur differs from the formula of its molecule.

concepts.name: A subscript is not a coefficient
concepts.why: A subscript counts the atoms bonded together in one molecule, while a number written in front counts separate units. H₂ is one molecule of two bonded atoms, 2H is two separate atoms, and 2H₂ is two molecules, four different things for four ways of writing hydrogen.
concepts.evidence: Figure 2.18 draws H, 2H, H₂ and 2H₂ side by side, and the section states the distinction in the paragraph before it.

concepts.name: Structural formulas and molecular models
concepts.why: A structural formula shows which atoms are connected to which, with lines for bonds; a ball-and-stick model shows the arrangement of the atoms in space, and a space-filling model shows their relative sizes. Each representation adds something the molecular formula leaves out.
concepts.evidence: Figures 2.16, 2.17, 2.20 and 2.21 show methane, sulfur, benzene and acetic acid in several of these representations, and exercises ask for formulas read off structural drawings.

concepts.name: Finding an empirical formula
concepts.why: An empirical formula gives the simplest whole-number ratio of the atoms or ions in a compound, found by dividing the subscripts of the molecular formula by their largest common factor. A molecular formula is always a whole-number multiple of the empirical formula, so acetic acid, C₂H₄O₂, and glucose share the empirical formula CH₂O.
concepts.evidence: The section derives the empirical formulas of acetic acid and benzene, Example 2.6 and its Check Your Learning ask for the formulas of glucose and metaldehyde, and several exercises ask for empirical formulas.

concepts.name: Isomers
concepts.why: The same atoms can be connected in different ways, so compounds with the same molecular formula can have different structures and different properties. Structural isomers differ in how the atoms are connected, as acetic acid and methyl formate do, and spatial isomers differ only in the orientation of the atoms in space, as the two mirror-image forms of carvone do.
concepts.evidence: Figures 2.23 and 2.24 show the two kinds of isomer, and an exercise asks for two molecules built from two carbons, six hydrogens and one oxygen and what their relationship is called.

concepts.name: The periodic law
concepts.why: The properties of the elements are periodic functions of their atomic numbers. Mendeleev arranged the elements by atomic mass and used the pattern to predict elements not yet found, and by the twentieth century it was clear that atomic number, not mass, orders the table.
concepts.evidence: The section tells how Mendeleev’s predictions of gallium and germanium were confirmed, with his table in Figure 2.25, and states the modern law before the table of Figure 2.26.

concepts.name: Periods and groups
concepts.why: The modern periodic table arranges the elements in order of increasing atomic number in seven horizontal rows, called periods, and eighteen vertical columns, called groups, so that elements with similar properties fall in the same group. Each box gives the element’s atomic number, symbol and average atomic mass, and a mass in square brackets marks an element made only of radioactive isotopes.
concepts.evidence: Figure 2.26 is the table itself, and exercises ask the reader to find elements by group and by period.

concepts.name: Metals, nonmetals, and metalloids
concepts.why: Metals are shiny, malleable and ductile and conduct heat and electricity well; nonmetals are dull and conduct poorly; metalloids conduct moderately well and share properties of both. The three classes occupy regions of the periodic table, so an element’s position predicts its general properties.
concepts.evidence: Figure 2.26 shades the three classes, and exercises ask the reader to classify elements as metals or nonmetals using the table.

concepts.name: Main-group elements, transition metals, and the named groups
concepts.why: The groups 1, 2 and 13 to 18 hold the main-group elements, groups 3 to 12 the transition metals, and the two rows beneath the table the inner transition metals, the lanthanides and actinides. Several groups have names of their own, the alkali metals, alkaline earth metals, pnictogens, chalcogens, halogens and noble gases, and their members have similar chemical properties.
concepts.evidence: Figure 2.27 marks each family on the table, and exercises ask the reader to classify elements as main-group elements, transition metals or inner transition metals and to find the lightest and heaviest members of named groups.

concepts.name: Naming the group an element belongs to
concepts.why: Given an element, the reader should be able to find it in the periodic table and give the name of its group, and given a group name and a period, find the element. This is the fluency with the table that the next two sections rely on for predicting ions and naming compounds.
concepts.evidence: Example 2.7 and its Check Your Learning ask for the group names of eight elements, and exercises ask for the element that is a given kind in a given period.

concepts.name: Predicting the charge of a monatomic ion
concepts.why: Main-group metals tend to lose enough electrons to have as many as the preceding noble gas and form cations whose charge equals their group number, and nonmetals tend to gain enough electrons to match the next noble gas and form anions whose charge is the number of groups they lie to the left of the noble gases. The rule weakens toward the middle of the table, where metals such as iron and copper form ions of more than one charge.
concepts.evidence: Figure 2.29 gives the common charges across the table, and Examples 2.8 and 2.9 and their Check Your Learning items ask for the symbol and charge of an ion from its position or its particles.

concepts.name: Polyatomic ions and oxyanions
concepts.why: A polyatomic ion is a group of bonded atoms that carries an overall charge and acts as a single unit, and an oxyanion is one that contains oxygen. The book asks the reader to memorize the names, formulas and charges of the common ones, and the suffixes -ate and -ite and prefixes per- and hypo- mark more or fewer oxygen atoms.
concepts.evidence: Table 2.5 lists the common polyatomic ions with their related acids, and exercises ask the reader to name the ions in compounds such as ammonium carbonate.

concepts.name: Ionic bonds and covalent bonds
concepts.why: When electrons are transferred and ions form, the electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions is an ionic bond; when electrons are shared and molecules form, the attraction between the nuclei and the shared pairs of electrons is a covalent bond. Compounds are classified as ionic or molecular by the bonds present in them.
concepts.evidence: The section defines both kinds of bond before dividing compounds into the two classes, and Figure 2.28 shows a sodium atom losing an electron to become a cation.

concepts.name: Ionic compounds
concepts.why: A metal combined with one or more nonmetals usually forms an ionic compound, a solid held together by ionic bonds that melts at a high temperature and conducts electricity when molten but not when solid. Its formula gives the relative numbers of ions rather than a molecule, since an ionic compound has no discrete molecules.
concepts.evidence: Figure 2.30 shows molten sodium chloride conducting, and the section explains why sodium oxalate is written Na₂C₂O₄ rather than as an empirical formula.

concepts.name: Writing the formula of an ionic compound
concepts.why: An ionic compound is electrically neutral, so its formula takes the ions in the ratio that makes the positive and negative charges equal, with a polyatomic ion treated as a unit in parentheses when more than one is needed. Two Al³⁺ and three O²⁻ give Al₂O₃, and one Ca²⁺ with two H₂PO₄⁻ gives Ca(H₂PO₄)₂.
concepts.evidence: Examples 2.10 and 2.11 and their Check Your Learning items predict four formulas, and exercises ask for the formula of the compound formed by each pair of ions.

concepts.name: Molecular compounds
concepts.why: Compounds of nonmetals usually consist of discrete, neutral molecules held together by covalent bonds, and under normal conditions they are often gases, low-boiling liquids or low-melting solids. The book notes that predicting this from positions in the periodic table is a simplistic approach with interesting exceptions.
concepts.evidence: The section contrasts molecular compounds with ionic ones and names aluminum chloride as an exception to the metal-and-nonmetal rule.

concepts.name: Predicting whether a compound is ionic or molecular
concepts.why: Given a formula, the reader should be able to find its elements in the periodic table and predict that a metal with nonmetals, or a compound with a polyatomic ion, is ionic, and that nonmetals alone form a molecular compound. It is the first question asked before naming any compound in the next section.
concepts.evidence: Example 2.12 and its Check Your Learning classify eight compounds, and exercises ask the reader to classify chlorides and other compounds and to write the ions of those that are ionic.

concepts.name: Naming ionic compounds
concepts.why: An ionic compound is named cation first and anion second: the metal’s name, then the nonmetal’s name with its ending replaced by -ide, or the name of the polyatomic ion as it stands. Because the charges fix the ratio of the ions, the name does not need to state how many of each there are.
concepts.evidence: Tables 2.6 to 2.8 give examples of binary and polyatomic ionic compounds and their everyday uses, and exercises ask the reader to name compounds and to write formulas from names.

concepts.name: Naming compounds of metals with variable charge
concepts.why: When a metal can form ions of more than one charge, the charge of its ion is worked out from the formula and the anion’s fixed charge and written as a Roman numeral in parentheses after the metal’s name, as in iron(II) chloride and iron(III) chloride. The older suffixes -ous and -ic for the lower and higher charges survive in some industries.
concepts.evidence: Table 2.9 lists variably charged metal compounds, Example 2.13 names five compounds, and exercises ask for IUPAC names of compounds such as ferric nitrate and cupric bromide.

concepts.name: Naming and writing formulas of ionic hydrates
concepts.why: A hydrate is named by adding to the name of the anhydrous compound a Greek prefix for the number of water molecules per formula unit followed by the word hydrate, and its formula appends a centered dot, that number and H₂O. Copper(II) sulfate pentahydrate is CuSO₄·5H₂O.
concepts.evidence: The section names copper(II) sulfate pentahydrate and sodium carbonate decahydrate with Table 2.10 of prefixes, and Example 2.13 and its Check Your Learning include a hydrate each.

concepts.name: Naming binary molecular compounds
concepts.why: Two nonmetals can combine in several ratios, so the name of a binary molecular compound gives the number of each atom with a Greek prefix: the more metallic element first, the other second with the suffix -ide, and mono- dropped from the first. CO is carbon monoxide and N₂O₄ is dinitrogen tetroxide.
concepts.evidence: Table 2.11 lists ten molecular compounds and their names, and Example 2.14 and its Check Your Learning ask for names and formulas of eight covalent compounds.

concepts.name: Naming binary acids
concepts.why: A compound of hydrogen and one other nonmetal dissolved in water is named as an acid by turning hydrogen into the prefix hydro-, adding -ic to the other element’s name, and adding the word acid, so that hydrogen chloride in water is hydrochloric acid.
concepts.evidence: Table 2.12 names five gases and the acids they form in water.

concepts.name: Naming oxyacids
concepts.why: An oxyacid is named from its oxyanion by omitting hydrogen, replacing -ate with -ic or -ite with -ous, and adding acid, so that H₂CO₃ is carbonic acid and HNO₂ is nitrous acid. Sulfuric and sulfurous acids are the book’s named exceptions.
concepts.evidence: Table 2.13 names eight oxyacids beside their anions, and an exercise asks for the formula of sulfuric acid.

concepts.name: Intermolecular and intramolecular forces
concepts.why: Intramolecular forces are the bonds within a molecule that keep it together; intermolecular forces are the attractions between molecules, and they decide many of a substance’s physical properties. The intermolecular forces between small molecules are usually weak compared to the bonds within them.
concepts.evidence: Figure 10.5 draws the two kinds of force between HCl molecules, and the text compares about 17 kJ to vaporize a mole of liquid HCl with about 430 kJ to break its H–Cl bonds.

concepts.name: The phase of a substance depends on its intermolecular forces and kinetic energy
concepts.why: Intermolecular forces hold particles close together, whereas the particles’ kinetic energy works to separate them, so the phase of a substance depends on the balance between the two. Cooling a gas or compressing it lets the attractions win and it condenses; cooling a liquid far enough lets it freeze.
concepts.evidence: Figure 10.2 sets a crystalline solid, a liquid and a gas side by side along arrows of increasing kinetic energy and increasing intermolecular forces, and the condensation on a cold glass and the liquid butane in a lighter are the book’s examples.

concepts.name: London dispersion forces
concepts.why: Because the electrons of an atom or molecule are in constant motion, it can develop an instantaneous dipole, which in turn induces a dipole in a neighbor; the two temporary dipoles attract. This dispersion force is present in all condensed phases, whatever the atoms or molecules.
concepts.evidence: Figure 10.6 illustrates the temporary dipoles of two nonpolar diatomic molecules, and the glossary defines the dispersion force, the instantaneous dipole and the induced dipole.

concepts.name: Larger, more polarizable particles have stronger dispersion forces
concepts.why: In a larger atom the valence electrons are farther from the nucleus and less tightly held, so the electron cloud is more easily distorted; a more polarizable particle has larger dispersion forces and a higher melting and boiling point.
concepts.evidence: Table 10.1 lists the melting and boiling points of the halogens rising with molar mass and atomic radius, and Example 10.1 orders CH₄, SiH₄, GeH₄ and SnH₄ by boiling point.

concepts.name: Molecular shape and contact area affect dispersion forces
concepts.why: Molecules with the same formula can have different dispersion forces: an elongated molecule offers more surface area for contact with its neighbors than a compact one, and so it is held more strongly.
concepts.evidence: Figure 10.7 compares the pentane isomers, whose boiling points fall from 36 °C for n-pentane to 9.5 °C for neopentane as the molecule becomes more compact.

concepts.name: Dipole-dipole attractions
concepts.why: A polar molecule has a partial positive end and a partial negative end, and the positive end of one polar molecule attracts the negative end of another. These attractions add to the dispersion forces, so a polar substance boils higher than a nonpolar one of similar mass.
concepts.evidence: Figure 10.9 shows two arrangements of HCl molecules; the text compares HCl (188 K) with F₂ (85 K), and Example 10.2 predicts that CO boils higher than N₂.

concepts.name: Hydrogen bonding
concepts.why: When hydrogen is bonded to fluorine, oxygen or nitrogen, the large difference in electronegativity and the small sizes of the atoms concentrate the partial charges, and the attraction to a similar group in a nearby molecule is a particularly strong dipole-dipole attraction called a hydrogen bond. It is much weaker than a covalent bond but stronger than other intermolecular attractions.
concepts.evidence: Figure 10.10 draws hydrogen bonds between water molecules, Figures 10.11 and 10.12 show the anomalously high boiling points of NH₃, H₂O and HF, and the DNA feature shows base pairs held by hydrogen bonds.

concepts.name: Identifying the intermolecular forces in a substance and ranking boiling points
concepts.why: To compare substances, we identify the forces each can have from its structure: dispersion forces always, dipole-dipole attractions if the molecule is polar, and hydrogen bonding if it has an H–F, H–O or H–N group. With similar sizes, the substance with the stronger forces has the higher boiling point; with the same kind of force, the larger molecule does.
concepts.evidence: Examples 10.1, 10.2 and 10.3 and most of the end-of-section exercises ask the reader to identify the forces present and to order compounds by boiling or melting point.

concepts.name: Viscosity
concepts.why: The viscosity of a liquid is its resistance to flow. It is greater for liquids of structurally complex molecules with strong intermolecular forces, and it decreases as the temperature rises and the molecules move more rapidly.
concepts.evidence: Table 10.2 lists viscosities from octane to honey, and the exercises ask about motor oils, molasses in winter and a warm engine.

concepts.name: Cohesive and adhesive forces
concepts.why: Cohesive forces are the attractions between identical molecules of a liquid; adhesive forces are the attractions between the liquid and different molecules, such as those of a surface. Their relative strength decides whether a liquid wets a surface and which way its meniscus curves.
concepts.evidence: The text contrasts water, which wets glass and forms a concave meniscus, with mercury, which forms a convex one (Figure 10.18), and Figure 10.16 names both forces on a drop of water on a spider’s web.

concepts.name: Surface tension
concepts.why: Molecules at the surface of a liquid are attracted by only about half as many neighbors as molecules within it, so the liquid contracts to the smallest surface. Surface tension is the energy required to increase the surface area of a liquid; it makes a small drop spherical and lets a water strider stand on water.
concepts.evidence: Table 10.3 lists surface tensions, with water high because of hydrogen bonding, and Figures 10.16 and 10.17 draw the unbalanced forces on surface molecules.

concepts.name: Capillary action
concepts.why: When the adhesive forces between a liquid and a narrow tube or porous material are strong, combined with the cohesive forces within the liquid, the liquid flows upward against gravity until its weight balances the attraction. The narrower the tube, the higher the liquid climbs.
concepts.evidence: Figures 10.19 and 10.20 show wine wicking up a paper towel and water rising and mercury falling in capillary tubes, and the feature on drawing blood relies on it.

concepts.name: The height of capillary rise, $h = 2T\cos\theta / r\rho g$
concepts.why: The height to which a liquid rises in a capillary tube is directly proportional to its surface tension and to the cosine of the contact angle, and inversely proportional to the radius of the tube and the density of the liquid. For water in glass the contact angle is 0°.
concepts.evidence: The section states the equation and Example 10.4 computes a rise of 12 cm for water in a tube of 0.25 mm diameter.

concepts.name: Vapor pressure and dynamic equilibrium
concepts.why: In a closed container, a liquid vaporizes until the rate of condensation equals the rate of vaporization; the amounts of liquid and vapor then stop changing, though molecules continue to be exchanged. The pressure of the vapor in this dynamic equilibrium is the liquid’s vapor pressure, and it does not depend on the surface area or the size of the vessel.
concepts.evidence: Figure 10.22 follows a manometer as the equilibrium is reached, and the glossary defines dynamic equilibrium and vapor pressure.

concepts.name: Stronger intermolecular forces mean a lower vapor pressure
concepts.why: Strong intermolecular attractions impede vaporization and favor the recapture of gas molecules, so a liquid with stronger forces has a lower vapor pressure.
concepts.evidence: Example 10.5 orders diethyl ether, ethanol, water and ethylene glycol by vapor pressure, and its Check Your Learning explains the vapor pressures of four alcohols.

concepts.name: Vapor pressure rises with temperature
concepts.why: At a higher temperature a greater fraction of the molecules have enough kinetic energy to escape the liquid, and those that escape move faster, so the vapor pressure increases.
concepts.evidence: Figure 10.23 shows the distribution of kinetic energies at two temperatures against the minimum needed to escape, and Figure 10.24 plots vapor pressure against temperature for four liquids.

concepts.name: Boiling point and normal boiling point
concepts.why: A liquid boils when its vapor pressure equals the pressure of the gas above it, so its boiling point depends on the surrounding pressure; the normal boiling point is the boiling point at 1 atm (101.3 kPa). A vapor pressure curve can be read as the boiling point at each pressure.
concepts.evidence: Example 10.6 reads the boiling point of water in Leadville, Colorado, from Figure 10.24, and the exercises ask about cooking an egg at altitude.

concepts.name: The Clausius-Clapeyron equation
concepts.why: The vapor pressure of a liquid depends exponentially on temperature, $P = Ae^{-\Delta H_{\text{vap}}/RT}$, so a plot of ln P against 1/T is a straight line whose slope is −ΔH<sub>vap</sub>/R. Temperature must be in kelvin.
concepts.evidence: The section derives the logarithmic and two-point forms from the exponential equation, and all three are the section’s key equations.

concepts.name: Using the two-point Clausius-Clapeyron equation
concepts.why: Given the vapor pressure at two temperatures, we can solve the two-point form for the enthalpy of vaporization; given one pair and the enthalpy of vaporization, we can find the vapor pressure at another temperature or the boiling point at another pressure.
concepts.evidence: Examples 10.7 and 10.8 estimate the enthalpy of vaporization of isooctane and the boiling point of benzene in Denver, and an exercise estimates the normal boiling point of CCl₄.

concepts.name: Enthalpies of vaporization, fusion, and sublimation
concepts.why: Melting, vaporization and sublimation are endothermic, and freezing, condensation and deposition release the same heat with the opposite sign. Melting only partly overcomes the intermolecular attractions while vaporization overcomes them completely, so ΔH<sub>fus</sub> is less than ΔH<sub>vap</sub>, and by Hess’s law ΔH<sub>sub</sub> is about their sum.
concepts.evidence: The section gives ΔH<sub>vap</sub> = 44.01 kJ/mol and ΔH<sub>fus</sub> = 6.01 kJ/mol for water and ΔH<sub>sub</sub> = 26.1 kJ/mol for CO₂, Figure 10.28 draws the three enthalpies on one energy diagram, and Example 10.9 computes the heat carried off by sweat.

concepts.name: Heating and cooling curves
concepts.why: As a substance is heated at a steady rate, its temperature rises within each phase, as q = mcΔT describes, and stays constant at each phase transition while the heat goes into overcoming intermolecular attractions. The plateaus of a heating curve are its phase transitions.
concepts.evidence: Figure 10.26 photographs ice held at 0 °C while it melts, and Figure 10.29 draws the heating curve of water with its melting and boiling plateaus.

concepts.name: Calculating the total heat to change temperature and phase
concepts.why: The heat for a change through several phases is the sum of the steps: q = mcΔT for each warming or cooling within a phase, with the specific heat of that phase, and q = nΔH for each transition.
concepts.evidence: Example 10.10 sums five steps to find 416 kJ to turn 135 g of ice at −15 °C into steam at 120 °C, and exercises ask the same for water and TiCl₄.

concepts.name: Phase diagrams
concepts.why: A phase diagram combines the pressure-temperature curves of the liquid-gas, solid-liquid and solid-gas equilibria of a substance. Each region is the phase that is stable under those conditions, and each curve gives a transition temperature as a function of pressure.
concepts.evidence: Figure 10.30 labels the regions, curves and transitions of a typical phase diagram, and Figures 10.31 and 10.34 are the diagrams of water and carbon dioxide.

concepts.name: Reading states and phase changes from a phase diagram
concepts.why: To find the state of a substance, we locate the temperature and pressure on its phase diagram and read the region; to find the phase changes on heating at constant pressure, or on compression at constant temperature, we follow a horizontal or vertical line and note the curves it crosses.
concepts.evidence: Examples 10.11 and 10.12 and their Check Your Learning items read the diagrams of water and CO₂, and several exercises do the same.

concepts.name: The triple point
concepts.why: The triple point is the temperature and pressure at which the solid, liquid and gas phases are in equilibrium. Below the triple-point pressure a substance cannot exist as a liquid, so it sublimes; freeze-drying and dry ice depend on this.
concepts.evidence: Point B of Figure 10.31 is water’s triple point at 0.01 °C and 0.6 kPa, Figure 10.32 shows freeze-dried ice cream, and the text notes that CO₂’s triple point lies well above 1 atm.

concepts.name: The slope of the solid-liquid curve
concepts.why: For most substances the solid-liquid curve has a positive slope, so the melting point rises with pressure; for water it has a slight negative slope, so pressure lowers the melting point of ice.
concepts.evidence: The text contrasts curve BD of water’s diagram with the positive slope for CO₂ and connects water’s behavior to the movement of glaciers (Figure 10.33).

concepts.name: The critical point and supercritical fluids
concepts.why: The liquid-gas curve ends at the critical point; above the critical temperature a gas cannot be liquefied however much pressure is applied, and the substance is a supercritical fluid whose properties are intermediate between those of a liquid and a gas.
concepts.evidence: The section lists critical temperatures and pressures, Figure 10.35 shows CO₂ passing through its critical point, Example 10.13 explains the CO₂ fire extinguisher on a hot day, and the decaffeination feature uses supercritical CO₂.

concepts.name: Crystalline and amorphous solids
concepts.why: In a crystalline solid the particles are arranged in a definite repeating pattern, so every particle is held with the same forces and the solid melts at a precise temperature; in an amorphous solid they are arranged randomly, the attractions vary, and the solid softens over a range of temperatures.
concepts.evidence: Figures 10.37 and 10.38 contrast the two arrangements, including quartz and fused silica, and the text explains why amorphous materials soften gradually.

concepts.name: Ionic, metallic, covalent network, and molecular solids
concepts.why: Crystalline solids are classified by the forces between their particles, and these forces explain their properties: ionic solids are hard, brittle and conduct only when molten; metallic solids are malleable conductors; covalent network solids are very hard with very high melting points; molecular solids are soft with low melting points.
concepts.evidence: Figures 10.39 to 10.42 show an example of each type, and Table 10.4 summarizes their particles, attractions, properties and examples.

concepts.name: Classifying a crystalline solid
concepts.why: From a formula we identify the particles (ions, metal atoms, network-forming atoms or molecules) and so the type of solid; from observed properties such as hardness, conductivity and melting point we reason back to the type.
concepts.evidence: Most of the section’s exercises ask the reader to classify substances by formula or by a table of properties.

concepts.name: Crystal defects
concepts.why: The repeating pattern of a crystal may contain defects: vacancies where a particle is missing, particles in interstitial sites, and impurities substituted into the lattice. Defects change physical properties, and doping silicon creates them on purpose for semiconductors.
concepts.evidence: Figure 10.45 draws a vacancy, an interstitial impurity and a substitution impurity, and the glossary defines vacancy and interstitial sites.

concepts.name: The unit cell and the lattice systems
concepts.why: The structure of a crystal is described by its unit cell, its simplest repeating unit, whose lattice points mark the locations of atoms or ions and which repeats in three dimensions. A unit cell is defined by three edge lengths and three angles, giving seven lattice systems and fourteen unit cells.
concepts.evidence: Figure 10.46 repeats a cubic unit cell, and Figures 10.55 and 10.56 show the axes and angles and the fourteen unit cells.

concepts.name: Simple, body-centered, and face-centered cubic unit cells
concepts.why: Counting one-eighth of each corner atom, one-half of each face atom and all of a body-center atom, a simple cubic cell contains one atom, a body-centered cubic cell two and a face-centered cubic cell four. Their coordination numbers are 6, 8 and 12, and they fill about 52%, 68% and 74% of the space.
concepts.evidence: Figures 10.47 to 10.52 build the three cubic cells, count their atoms and their neighbors, and the glossary defines the coordination number.

concepts.name: Hexagonal and cubic closest packing
concepts.why: Identical spheres pack most closely in hexagonal layers, each layer sitting in the hollows of the one below. Stacking ABAB… gives hexagonal closest packing and ABCABC… gives cubic closest packing, which is the face-centered cubic structure; both have a coordination number of 12, and about two-thirds of metals crystallize this way.
concepts.evidence: Figure 10.53 shows why cubic closest packing is face-centered cubic, and Figure 10.54 compares the two stackings.

concepts.name: Calculating a radius and a density from a unit cell
concepts.why: Where the atoms touch (along an edge in a simple cubic cell, along a face diagonal in a face-centered cubic cell, along a body diagonal in a body-centered one) the edge length gives the radius; the atoms per cell times the mass of an atom, divided by the cell’s volume, gives the density. The same geometry gives ionic radii from the edge length of an ionic crystal.
concepts.evidence: Examples 10.14 and 10.15 find the radius and density of polonium and calcium, Example 10.18 finds the radius of the chloride ion in LiCl, and several exercises ask the same for other metals and salts.

concepts.name: Tetrahedral, octahedral, and cubic holes
concepts.why: In simple ionic structures the larger anions usually form a closest-packed array and the smaller cations occupy the holes between them: tetrahedral holes, two per anion, for small cations; octahedral holes, one per anion, for larger ones; and cubic holes in a simple cubic array for the largest.
concepts.evidence: Figures 10.57 and 10.58 show the holes and the ranges of cation-to-anion radius ratio that fill each.

concepts.name: Finding a formula from the holes occupied
concepts.why: Knowing the number of holes of each kind per anion, the fraction of them the cations occupy gives the ratio of cations to anions, and so the formula of the compound.
concepts.evidence: Examples 10.16 and 10.17 find the formulas of zinc sulfide and aluminum oxide, and several exercises ask the same for other compounds.

concepts.name: Unit cells of ionic compounds
concepts.why: Ionic compounds with ions of similar size in a 1:1 ratio, such as CsCl, form a simple cubic structure; those whose ions differ more in size, such as NaCl and ZnS, form a face-centered cubic cell with the cations in octahedral or tetrahedral holes; CaF₂ is face-centered cubic with fluoride ions in all the tetrahedral holes. The contents of the cell give the formula.
concepts.evidence: Figures 10.59 to 10.62 show the CsCl, NaCl, ZnS and CaF₂ cells and count the ions in each.

concepts.name: X-ray diffraction and the Bragg equation, $n\lambda = 2d\sin\theta$
concepts.why: X-rays scattered by atoms in adjacent crystal planes interfere constructively only when the extra distance traveled is a whole number of wavelengths, which happens at the angle given by the Bragg equation; measuring the diffraction angles gives the spacing of the planes.
concepts.evidence: Figures 10.63 to 10.65 show constructive and destructive interference and a diffractometer, and Example 10.19 finds the plane spacing in copper.

concepts.name: Chemical equations
concepts.why: A chemical equation represents a reaction symbolically: the formulas of the reactants on the left, the formulas of the products on the right, plus signs between formulas and an arrow between the two sides. Parenthetical abbreviations give the physical state of each substance (s, l, g, aq), and a word or symbol over the arrow, such as Δ for heating, names a special condition. It is the language every later chapter writes its reactions in.
concepts.evidence: The section opens with the combustion of methane written as an equation and drawn in space-filling models in Figure 4.2, lists the fundamental aspects of any chemical equation, and illustrates state notation with sodium in water and a condition over the arrow with the decomposition of calcium carbonate.

concepts.name: Coefficients give relative numbers
concepts.why: The coefficients of a balanced equation state the relative numbers of reactant and product species, so they may be read as ratios in any amount unit: one molecule of methane and two of oxygen, one dozen and two dozen, or one mole and two moles. Note that the convention is to use the smallest whole-number coefficients, and that this reading is what makes an equation a statement about amounts rather than only about identities.
concepts.evidence: The section reads the methane equation three ways, Figure 4.3 shows that the 1:2:1:2 ratio holds whatever the absolute numbers of molecules, and the ammonia equation 3N2 + 9H2 ⟶ 6NH3 is reduced to its smallest whole-number coefficients by dividing by 3.

concepts.name: A balanced equation conserves atoms
concepts.why: An equation is balanced when equal numbers of atoms of each element are represented on the reactant and product sides, which is what the law of conservation of matter requires. The number of atoms of an element is the coefficient of each formula containing it multiplied by the element's subscript in that formula, added over every formula on that side.
concepts.evidence: The section defines a balanced equation, counts the oxygen atoms on the product side of the methane equation and tabulates element by element that it is balanced, and an exercise asks what it means for an equation to be balanced and why it matters.

concepts.name: Balancing an equation by inspection
concepts.why: Balancing by inspection changes coefficients, never subscripts, one element at a time until every element balances; changing a subscript would change the identity of a substance, as turning H2O into H2O2 turns water into hydrogen peroxide. A fractional coefficient may be used along the way and then cleared by multiplying through by a whole number.
concepts.evidence: The section balances the decomposition of water step by step with a counting table after each change, Example 4.1 balances the formation of dinitrogen pentoxide, the ethane combustion is balanced through a coefficient of 7/2, and five exercises ask for balanced equations from unbalanced ones or from narrative descriptions.

concepts.name: Molecular, complete ionic, and net ionic equations
concepts.why: A reaction between ionic compounds in water may be written with different levels of detail. A molecular equation writes every substance as a neutral formula; a complete ionic equation writes the dissolved ionic compounds as their dissociated ions; and a net ionic equation leaves out the spectator ions, which appear unchanged on both sides, so that it shows only the species that actually change.
concepts.evidence: The section works the reaction of calcium chloride with silver nitrate through all three forms and cancels the spectator ions, Example 4.2 does the same for carbon dioxide in sodium hydroxide, and an exercise asks how the three kinds of equation differ and when the complete and net ionic equations are identical.

concepts.name: Writing a net ionic equation
concepts.why: Given a balanced molecular equation, the reader dissociates every dissolved ionic compound into its ions, identifies the spectator ions present in identical form on both sides, removes them, and reduces the coefficients to the smallest whole numbers. The result says, for example, that solid silver chloride forms from dissolved silver and chloride ions whatever their source.
concepts.evidence: Example 4.2 and its Check Your Learning, on the electrolysis of brine, write all three equations, and two exercises ask for complete and net ionic equations from molecular ones, among them the precipitation of calcium fluoride.

concepts.name: Precipitation reactions and solubility
concepts.why: A precipitation reaction is one in which dissolved substances react to form one or more solid products, often by an exchange of ions between ionic compounds. A substance precipitates when its concentration exceeds its solubility, the maximum concentration that can be achieved under specified conditions, so the insoluble compounds are the ones that come out of solution.
concepts.evidence: The section defines precipitation reaction, solubility, soluble, insoluble and precipitate, and shows yellow lead iodide forming from potassium iodide and lead nitrate in Figure 4.4 with its net ionic equation.

concepts.name: Predicting a precipitate from solubility guidelines
concepts.why: To predict whether mixing two solutions gives a precipitate, identify every ion present, consider each new cation and anion pairing, and look each up in the solubility guidelines. If one pairing is insoluble, a precipitation reaction is expected and its net ionic equation can be written.
concepts.evidence: Table 4.1 gives the solubility guidelines, the section predicts silver chloride from silver nitrate and sodium chloride, Example 4.3 predicts three precipitates, and its Check Your Learning asks which sodium salt would precipitate barium ion from a water sample.

concepts.name: Acids, bases, and acid-base reactions
concepts.why: An acid-base reaction is one in which a hydrogen ion is transferred from one species to another. In water, an acid is a substance that yields hydronium ions, as hydrogen chloride does by transferring H+ to water molecules, and a base is one that yields hydroxide ions, either by dissociating, as ionic hydroxides do, or by reacting with water, as ammonia does.
concepts.evidence: The section defines acid-base reaction, acid and base, shows hydrogen chloride transferring protons to water in Figure 4.5 and ammonia's uses in Figure 4.7, and Example 4.4 writes the reaction of the weak acid hypochlorous acid with water.

concepts.name: Strong and weak acids and bases
concepts.why: A strong acid reacts completely with water, so virtually every dissolved molecule yields a hydronium ion, and a strong base, such as an ionic hydroxide, dissociates completely. A weak acid or weak base reacts only partially, leaving most of its molecules in their original form, which is why its equation is written with a double arrow; only about 1% of acetic acid or of ammonia is ionized under typical conditions.
concepts.evidence: The section defines the four terms, Table 4.2 lists the six common strong acids, Figure 4.6 shows citrus fruits and vinegar as sources of weak acids, and Example 4.4 explains why a double arrow is used for hypochlorous acid.

concepts.name: Neutralization reactions
concepts.why: A neutralization reaction is an acid-base reaction whose reactants are an acid and a base (but not water), and whose products are often a salt and water. The net ionic equation for the neutralization of any strong acid by an ionic hydroxide is the same, hydronium ion and hydroxide ion giving water.
concepts.evidence: The section defines neutralization and salt, writes the reaction of milk of magnesia with stomach acid, Example 4.4 neutralizes barium hydroxide with nitric acid and its Check Your Learning asks for the general net ionic equation, the Stomach Antacids and Culinary Aspects of Chemistry notes and Figure 4.8 give everyday cases, and several exercises ask the reader to complete and balance neutralizations.

concepts.name: Assigning oxidation numbers
concepts.why: The oxidation number of an element in a compound is the charge its atoms would have if the compound were ionic. It is assigned by four guidelines: zero in an elemental substance, the ion's charge for a monatomic ion, the usual values for hydrogen, oxygen and the halogens, and a sum equal to the charge of the molecule or ion, which fixes the one unknown. Note that an oxidation number is written sign first (+2), a charge number first (2+).
concepts.evidence: The section states the guidelines, Example 4.5 assigns the oxidation numbers of sulfur in H2S, sulfite and sodium sulfate, its Check Your Learning asks for four more, and three exercises ask for the oxidation states of the elements in nineteen compounds.

concepts.name: Oxidation-reduction reactions
concepts.why: An oxidation-reduction (redox) reaction is one in which one or more elements undergo a change in oxidation number. Oxidation is an increase in oxidation number, or a loss of electrons, and reduction a decrease, or a gain; the reducing agent is the species oxidized and the oxidizing agent the species reduced. Defined this way, the class includes reactions such as hydrogen with chlorine in which no electrons are transferred outright.
concepts.evidence: The section develops the definitions from sodium and chlorine through half-reactions and extends them to hydrogen and chlorine through oxidation numbers, Figure 4.9 shows copper displacing silver from solution, and exercises ask which atoms are oxidized and reduced and which species are the oxidizing and reducing agents.

concepts.name: Classifying a reaction
