concepts.why: Given an equation or a description, the reader should be able to say whether it is a precipitation, an acid-base or a redox reaction, or more than one, and name a redox subclass where one fits: combustion, in which a fuel and an oxidant react vigorously to give heat and often light, single displacement, in which an ion in solution is replaced through the oxidation of a metal, or disproportionation, in which one element is both oxidized and reduced.
concepts.evidence: Example 4.6 identifies which of five equations are redox and names them, its Check Your Learning classifies the production of tin(II) chloride, and five exercises ask for the type or types of reaction an equation represents.

concepts.name: Balancing redox equations by half-reactions
concepts.why: A redox equation in aqueous solution can be hard to balance by inspection because water, hydronium ions and hydroxide ions take part. The half-reaction method writes the oxidation and the reduction separately, balances each for atoms (oxygen with water, hydrogen with H+) and then for charge with electrons, scales them to equal numbers of electrons and adds them, with extra steps that convert H+ to water in basic solution. Both atoms and charge must balance at the end.
concepts.evidence: The section lists the nine steps, Example 4.7 balances dichromate with iron(II) in acidic solution step by step and checks atoms and charge in a table, its Check Your Learning balances the disproportionation of chlorine in basic solution, and five exercises complete half-reactions or balance whole equations by the method.

concepts.name: Reaction stoichiometry
concepts.why: The stoichiometry of a reaction is the set of quantitative relationships between the amounts of the substances it consumes and produces, and the balanced equation states it. As a recipe for eight pancakes scales to twenty-four, the coefficients scale to any amount of any reactant or product.
concepts.evidence: The section defines stoichiometry, makes the pancake analogy, and states in its summary that coefficients are used for computations relating masses, molar amounts and other quantities.

concepts.name: Stoichiometric factors
concepts.why: A stoichiometric factor is a ratio of two coefficients from a balanced equation, such as 2 mol NH3 per 3 mol H2 in the synthesis of ammonia, and it may be written in any amount unit. It is the one step every reaction stoichiometry calculation shares, whatever quantities are given at its start and asked for at its end.
concepts.evidence: The section derives the factors relating ammonia to hydrogen in molecules, dozens and moles, every worked example of the section turns on one, and Figure 4.11 places the factor at the center of the flowchart of stoichiometry calculations.

concepts.name: Relating moles and numbers of molecules through an equation
concepts.why: Multiplying a given molar amount of one substance by the stoichiometric factor gives the molar amount of another, and Avogadro's number turns that molar amount into a number of molecules. This is the shortest stoichiometry calculation and the pattern the longer ones extend.
concepts.evidence: Example 4.8 finds the moles of iodine needed to react with 0.429 mol of aluminum and Example 4.9 the number of carbon dioxide molecules from 0.75 mol of propane, each with a Check Your Learning, and two exercises ask for numbers of molecules produced.

concepts.name: Relating masses and solution volumes through an equation
concepts.why: Since masses, not numbers of molecules, are what can be measured, a practical stoichiometry calculation converts a given mass (or a volume of a solution of known molarity) to moles, applies the stoichiometric factor, and converts the result back to a mass or a volume. The route is the same whether the two substances are a reactant and a product or two reactants.
concepts.evidence: Example 4.10 finds the mass of sodium hydroxide needed for 16 g of magnesium hydroxide and Example 4.11 the mass of oxygen consumed by 702 g of octane, each with a Check Your Learning, Figure 4.11 outlines the general route, and most of the section's exercises relate masses, moles and solution volumes.

concepts.name: Limiting and excess reactants
concepts.why: When reactants are not present in stoichiometric amounts, one is used up first and limits the amount of product; the others are in excess and some of each is left over. Eleven slices of cheese and twenty-eight slices of bread make eleven sandwiches with six slices of bread to spare, and three moles of hydrogen with two of chlorine make four moles of hydrogen chloride with one mole of hydrogen to spare.
concepts.evidence: The section introduces the idea with the sandwiches of Figure 4.13, defines limiting and excess reactant, and shows hydrogen in excess and chlorine limiting in Figure 4.14.

concepts.name: Identifying the limiting reactant
concepts.why: There are two ways. Compare the molar ratio of the reactants provided with the stoichiometric ratio of the equation, or compute the amount of product each reactant alone would give; the reactant that gives the lesser amount is the limiting one.
concepts.evidence: The section does both for hydrogen and chlorine, Example 4.12 does both for silicon and nitrogen forming silicon nitride, its Check Your Learning asks about hydrogen and oxygen forming water, and several exercises ask for the limiting reactant from masses, moles or numbers of molecules.

concepts.name: Theoretical and actual yield
concepts.why: The theoretical yield is the amount of product the stoichiometry of the balanced equation predicts from the limiting reactant; the actual yield is the amount obtained, and it is often less because of side reactions, incomplete reactions and losses in collecting the product.
concepts.evidence: The section defines both yields and gives the reasons the actual yield falls short, Example 4.13 computes a theoretical yield of copper before comparing it with the amount obtained, and an exercise asks which postulate of Dalton's atomic theory makes a theoretical yield calculable.

concepts.name: Percent yield
concepts.why: Percent yield is the actual yield divided by the theoretical yield, times 100%, and it measures how efficiently a reaction delivered the product the stoichiometry allows. Both yields may be masses, molar amounts or any other measure, so long as they are in the same units, which then cancel.
concepts.evidence: The section states the definition, which is its one key equation, Example 4.13 finds a 77.3% yield of copper and its Check Your Learning the yield of a Freon, and several exercises ask for percent yields from masses and volumes.

concepts.name: Atom economy
concepts.why: The atom economy of a process is the mass of the desired product as a percentage of the mass of all the reactants used, a measure of how much of what goes in ends up in the product. It looks like percent yield but compares the theoretical efficiencies of different processes, whereas percent yield compares what one process actually gives with what it could give.
concepts.evidence: The Green Chemistry and Atom Economy note defines atom economy and contrasts it with percent yield, and Figure 4.15 compares the six-step synthesis of ibuprofen at 40% with the three-step BHC process at about 80%.

concepts.name: Quantitative chemical analysis
concepts.why: Quantitative analysis is the determination of the amount or concentration of a substance in a sample, and reaction stoichiometry is one of its foundations: the amount of a reactant that combines with the analyte, or of a product it gives, measures how much analyte there was.
concepts.evidence: The section defines quantitative analysis through the eighteenth-century test of vinegar's strength with potassium carbonate, and its summary names titration and gravimetric analysis as two methods built on stoichiometry.

concepts.name: Titration analysis
concepts.why: In a titration, a titrant of known concentration is added from a buret to a sample of the analyte until the reaction between them is complete. The volume of titrant needed to reach this equivalence point, detected as an end point by a change such as an indicator's color, measures the amount of analyte through the reaction's stoichiometry.
concepts.evidence: The section defines titration analysis, buret, titrant, analyte, equivalence point, end point and indicator, and Figure 4.16 shows a buret being filled and read to the nearest 0.01 mL.

concepts.name: Calculating a concentration from titration data
concepts.why: The volume and molarity of the titrant give its molar amount, the stoichiometric factor gives the molar amount of analyte, and dividing by the sample volume gives the analyte's molarity. Since molarity is also millimoles per milliliter, the calculation can be done in milliliters throughout.
concepts.evidence: Example 4.14 finds the molarity of hydrochloric acid titrated with sodium hydroxide both ways, its Check Your Learning titrates oxalic acid with permanganate, and most of the section's exercises ask for a volume or a concentration from titration data.

concepts.name: Gravimetric analysis
concepts.why: In a gravimetric analysis the analyte is separated from the sample by a change of state, often by precipitation and filtration, and weighed; the mass of the isolated substance, carried through the stoichiometry, gives the mass of the analyte and its percent of the sample.
concepts.evidence: The section defines gravimetric analysis and shows a precipitate being filtered in Figure 4.17, Example 4.15 finds the percent of magnesium sulfate in a mixture from the mass of barium sulfate it precipitates, its Check Your Learning finds a percent of chloride, and an exercise computes the percent of gallium in gallium bromide.

concepts.name: Combustion analysis
concepts.why: A weighed sample of a compound of carbon and hydrogen is burned completely in oxygen, and the carbon dioxide and water it gives are collected in separate preweighed absorbers. The mass of each product gives the moles of carbon and of hydrogen in the sample, and their smallest whole-number ratio gives the empirical formula.
concepts.evidence: The section describes the method and draws the apparatus in Figure 4.18, Example 4.16 finds the empirical formula of polyethylene and its Check Your Learning that of polystyrene, and exercises find the formulas of a boron hydride and a tungsten chloride.

concepts.name: Energy as the capacity to supply heat or do work
concepts.why: Energy is defined in this book by what it can do, and work is one of the two things it does: matter is moved against an opposing force, as the air in a pump is pushed into a tire. Every later idea of the chapter, heat, internal energy and enthalpy, is a way of keeping account of this capacity.
concepts.evidence: The section opens its account of energy with this definition and the bicycle tire, and the summary repeats it as its first sentence.

concepts.name: Potential energy and kinetic energy
concepts.why: One scheme sorts energy into two kinds: potential energy, which an object has because of its position, composition, or condition, and kinetic energy, which it has because of its motion. The chemical energy stored in gasoline is potential energy, and thermal energy is kinetic, so the distinction is how the chapter says where the energy of a reaction comes from and where it goes.
concepts.evidence: The section defines both terms, Figure 5.3 shows water at the top of Victoria Falls and flowing through the Hoover Dam, and an exercise asks for a table of the energy transitions in an automobile.

concepts.name: The law of conservation of energy
concepts.why: During a chemical or physical change, energy can be neither created nor destroyed, although it can be changed in form. This is the rule that makes every calorimetry calculation possible, since the heat a reaction gives off must turn up somewhere else, and it is one version of the first law of thermodynamics that 5.3 states as an equation.
concepts.evidence: The section states the law and sets it beside the law of conservation of matter, and the summary names it as the first law of thermodynamics.

concepts.name: Thermal energy and temperature
concepts.why: Thermal energy is the kinetic energy of the random motion of atoms and molecules, and temperature is a measure of how hot or cold a sample is, which rises as the average kinetic energy of its particles rises. The two are not the same thing: a bonfire and a match may share a temperature and hold very different amounts of thermal energy.
concepts.evidence: The section defines both, Figure 5.4 sets the fast molecules of hot water beside the slow ones of cold water, Figure 5.5 shows how thermometers read the change, and the first exercise asks why a match does not warm us as a bonfire does.

concepts.name: Heat as the transfer of thermal energy
concepts.why: Heat is the transfer of thermal energy between two bodies at different temperatures. It flows spontaneously from the hotter body to the cooler one, lowering the average kinetic energy of the first and raising that of the second, until the two reach thermal equilibrium at one temperature. Calorimetry in 5.2 is built on exactly this exchange.
concepts.evidence: The section defines heat and follows substances H and L from contact to thermal equilibrium in Figure 5.6, and 5.2 repeats the argument for a hot metal dropped into cool water.

concepts.name: Exothermic and endothermic processes
concepts.why: A change that releases heat is exothermic and a change that absorbs heat is endothermic. The sign of every heat and every enthalpy change in the rest of the chapter is read against these two words, so the reader must be able to tell which is which from what happens to the temperature of the surroundings.
concepts.evidence: The section defines both terms with the oxyacetylene torch and the cold pack of Figure 5.7, and calorimetry exercises in 5.2 ask whether each dissolution is exothermic or endothermic.

concepts.name: Converting between joules, calories, and Calories
concepts.why: The SI unit of energy is the joule, but the calorie is still frequently used, and food energy is quoted in Calories, each of which is a kilocalorie. Since 1 calorie is defined as exactly 4.184 joules, the reader must move between these units with ease to read a food label or to compare a result given in either.
concepts.evidence: The section defines the calorie, the Calorie, and the joule and states the conversion, and exercises in 5.1 ask for heat capacities and heats in both joules and calories.

concepts.name: Heat capacity and specific heat
concepts.why: The heat capacity of a body is the heat it absorbs or releases for a temperature change of 1 °C, and it grows with the amount of material, so it is extensive. The specific heat is the heat needed to raise 1 gram of a substance by 1 °C, and it depends only on the kind of substance, so it is intensive. The two frying pans of the text differ fivefold in heat capacity and share one specific heat.
concepts.evidence: The section defines both with their equations, works through the small and large cast iron pans of Figure 5.8, lists specific heats in Table 5.1, and an exercise asks the reader to explain the difference between the two.

concepts.name: Heat, specific heat, mass, and temperature change, $q = c \times m \times \Delta T$
concepts.why: The heat entering or leaving a substance is the product of its specific heat, its mass, and its temperature change, taken as the final temperature minus the initial one. The sign of q follows from that difference, positive when the substance warms and negative when it cools, and any one of the four quantities can be found when the other three are known.
concepts.evidence: The section derives the relation and uses it in Example 5.1 to find the heat absorbed by water and in Example 5.2 to identify an unknown metal from its specific heat; most of the section's exercises apply it.

concepts.name: The system and its surroundings
concepts.why: Measuring a heat requires dividing the world in two: the system, the substances undergoing the change, and the surroundings, everything else that gives heat to the system or takes it away. The sign of every q in the chapter is stated from the point of view of the system, so the reader must be able to name which is which in each experiment.
concepts.evidence: The section defines both terms at its start, Figure 5.11 labels the reaction as system and the solution as surroundings, and Figure 5.14 labels the hot metal and the cool water the same way.

concepts.name: The heats exchanged in a calorimeter sum to zero
concepts.why: When a hot metal is placed in cool water in an ideal calorimeter, all the heat lost by one is gained by the other, so the two heats add up to zero and one is the negative of the other. The negative sign records the opposite direction of flow and does not by itself give either value its sign.
concepts.evidence: The section states the balance and its rearrangement, and Examples 5.3 and 5.4 use it to find the initial temperature of a piece of rebar and the specific heat of an unknown metal.

concepts.name: The heat of a reaction from the heat of the solution, $q_{\text{reaction}} = -q_{\text{solution}}$
concepts.why: Because energy is neither created nor destroyed, the heat produced or consumed by a reaction in a calorimeter equals the heat absorbed or lost by the solution around it, with the opposite sign. This is the concept that lies at the heart of all calorimetry problems: the temperature change of the solution is measured, and the heat of the reaction is read from it.
concepts.evidence: The section states it after the metal-and-water examples and applies it in Example 5.5, the neutralization of HCl by NaOH, and Example 5.6, the instant ice pack.

concepts.name: Calculating a heat from coffee cup calorimetry data
concepts.why: With a coffee cup calorimeter the reader measures a temperature change and must make and state reasonable assumptions to turn it into a heat: that no heat is exchanged with the outside or absorbed by the cup, and that a dilute solution has the specific heat and density of water. The skill is carrying those assumptions through to a heat with the right sign.
concepts.evidence: Examples 5.3 to 5.6 and their Check Your Learning items ask for the heat, a temperature, or a specific heat and for the assumptions made, and most of the section's exercises set the same task.

concepts.name: Calculating a heat of combustion from bomb calorimetry
concepts.why: A bomb calorimeter works at constant volume and is used for reactions, such as combustions, that give off much heat and gaseous products. The heat of the reaction is shared between the water and the steel bomb, so the calculation adds the heat taken in by the water to the heat capacity of the bomb times the temperature rise.
concepts.evidence: The section describes the bomb calorimeter and its calibration with Figure 5.17, Example 5.7 finds the heat produced by burning glucose, and exercises burn fructose, TNT, and coal.

concepts.name: Counting the Calories in a food
concepts.why: Food labels give energy in Calories, computed by the Atwater system from the grams of protein, carbohydrate, and fat in a serving and their average Calories per gram, values that were themselves found by bomb calorimetry. The reader who can do this sum can check a label and compare foods.
concepts.evidence: The Measuring Nutritional Calories note works the label of Figure 5.18 to 252 Calories, and exercises ask for the Calories in cereal and the mass of fat or carbohydrate for a given Calorie count.

concepts.name: The first law of thermodynamics, $\Delta U = q + w$
concepts.why: The internal energy of a system changes only through heat flowing into or out of it and work done on or by it. The signs are fixed from the system's side: q is positive for heat flowing in and w is positive for work done on the system, so a system that loses heat and does work loses internal energy on both counts, as the gases in an engine cylinder do.
concepts.evidence: The section defines internal energy, states the equation, and draws the four arrows into and out of the system in Figure 5.19; the equation is one of the section's key equations.

concepts.name: State functions
concepts.why: The value of a state function depends only on the state a system is in, and not on how that state was reached. Internal energy and enthalpy are state functions, while heat and work are not, just as the altitude of a summit does not depend on the route climbed but the distance walked does. Hess's law rests on this property.
concepts.evidence: The section defines the term with the two paths up Mt. Kilimanjaro in Figure 5.20 and later says Hess's law is valid because enthalpy is a state function.

concepts.name: Enthalpy, and $\Delta H = q_{\text{p}}$ at constant pressure
concepts.why: Enthalpy is the sum of a system's internal energy and the product of its pressure and volume. For a process at constant pressure whose only work is expansion work, the enthalpy change equals the heat flow, which is why chemists, who usually work at the constant pressure of the atmosphere, use enthalpy to describe the heat of a reaction. The heat measured in a bomb calorimeter, at constant volume, is not ΔH.
concepts.evidence: The section defines enthalpy, derives ΔH = q<sub>p</sub> from the first law and the expansion work PΔV = −w, and contrasts the Bunsen burner with the bomb calorimeter.

concepts.name: Writing and scaling thermochemical equations
concepts.why: A thermochemical equation gives ΔH after a balanced equation, for the amounts in moles that the equation shows. Since ΔH is extensive, it scales with the coefficients, it changes sign when the equation is reversed, and it depends on the physical states written, so the reader must carry all three rules and account for the limiting reactant when turning a measured heat into ΔH.
concepts.evidence: The section states the conventions with the formation of liquid and gaseous water, Examples 5.8 and 5.9 write thermochemical equations from measured heats, and several exercises ask for ΔH per mole of a reactant.

concepts.name: Using a standard enthalpy of combustion
concepts.why: The standard enthalpy of combustion is the enthalpy change when 1 mole of a substance burns completely under standard state conditions. With it, and with the conversions of earlier chapters, the reader can find the heat given by any amount of a fuel, as the heat of 1.00 L of gasoline is found from the value for isooctane.
concepts.evidence: The section defines the quantity, lists values in Table 5.2, works Example 5.10 on gasoline, and sets exercises on acetylene, methanol, isooctane, and carbon monoxide.

concepts.name: Standard states and the standard enthalpy of formation
concepts.why: A standard state is an agreed set of reference conditions, 1 bar and 1 M, with 298.15 K assumed, and ΔH° marks an enthalpy change under them. The standard enthalpy of formation is ΔH° for forming exactly 1 mole of a substance from its elements in their most stable states, so an element in its most stable form has a value of zero and the formation equation often carries fractional coefficients.
concepts.evidence: The section defines the standard state and the enthalpy of formation, Example 5.11 finds it for ozone and Example 5.12 writes formation equations, and an exercise asks which enthalpies of combustion in Table 5.2 are also enthalpies of formation.

concepts.name: Hess’s law
concepts.why: If a process can be written as the sum of several stepwise processes, the enthalpy change of the total process equals the sum of the enthalpy changes of the steps. This lets the reader find the enthalpy change of a reaction that is hard or dangerous to carry out by adding reactions, reversed and scaled as needed, whose values are known.
concepts.evidence: The section states the law, shows carbon burning to CO<sub>2</sub> in one step or two in Figure 5.24, works Examples 5.13 and 5.14, and sets many exercises that combine given reactions.

concepts.name: Calculating a reaction enthalpy from enthalpies of formation
concepts.why: Hess's law applied to decomposing the reactants into their elements and re-forming the products gives the standard enthalpy change of any reaction as the sum of n times the enthalpies of formation of the products minus the same sum for the reactants. With the table of Appendix G the reader can compute ΔH° for reactions that no one has measured directly.
concepts.evidence: The section derives the equation, Example 5.15 uses it both directly and by summing four formation steps, and a large share of the section's exercises ask for ΔH° from the data in Appendix G.

concepts.name: Calculating the formula mass of a compound
concepts.why: The formula mass of a substance is the sum of the average atomic masses of all the atoms its formula represents. It is the first place where a chemical formula becomes a number, and every later calculation of the chapter, from molar mass to percent composition, begins by adding up the masses a formula names.
concepts.evidence: The section works chloroform, aspirin and sodium chloride in Figures 3.2 to 3.4, Examples 3.1 and 3.2 compute the masses of ibuprofen and aluminum sulfate, and several exercises ask for the molecular or formula mass of a list of compounds.

concepts.name: Molecular mass and the formula mass of an ionic compound
concepts.why: For a covalent substance the formula describes one molecule, so its formula mass may be called a molecular mass; an ionic compound has no discrete molecule, so its formula mass may not. The masses of neutral atoms are used for ions as well, since the mass of an electron is negligible beside that of an atom.
concepts.evidence: The section treats covalent substances and ionic compounds under separate headers, explains why the masses of neutral sodium and chlorine atoms serve for NaCl, and Example 3.2 rewrites Al<sub>2</sub>(SO<sub>4</sub>)<sub>3</sub> as Al<sub>2</sub>S<sub>3</sub>O<sub>12</sub> to count its atoms.

concepts.name: The mole
concepts.why: The mole is an amount unit like a pair or a dozen, and it links an easily measured property, bulk mass, to a fundamental one, the number of atoms or molecules. Chemists count particles they cannot see by weighing them, and the mole is the unit that makes that possible.
concepts.evidence: The section defines the mole as the amount containing 6.02214076 × 10<sup>23</sup> entities, Figures 3.5 and 3.6 set out one mole each of several elements and compounds, and an exercise compares 1 mole of H<sub>2</sub>, O<sub>2</sub> and F<sub>2</sub>.

concepts.name: Avogadro’s number, $N_A = 6.022 \times 10^{23}$/mol
concepts.why: One mole of any substance contains the same number of entities, 6.022 × 10<sup>23</sup>, so the number of atoms or molecules in a sample follows from its amount in moles. The size of the number is what lets a drop of water hold more molecules than can be clearly imagined.
concepts.evidence: The section names the constant and gives its unit of per mole, Figure 3.7 compares the molecules in a droplet with the number of people on earth, and Examples 3.5 and 3.8 multiply an amount by Avogadro’s number to count atoms and molecules.

concepts.name: Molar mass
concepts.why: The molar mass of a substance is the mass in grams of 1 mole of it, and it is numerically equal to the formula mass in amu, because the atomic mass unit and the mole are defined from the same reference, carbon-12. That equality turns a formula mass read from the periodic table into a conversion factor between grams and moles.
concepts.evidence: The section defines molar mass, explains its equality with the formula mass through <sup>12</sup>C, tabulates both for five elements, and exercises ask how molecular mass and molar mass are alike and how they differ and ask for the molar masses of many compounds.

concepts.name: Converting between mass and moles
concepts.why: Dividing a mass by the molar mass gives the amount in moles, and multiplying an amount by the molar mass gives the mass. This is the conversion the rest of the book leans on whenever a quantity weighed on a balance must become a count of particles or the reverse.
concepts.evidence: Examples 3.3, 3.4, 3.6 and 3.7 convert grams of potassium, argon, glycine and vitamin C to moles and back, each with a ballpark estimate first, and many exercises ask for the moles in a given mass or the mass of a given amount.

concepts.name: Counting atoms and molecules from a mass
concepts.why: A mass is converted to moles with the molar mass and then to a number of entities with Avogadro’s number, and the formula then gives the number of each kind of atom. The two-step chain answers questions no balance can answer directly, such as how many carbon atoms a packet of sweetener holds.
concepts.evidence: Examples 3.5 and 3.8 count the copper atoms in 5.00 g of wire and the saccharin molecules and carbon atoms in 40.0 mg of sweetener, and exercises count the atoms in a diamond and the atoms of each element in a sample of zircon.

concepts.name: Percent composition
concepts.why: The percent composition of a compound is the percentage by mass of each element in it. Measuring the mass of each element is often the first step in finding an unknown compound’s formula, and the percentages are how that measurement is reported.
concepts.evidence: The section defines percent composition from the masses of hydrogen and carbon in a 10.0-g sample of gas, Example 3.9 computes it for a compound of carbon, hydrogen and nitrogen, and its Check Your Learning does the same for a compound of carbon, oxygen and chlorine.

concepts.name: Percent composition from a formula
concepts.why: When the formula is known, the percent composition follows from the atomic or molar masses alone, by taking one mole of the compound as the sample. This is how a fertilizer buyer compares the nitrogen in ammonia, ammonium nitrate and urea.
concepts.evidence: The section computes the percent composition of ammonia from its formula mass, Example 3.10 does the same for aspirin with molar masses, and exercises ask for the percent composition of ammonia, hypo, hydrazoic acid and TNT and the percent of water in a hydrate.

concepts.name: Deriving an empirical formula from the masses of the elements
concepts.why: A formula states the relative numbers of atoms, not their masses, so each element’s mass is converted to moles, the amounts are divided by the smallest, and the result is multiplied by an integer if needed to reach whole numbers. The procedure turns an analysis on a balance into a chemical formula.
concepts.evidence: The section derives CH<sub>2</sub> and Cl<sub>2</sub>O<sub>7</sub> from measured masses, Figure 3.11 sets the procedure out as a flowchart, and Example 3.11 finds the formula of hematite, Fe<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub>, from 34.97 g of iron and 15.03 g of oxygen.

concepts.name: Deriving an empirical formula from percent composition
concepts.why: When only the percentages are known, a 100-g sample is assumed, so that each element’s mass in grams is numerically its mass percentage, and the usual procedure follows.
concepts.evidence: Example 3.12 finds that the gas from fermentation, 27.29% C and 72.71% O, is CO<sub>2</sub>, and exercises ask for the empirical formulas of compounds and of five polymers from their percent compositions.

concepts.name: Deriving a molecular formula from an empirical formula
concepts.why: An empirical formula gives only the relative numbers of atoms. Dividing the molecular or molar mass by the empirical formula mass gives the number of formula units in each molecule, and multiplying every subscript by that number gives the molecular formula.
concepts.evidence: The section shows that CH<sub>2</sub>O with a molecular mass of 180 amu is C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>12</sub>O<sub>6</sub>, Example 3.13 finds nicotine to be C<sub>10</sub>H<sub>14</sub>N<sub>2</sub>, and exercises ask what information is needed and find the formulas of benzene, dichloroethane, chrysotile and a yellow dye.

concepts.name: Solvent, solute, and aqueous solutions
concepts.why: A solution is a homogeneous mixture, and it usually has one component, the solvent, present at a much greater concentration than the others, the solutes, which are dissolved in it. A solution in water is an aqueous solution, the kind this book meets most often.
concepts.evidence: The section recalls that solutions are homogeneous mixtures and defines concentration, solvent, dissolved, aqueous solution and solute in turn, and the summary repeats the definitions.

concepts.name: Concentration
concepts.why: The relative amount of a given component of a solution is its concentration, and the properties of a mixture depend on it, as the sweetness of a coffee depends on its sugar. A solution is called dilute or concentrated in words before any unit puts a number on it.
concepts.evidence: The section opens on the composition of atmospheres, steels, medicines and drinks, Figure 3.14 shows the sugar in a coffee, the terms dilute and concentrated are defined, and exercises ask in what ways two samples of the same solution are identical and how they differ.

concepts.name: Molarity, $M$ = mol solute / L solution
concepts.why: Molarity is the number of moles of solute in exactly 1 liter of solution, and it is the concentration unit of most of chemistry. The liter is of the whole solution, not of the solvent that was added.
concepts.evidence: The section defines molarity with its equation, Example 3.14 finds the molarity of sucrose in a soft drink, and an exercise asks what information is needed to calculate the molarity of a sulfuric acid solution.

concepts.name: Calculating with molarity
concepts.why: The definition of molarity links three quantities, so any one of the amount of solute, the volume of solution and the molarity follows from the other two, and a molar mass brings in the mass of solute as well. Keeping a guard digit, or working the calculation in one step, keeps the rounding error out of the answer.
concepts.evidence: Examples 3.15 to 3.18 find the sugar in a sip, the molarity of vinegar from its mass of acetic acid, the mass of NaCl in a volume of solution and the volume of vinegar that holds a mass of acid, the section explains the guard digit with Example 3.17, and many exercises ask for molarities, amounts and masses of solute.

concepts.name: Dilution
concepts.why: Dilution lowers the concentration of a solution by adding solvent, and it leaves the amount of solute unchanged. It is how melting ice weakens iced tea and how a laboratory prepares a working solution from a concentrated stock.
concepts.evidence: The section defines dilution, Figure 3.16 shows two solutions with the same mass of copper nitrate in different amounts of solvent, and an exercise asks what changes and what stays the same when a solution of NaCl is diluted from 1.00 L to 1.80 L.

concepts.name: The dilution equation, $C_1V_1 = C_2V_2$
concepts.why: Since n = ML and the amount of solute does not change on dilution, the product of concentration and volume is the same before and after. The relation works in any units of concentration and volume that cancel, so it is written C<sub>1</sub>V<sub>1</sub> = C<sub>2</sub>V<sub>2</sub>.
concepts.evidence: The section derives the equation from n<sub>1</sub> = n<sub>2</sub>, Examples 3.19 to 3.21 solve it for the diluted concentration, the diluted volume and the stock volume, and exercises dilute and evaporate solutions of iron nitrate, propanol, phosphoric acid, sucrose and NaCl.

concepts.name: Mass percentage
concepts.why: The mass percentage of a component is the ratio of its mass to the mass of the solution, expressed as a percentage. It is the unit on the labels of consumer products, and it needs only that both masses be in the same unit.
concepts.evidence: The section defines mass percentage and its other names, Figure 3.17 shows a bleach bottle labelled 7.4% NaOCl, and Example 3.22 finds the percent by mass of glucose in spinal fluid.

concepts.name: Volume percentage
concepts.why: A liquid dissolved in a liquid is conveniently described by the ratio of the volume of solute to the volume of solution, expressed as a percentage, since liquid volumes are easily measured.
concepts.evidence: The section defines volume percentage, and Example 3.24 finds the mass of isopropyl alcohol in a bottle of 70%vol rubbing alcohol, with a Check Your Learning on the ethanol in a bottle of wine.

concepts.name: Mass-volume percent
concepts.why: A mixed unit takes the mass of solute and the volume of solution, as physiological saline is 0.9 g of solute per 100 mL and blood sugar is reported in milligrams per deciliter. Such units are common in biochemical and medical settings.
concepts.evidence: The section defines mass-volume percent with saline and blood glucose as its examples, Figure 3.18 shows both, and an exercise converts a blood glucose reading between millimoles per liter and milligrams per deciliter.

concepts.name: Parts per million and parts per billion
concepts.why: Very low concentrations are expressed as parts per million or parts per billion, the mass ratio multiplied by 10<sup>6</sup> or 10<sup>9</sup>, just as a percentage is a part per hundred. They are the units of trace contaminants in water.
concepts.evidence: The section gives the mass-based definitions, Figure 3.19 shows tap water and an inline filter, Example 3.25 converts the EPA’s 15 ppb lead limit to ppm and to micrograms in a glass of water, and exercises ask about water hardness and mercury in a stream.

concepts.name: Converting between concentration units with a density
concepts.why: A solution’s density converts its volume to its mass, and a molar mass converts a mass of solute to moles, so a concentration given in one unit can be expressed in another, from a mass percentage to a mass of solute or to a molarity.
concepts.evidence: Example 3.23 uses the density of concentrated hydrochloric acid to find the mass of HCl in 0.500 L of it, and exercises find the molarities of a throat spray, a cough syrup, D5W and sulfuric acid from their mass percentages and densities.

concepts.name: Bond angles and bond distances
concepts.why: A Lewis structure is drawn flat, but a molecule is not: it occupies space, and describing it means giving the distances between the nuclei and the angles between the bonds. A bond angle is the angle between two bonds that share an atom, measured in degrees, and a bond distance is the distance between the nuclei of two bonded atoms, measured in Ångstroms or picometers. These two measurements are what every later statement about a molecule's shape is finally about.
concepts.evidence: The section opens by defining both terms and Figure 7.14 gives the formaldehyde molecule its measured angle of 118° and its measured C=O distance of 1.21 Å; the bond angles named for every geometry that follows, 180°, 120°, 109.5°, 90°, are the same measurement made on the shapes VSEPR theory predicts.

concepts.name: Valence shell electron-pair repulsion theory
concepts.why: VSEPR theory predicts the shape of a molecule from one assumption: the regions of high electron density in the valence shell of the central atom, whether they are bonding pairs or lone pairs, repel one another, and they settle into the arrangement that puts them as far apart as possible. It is worth noting that the theory considers electron-pair repulsions alone, and that nuclear-nuclear repulsions and nuclear-electron attractions are also at work in the arrangement a molecule finally adopts.
concepts.evidence: The section states the assumption and works it through on BeF2, where two bonds and no lone pairs give a bond angle of 180° (Figure 7.15), and the four-step procedure that follows begins with a Lewis structure and ends with a predicted shape.

concepts.name: The five electron-pair geometries
concepts.why: The number of regions of electron density around a central atom decides the arrangement, and there are only five of them: two regions are linear, three are trigonal planar, four are tetrahedral, five are trigonal bipyramidal and six are octahedral. A single, a double and a triple bond each count as one region, so the count is a count of directions rather than of electrons, and the whole of the shape prediction rests on getting it right.
concepts.evidence: Figure 7.16 draws the five arrangements with their angles, the section names each one as it is defined in the glossary, and the worked examples count the regions of CO2, BCl3, the ammonium ion, water, SF4 and XeF4 before naming any shape.

concepts.name: Molecular structure is not electron-pair geometry
concepts.why: The electron-pair geometry describes where all the regions of electron density are, bonds and lone pairs together; the molecular structure describes where the atoms are and says nothing about the lone pairs. The two are the same when the central atom carries no lone pair and they differ whenever it carries one, which is why methane is tetrahedral while ammonia, with the same four regions, is trigonal pyramidal and water is bent.
concepts.evidence: The section defines both terms and contrasts methane (Figure 7.17) with ammonia (Figure 7.18), Figure 7.19 sets out the molecular structures that follow from each electron-pair geometry as lone pairs are added, and Examples 7.13, 7.14 and 7.15 name a different electron-pair geometry and molecular structure for water, SF4 and XeF4.

concepts.name: The order of repulsions and the space a region occupies
concepts.why: The ideal angles are only approximate, because the regions of electron density are not all the same size. A lone pair repels more strongly than a bonding pair, and it occupies more space than a triple bond, which occupies more than a double bond, which occupies more than a single bond. That order is what explains the small distortions from the ideal angles, and it is what decides which arrangement is chosen when more than one is possible.
concepts.evidence: The section states both orders as displayed relations, explains the H–N–H angle of ammonia as slightly smaller than 109.5° because the lone pair-bonding pair repulsion is the greater one (Figure 7.18), and reads the 121° and 118° angles of formaldehyde off the larger space the double bond takes.

concepts.name: Axial and equatorial positions in a trigonal bipyramid
concepts.why: In the linear, trigonal planar and tetrahedral arrangements every terminal position is equivalent, so it does not matter which one a lone pair takes. A trigonal bipyramid has two kinds of position: an axial position surrounded by 90° angles and an equatorial position with more room because of its 120° angles. A lone pair always takes an equatorial position, and in an octahedron with two lone pairs the two sit 180° apart, which is what makes ClF3 T-shaped and XeF4 square planar.
concepts.evidence: Figure 7.20 draws the trigonal bipyramid's two kinds of position and the three arrangements possible for ClF3, of which only the T-shaped one is observed; Example 7.14 places the lone pair of SF4 in an equatorial position to give a seesaw, and Example 7.15 puts the two lone pairs of XeF4 on opposite sides of the octahedron.

concepts.name: Predicting electron-pair geometry and molecular structure
concepts.why: The prediction is a four-step procedure and it is the skill the section is written to teach: write the Lewis structure, count the regions of electron density around the central atom, read off the electron-pair geometry, and use the number of lone pairs to name the molecular structure, choosing the arrangement that minimizes repulsion where more than one is possible. A molecule with no single central atom is handled one interior atom at a time, each with a local geometry of its own.
concepts.evidence: The section sets out the four steps and then applies them in Examples 7.11 to 7.16, to CO2, BCl3, the ammonium ion, water, SF4, XeF4 and the amino acid glycine, and the end-of-chapter exercises ask for the electron-pair geometry and the molecular structure of some forty molecules and ions.

concepts.name: The bond dipole moment
concepts.why: A polar covalent bond leaves one atom with a partial positive charge and the other with a partial negative charge, and the separation of charge is measured by the bond dipole moment, the product of the magnitude of the partial charges and the distance between them. It is drawn as a vector pointing from the less electronegative atom toward the more electronegative one, with a small plus sign at the positive end and a length proportional to the electronegativity difference.
concepts.evidence: The section gives the formula and defines the vector that represents it, and Figure 7.26 draws the short vector of a C–H bond beside the much longer vector of a B–F bond.

concepts.name: Assessing the polarity of a molecule
concepts.why: A molecule is polar only if it contains at least one polar bond and its bond moments, added as vectors in three dimensions, do not cancel. Geometry is therefore as much of the answer as electronegativity: carbon dioxide has two polar bonds pointing in opposite directions and is nonpolar, while water has the same two bonds bent toward one another and is polar. Molecules of high symmetry such as BF3, CH4, PF5 and SF6 are nonpolar for the same reason, and polar molecules are the ones that align in an electric field and dissolve readily in polar solvents.
concepts.evidence: The section states the two conditions for polarity, contrasts CO2 with water in Figure 7.27, works through OCS, chloromethane, H2S and ammonia in turn, and Figure 7.28 shows HF molecules lying at random until a field is applied and then lining up with it; nine end-of-chapter exercises ask which molecules of a list have dipole moments.

concepts.name: Writing a Lewis structure
concepts.why: A Lewis structure shows every valence electron of a molecule or polyatomic ion, as a shared pair on a bond or as a lone pair on an atom. It is where a prediction of shape begins, because the count of bonding regions and lone pairs that VSEPR theory needs is read straight off it.
concepts.evidence: The section sets out the five steps and works them on SiH4, CHO2−, NO+ and OF2, and Examples 7.4 and 7.5 write the structures of HCN, ethane, acetylene, ammonia, XeF2 and XeF6; nine exercises ask for Lewis structures. A Sim walks the five steps for six molecules and ions.

concepts.name: Polar covalent bonds and electronegativity
concepts.why: When two bonded atoms differ in electronegativity the shared electrons are pulled toward the more electronegative one, leaving it with a partial negative charge and its partner with a partial positive charge. The size of that difference is what sets the size of a bond's dipole moment, and a molecule with no polar bond at all can have no dipole moment.
concepts.evidence: The section contrasts the pure covalent bonds of H2 and Cl2 with the polar H–Cl bond of Figure 7.5, with its partial charges marked δ+ and δ−, and Example 7.3 designates the positive and negative atoms of six bonds; exercises ask which atoms give sulfur a positive partial charge and which molecules contain polar bonds.

concepts.name: Ionic bonds and the properties of ionic compounds
concepts.why: An ionic bond is the electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged cations and anions, typically formed when a metal atom transfers electrons to a nonmetal atom. The bond is strong, which is why ionic solids are rigid and brittle with high melting points, and the ions are held in place, which is why the solid conducts poorly while the melt or the solution conducts well.
concepts.evidence: The section defines the ionic bond, reads its strength off the properties of ionic solids, and contrasts sodium metal and chlorine gas with the salt they form in Figure 7.2; an exercise asks which atoms of a list form cations and which form anions.

concepts.name: An ionic formula describes a lattice, not a molecule
concepts.why: Because every compound is electrically neutral, the formula of an ionic compound gives the simplest ratio of ions whose charges cancel, as Al2O3 does with two Al3+ ions for every three O2− ions. The formula does not describe a molecule: the attraction between ions is the same in all directions, so each ion is drawn to all its neighbors of opposite charge and the ions build a three-dimensional lattice.
concepts.evidence: The section works the charge balance of aluminum oxide, explains why it is incorrect to speak of a sodium chloride molecule, and Figure 7.3 draws the sodium chloride lattice with each ion surrounded by six of the other kind; an exercise asks why a molecule of solid NaCl cannot be spoken of.

concepts.name: Predicting the charge of a monatomic ion
concepts.why: A main group metal atom tends to lose all its valence electrons and a nonmetal atom tends to gain enough to fill its valence s and p orbitals, so in each case the ion takes the electron configuration of a noble gas and its charge can be read from the group. The heavy elements of groups 13 to 15 may also keep their valence s pair, the inert pair effect, which is why Tl+, Sn2+, Pb2+ and Bi3+ exist beside the expected ions.
concepts.evidence: The section derives the charges of the group 1, group 2 and group 13 to 17 ions, names the exceptions of the inert pair effect and the mercury(I) ion, and three exercises ask for the charges of the monatomic ions formed from lists of atoms.

concepts.name: Writing the electron configuration of an ion
concepts.why: The configuration of a cation is written by removing electrons from the neutral atom, and the configuration of an anion by adding them. For a transition metal the outermost s electrons are lost first, before any d electron, even though the d orbitals were the last to fill; so iron becomes Fe2+ by losing its 4s pair and Fe3+ by losing one 3d electron as well.
concepts.evidence: The section works the configurations of Ca2+, Fe2+ and Fe3+, and Examples 7.1 and 7.2 write the configurations of Cr3+, Zn2+, Se2− and I−; four exercises ask for the configurations of ions.

concepts.name: How a covalent bond forms, and the bond length
concepts.why: A covalent bond is formed when two atoms share a pair of electrons that is attracted by both nuclei. As two hydrogen atoms approach, the potential energy falls while each electron is drawn to both nuclei and then rises steeply as the nuclei repel, and the bond length is the distance at which the energy is lowest. Breaking a bond always takes energy and forming one always releases it.
concepts.evidence: The section explains the formation of H2 against the potential energy curve of Figure 7.4, which marks the bond length of 74 pm, and states that 436 kJ must be added to break the bonds in a mole of hydrogen molecules and is released when they form.

concepts.name: Electronegativity and its periodic trend
concepts.why: Electronegativity is the tendency of an atom to attract the electrons of a bond toward itself. On Pauling's scale it increases from left to right across a period and decreases down a group, so the nonmetals of the upper right are the most electronegative, fluorine above all at 4.0, and the group 1 metals are the least. It is a calculated, dimensionless number and should not be confused with electron affinity, which is a measured energy of an isolated atom.
concepts.evidence: The section defines electronegativity, Figure 7.6 sets out Pauling's values across the periodic table, and a subsection separates it from electron affinity; four exercises ask which atom of a pair is more electronegative or ask for a series in order of increasing electronegativity.

concepts.name: Judging bond type from the electronegativity difference
concepts.why: The absolute difference in electronegativity between two bonded atoms is a rough measure of the bond's character: a small difference gives a pure covalent bond, an intermediate one a polar covalent bond, and a large one an ionic bond. It is only a guide, and the better one is the kind of atoms involved, since bonds between two nonmetals are generally covalent and bonds between a metal and a nonmetal are often ionic.
concepts.evidence: The section gives the differences for H–H, H–Cl and Na–Cl, Figure 7.8 relates the difference to the bond type, and Example 7.3 orders six bonds of the amino acids by polarity in Table 7.1; exercises ask which compounds are ionic and which bond of each pair is the more polar.

concepts.name: Writing Lewis symbols for atoms and ions
concepts.why: A Lewis symbol is the symbol of an element surrounded by one dot for each of its valence electrons. The same notation shows a cation forming as dots are lost and an anion forming as dots are gained, and so it shows the transfer of electrons when an ionic compound forms without the total number of electrons changing.
concepts.evidence: The section defines the Lewis symbol, Figure 7.9 gives the symbols of the third-period elements, and Figure 7.10 draws the formation of sodium chloride, magnesium oxide and calcium fluoride; three exercises ask for the Lewis symbols of ions.

concepts.name: The octet rule
concepts.why: Main group atoms tend to form enough bonds to have eight valence electrons around them, counting the shared electrons of each bond as belonging to both atoms. The number of bonds an atom forms can often be predicted from the number of electrons it needs to reach eight, so carbon forms four bonds, nitrogen three, oxygen two and fluorine one; hydrogen, which needs only two, is the exception.
concepts.evidence: The section states the rule for the halogens and applies it to CCl4, SiH4, NH3, H2O and HF.

concepts.name: Single, double, and triple bonds
concepts.why: A single bond shares one pair of electrons between two atoms, a double bond shares two pairs and a triple bond shares three. Atoms share more than one pair when that is what it takes to give each of them an octet, as in formaldehyde and ethylene with their double bonds and carbon monoxide and the cyanide ion with their triple bonds.
concepts.evidence: The section defines all three bonds with the Lewis structures of Cl2, CH2O, C2H4, CO and CN−, and an exercise asks how single, double and triple bonds are similar and how they differ.

concepts.name: Exceptions to the octet rule
concepts.why: Three kinds of molecule cannot give every atom eight electrons. An odd-electron molecule, or free radical, such as NO, must leave one electron unpaired; an electron-deficient molecule such as BF3 has a central atom with fewer than eight; and a hypervalent molecule such as PCl5 or SF6 has a central atom of the third period or beyond that holds more than eight.
concepts.evidence: The section works each case in turn, NO, BeH2 and BF3, then PCl5 and SF6 in Figure 7.12 and IF5 and XeF4, and Example 7.5 writes the structures of XeF2 and XeF6; exercises ask for the Lewis structures of ClF3, PCl5, BF3, SeF6 and XeF4.

concepts.name: Calculating formal charge
concepts.why: The formal charge of an atom in a Lewis structure is the charge it would have if the electrons of each bond were shared equally: the valence electrons of the free atom, less its lone pair electrons, less half its bonding electrons. The formal charges of a molecule add up to zero and those of an ion add up to its charge, which checks the arithmetic. A formal charge is bookkeeping and not the actual charge on the atom.
concepts.evidence: The section gives the formula and Examples 7.6 and 7.7 assign the formal charges of ICl4− and BrCl3; four exercises ask for the formal charges of the atoms in lists of molecules and ions. A Sim marks the lone pair and bonding electrons of each atom in the eight candidate structures the section compares.

concepts.name: Choosing the most likely Lewis structure by formal charge
concepts.why: When more than one Lewis structure can be written, the preferred one has formal charges of zero, or else the smallest nonzero formal charges, with adjacent formal charges zero or of opposite sign, and with any negative formal charge on the more electronegative atom. These guidelines explain why the least electronegative atom usually takes the central position.
concepts.evidence: The section states the four guidelines and applies them to three structures of CO2 and three arrangements of the thiocyanate ion, and Example 7.8 chooses the structure of nitrous oxide; exercises ask for the likely arrangement of the atoms in nitrosyl chloride, hypochlorous acid and sulfur dioxide.

concepts.name: Resonance forms and the resonance hybrid
concepts.why: When two or more Lewis structures with the same arrangement of atoms can be written, none of them alone describes the molecule; the actual distribution of electrons is their average, the resonance hybrid. The molecule never switches between its resonance forms, which is why both N–O bonds of the nitrite ion and all three C–O bonds of the carbonate ion are found to be identical.
concepts.evidence: The section introduces resonance on the nitrite ion, tells Wheland's analogy of the rhinoceros described as a dragon and a unicorn, and draws the three resonance forms of the carbonate ion; six exercises ask for resonance forms. A Sim draws the resonance hybrids of the nitrite and carbonate ions beneath their forms.

concepts.name: Bond energy
concepts.why: The strength of a covalent bond is measured by its bond energy, the energy needed to break one mole of that bond in gaseous molecules, which for a diatomic molecule is the standard enthalpy change of its dissociation. In a molecule with several bonds of one kind the tabulated value is an average, since the first bond broken does not need the same energy as the rest.
concepts.evidence: The section defines the bond energy by the dissociation of XY and of H2, derives the average C–H bond energy of 415 kJ/mol from the 1660 kJ needed to break all four bonds of methane, and tabulates bond energies in Table 7.2.

concepts.name: Bond strength, bond order, and bond length
concepts.why: The more electron pairs two atoms share, the stronger and the shorter their bond, so a triple bond is stronger and shorter than a double bond between the same atoms and a double bond is stronger and shorter than a single one. When one atom bonds to the members of a group, the bond grows weaker going down the group.
concepts.evidence: The section states both trends and quotes C–F, C–Cl and C–Br, and Table 7.3 sets the lengths and energies of the single, double and triple bonds of carbon to carbon, nitrogen and oxygen side by side; exercises ask which bond of each pair is the strongest and which bond of a structure is the longest.

concepts.name: Estimating an enthalpy of reaction from bond energies
concepts.why: The enthalpy change of a reaction is approximately the energy needed to break every bond of the reactants less the energy released in forming every bond of the products. The estimate needs the Lewis structures of all the species, to know which bonds are single, double or triple, and it is rough because the bond energies are averages.
concepts.evidence: The section estimates ΔH for the formation of HCl as −185 kJ against −184.6 kJ from enthalpies of formation, and Example 7.9 estimates −107 kJ for the synthesis of methanol against −90.5 kJ from the tables; exercises ask for the approximate enthalpy changes of several reactions.

concepts.name: Lattice energy
concepts.why: The lattice energy of an ionic compound is the energy needed to separate one mole of the solid into its gaseous ions, a positive quantity under the convention the book uses. It measures the strength of the attraction that holds an ionic solid together, and it is much larger than a covalent bond energy because it sums the interactions of every ion with the whole lattice.
concepts.evidence: The section defines the lattice energy, gives 769 kJ for sodium chloride, warns that some texts use the opposite sign, and compares the range of lattice energies with that of covalent bond energies; exercises ask which compound of a list needs the least or the most energy to separate into ions.

concepts.name: Lattice energy grows with ionic charge and shrinks with ionic size
concepts.why: Derived from Coulomb's law, the lattice energy is proportional to the product of the ionic charges and inversely proportional to the distance between the ions. Doubling both charges quadruples it, which is why MgO has nearly four times the lattice energy of LiF, and smaller ions give a larger lattice energy, which is why MgF2 exceeds MgI2.
concepts.evidence: The section gives the relation and compares LiF with MgO and MgF2 with MgI2, and Example 7.10 compares Al2O3 with Al2Se3; five exercises ask which compound of a pair has the larger lattice energy or which value best approximates one.

concepts.name: Calculating a lattice energy with the Born-Haber cycle
concepts.why: Lattice energies cannot be measured directly, but the Born-Haber cycle breaks the formation of an ionic solid from its elements into steps whose enthalpies are known: the sublimation of the metal, the dissociation of the nonmetal, the ionization of the metal atom, the electron affinity of the nonmetal atom, and the negative of the lattice energy. By Hess's law the steps add up to the enthalpy of formation, so any one of them can be found from the others.
concepts.evidence: Figure 7.13 draws the cycle for cesium fluoride, Table 7.4 lists its steps, and the section solves the cycle for a lattice energy of 756.9 kJ/mol.

concepts.name: Valence bond theory
concepts.why: Valence bond theory describes a covalent bond as the overlap of two half-filled atomic orbitals on different atoms, so that the single electrons in each orbital combine to form a pair shared between the two nuclei. The mutual attraction between this electron pair and the two positively charged nuclei is what holds the atoms together, and the strength of the bond depends on how much the orbitals overlap.
concepts.evidence: The section states the two conditions for a covalent bond, an overlap of orbitals and the pairing of their single electrons, and the glossary defines valence bond theory and overlap in the same terms; every bond described in the rest of the chapter until molecular orbital theory is described this way.

concepts.name: Bond distance and bond energy from the energy of two atoms
concepts.why: As two atoms approach, the energy of the system first falls, because each electron feels the attraction of the other nucleus, and then rises steeply, because the repulsions between the nuclei and between the electrons grow stronger than the attractions. The bond distance is the distance at which the energy is lowest, and the bond energy is the difference between that minimum and the energy of the separated atoms, which is the energy released when the bond forms and needed to break it.
concepts.evidence: Figure 8.2 follows two hydrogen atoms to the minimum at 74 pm, 7.24 × 10⁻¹⁹ J below the separated atoms, which the text converts to 4.36 × 10⁵ J for a mole of H–H bonds; Table 8.1 lists average bond lengths and energies, and exercises ask why atoms stop at a specific average distance.

concepts.name: Sigma and pi bonds
concepts.why: A σ bond forms when orbitals overlap end to end along the internuclear axis, as two s orbitals, an s and a p orbital, or two p orbitals pointed at each other do, so that the electron density is concentrated on the line between the nuclei. A π bond forms from the side-by-side overlap of two p orbitals, with the electron density on opposite sides of the internuclear axis and a node along the axis itself. Greater overlap is possible end to end, so a π bond is generally weaker than a σ bond between the same two atoms.
concepts.evidence: Figures 8.3, 8.4 and 8.5 draw the end-to-end and side-by-side overlaps, the glossary defines both bonds and the node, and the Check Your Learning of Example 8.1 asks the reader to identify three overlaps as σ or π.

concepts.name: What single, double, and triple bonds are made of
concepts.why: Between any two atoms the first bond formed is always a σ bond, and there can be only one σ bond in any one location. A single bond is therefore one σ bond, a double bond is one σ bond and one π bond, and a triple bond is one σ bond and two π bonds, which is why a carbon-carbon double bond is stronger than a single bond but not twice as strong.
concepts.evidence: The section reads the Lewis structures of HCl, O2 and N2 in these terms and uses Table 8.1 to show that each π bond adds less than the σ bond does (347, 614 and 839 kJ/mol for C–C, C=C and C≡C); the 8.3 exercise on the C≡C bond asks for the same explanation.

concepts.name: Counting the σ and π bonds in a molecule
concepts.why: Given a Lewis structure, we can count the σ and π bonds directly: every bond line contributes one σ bond, and each double bond adds one π bond and each triple bond adds two. The count is the first place the reader applies the valence bond description to a whole molecule.
concepts.evidence: Example 8.1 counts nine σ bonds and two π bonds in butadiene, and the end-of-section exercises ask for the σ and π bonds in HCN, CO2 and CO and whether N2 has three π bonds.

concepts.name: Hybridization of atomic orbitals
concepts.why: The overlap of unmodified atomic orbitals predicts the wrong shapes: two O–H bonds made from oxygen's perpendicular 2p orbitals would meet at 90°, while the observed angle in water is 104.5°. Hybridization combines the wave functions of an atom's valence orbitals by the linear combination of atomic orbitals into a new set of hybrid orbitals whose directions match the observed geometry, so valence bond theory must include it to give accurate predictions.
concepts.evidence: The section opens with the 90° prediction of Figure 8.6 against the observed 104.5°, then describes the four tetrahedral hybrid orbitals of oxygen in Figure 8.7; the first exercise asks why the concept of hybridization is required in valence bond theory.

concepts.name: The properties of a set of hybrid orbitals
concepts.why: Hybrid orbitals exist only in covalently bonded atoms, they have shapes and orientations very different from those of the atomic orbitals they come from, and a set contains as many hybrid orbitals as atomic orbitals were combined to make it. All the orbitals of a set are equivalent in shape and energy, the kind of set depends on the atom's electron-pair geometry, and hybrid orbitals form σ bonds while unhybridized orbitals form π bonds.
concepts.evidence: The section lists these six ideas before the first kind of hybridization is described, and each later subsection checks them: the sp set of Figure 8.8 is two orbitals from two, and the orbital energy-level diagrams of Figures 8.9, 8.13 and 8.16 show every hybrid of a set at one energy.

concepts.name: The sp, sp², and sp³ hybrid orbitals
concepts.why: Mixing the valence s orbital with one p orbital gives two sp hybrids pointing 180° apart; with two p orbitals, three sp² hybrids at 120° in a plane, leaving one unhybridized p orbital perpendicular to it; with all three p orbitals, four sp³ hybrids pointing to the corners of a tetrahedron at 109.5°. Each hybrid holds a bonding pair or a lone pair, so the linear BeCl2, the trigonal planar BH3 and the tetrahedral CH4, NH3 and H2O are all described this way.
concepts.evidence: Figures 8.8, 8.10 and 8.15 build the three sets from their atomic orbitals, Figures 8.12 and 8.17 show them bonding in BH3 and ethane, and the glossary defines each set by its arrangement; the text names HgCl2, CO2, ClNO, CH2O, CCl4 and NCl3 as further examples.

concepts.name: The sp³d and sp³d² hybrid orbitals
concepts.why: Five hybrid orbitals directed to the corners of a trigonal bipyramid need one d orbital as well as the s and three p orbitals, and six directed to the corners of an octahedron need two d orbitals. These hybridizations are possible only for atoms with d orbitals in their valence subshells, which rules out every atom of the first and second periods.
concepts.evidence: The section describes PCl5 with sp³d hybrids (Figure 8.19) and SF6 with sp³d² hybrids (Figure 8.20), names SF4, ClF3, XeF4 and the interhalogens as further examples, and the exercises ask why carbon cannot form five bonds and why NF5 does not exist while PF5 does.

concepts.name: Showing hybridization on an orbital energy-level diagram
concepts.why: An orbital energy-level diagram draws each orbital as a horizontal line at its energy and each electron as an arrow, and setting the isolated atom beside the bonded one shows the valence electrons redistributed into the hybrid set. The diagram makes plain which hybrids are half filled and ready to pair with an electron from another atom, and which orbitals stay unhybridized.
concepts.evidence: Figures 8.9, 8.13 and 8.16 draw the diagrams for beryllium in BeCl2, boron in BH3 and carbon in CH4, Figure 8.22 draws carbon in ethene, and the exercise on CO2 asks the reader to draw the diagram for its carbon.

concepts.name: Assigning the hybridization of a central atom
concepts.why: The hybridization of an atom follows from the number of regions of electron density around it: write the Lewis structure, count the regions with single bonds, multiple bonds, radicals and lone pairs each counting as one, and read the matching set from the table of arrangements, two regions sp, three sp², four sp³, five sp³d and six sp³d². VSEPR theory predicts the shape, and the hybrid orbitals explain how that shape is formed.
concepts.evidence: Figure 8.21 sets out the five arrangements with their hybridizations, Examples 8.2 and 8.3 assign sp³ to sulfur in sulfate and sp² to carbon in urea, their Check Your Learning items ask for SeF4 and acetic acid, and most of the section's exercises are this skill applied.

concepts.name: Where hybridization is needed and where it is not
concepts.why: Hybridization was devised to rationalize observed geometries, and it works well for small central atoms whose valence pairs are close together. For larger central atoms the pairs are farther from the nucleus and repel less, and the observed angles approach those of unhybridized p orbitals, so we invoke hybridization only where it is needed to explain the structure.
concepts.evidence: The section compares the H–O–H angle of 104.5° in water with 92.1° in H2S and 90° in H2Te, reading the last as the overlap of 5p orbitals without hybridization.

concepts.name: Multiple bonds from hybrid and unhybridized orbitals
concepts.why: In a molecule with a double or a triple bond, the hybrid orbitals of each atom form the σ framework and the unhybridized p orbitals left over overlap side by side to form the π bonds. Each carbon of ethene uses three sp² hybrids for its σ bonds and one p orbital, perpendicular to the plane, for its π bond; each carbon of acetylene uses two sp hybrids for σ bonds and two perpendicular p orbitals for two π bonds.
concepts.evidence: Figures 8.22 and 8.23 draw ethene's sp² hybrids and its π bond above and below the plane, Figures 8.24 and 8.25 draw acetylene's two π bonds around the C–C axis, and the exercises on acetonitrile and allene ask which orbitals form each σ and π bond.

concepts.name: Rotation about a double bond is restricted
concepts.why: Rotation about a single bond occurs easily, because the end-to-end overlap of a σ bond is symmetric about the internuclear axis and does not change as the atoms turn. Rotation about a double bond would twist the two p orbitals out of line and destroy their side-by-side overlap, essentially breaking the π bond, which is why all six atoms of ethene lie in one plane.
concepts.evidence: The section derives the planarity of ethene from the overlap of its p orbitals and contrasts it with the free rotation of the two CH3 groups of ethane described in 8.2; the allene exercise asks whether its hydrogen atoms lie in the same plane or in perpendicular planes.

concepts.name: Resonance, hybridization, and delocalized π electrons
concepts.why: Hybridization involves only σ bonds, lone pairs and single unpaired electrons, and resonance forms differ only in the arrangement of π bonds, which uses the unhybridized orbitals. Resonance therefore does not change the hybridization we assign, and either resonance form gives the same answer. The π electrons themselves are not located in one form or the other but are delocalized over the molecule, which valence bond theory does not easily describe.
concepts.evidence: The section assigns sp² to every carbon of benzene from either resonance form (Figure 8.26) and says its π electrons are delocalized throughout the ring; Example 8.4 assigns sp² to sulfur in SO2 from its resonance structures, and exercises ask whether the electrons of O3, CO2, NO2 and phosphate are delocalized.

concepts.name: Paramagnetism and diamagnetism
concepts.why: A substance whose molecules have unpaired electrons is paramagnetic and is attracted into a magnetic field, while one whose electrons are all paired is diamagnetic and is weakly repelled; neither is a permanent magnet. Liquid oxygen collects between the poles of a magnet, which shows that the O2 molecule has two unpaired electrons although its Lewis structure pairs every electron.
concepts.evidence: The section defines both terms, describes the Gouy balance of Figure 8.27 that measures the number of unpaired electrons, and returns to the liquid oxygen of Figure 8.1; the exercises ask whether a molecule with an odd or an even number of electrons can be diamagnetic or paramagnetic.

concepts.name: Molecular orbital theory
concepts.why: Molecular orbital theory describes the electrons of a molecule by molecular orbitals, formed by the linear combination of atomic orbitals, that extend over the whole molecule rather than belonging to one atom. Like an atomic orbital, a molecular orbital has a quantized energy and holds at most two electrons of opposite spin. The theory accounts for things valence bond theory cannot, among them the paramagnetism of oxygen and bonding described by several resonance forms.
concepts.evidence: The section introduces the theory against the problem of O2, compares it with valence bond theory in Table 8.2, and defines the molecular orbital, the homonuclear diatomic molecule and the linear combination of atomic orbitals in the glossary.

concepts.name: Bonding and antibonding molecular orbitals
concepts.why: Combining two atomic wave functions in phase is constructive interference and gives a bonding orbital, lower in energy than the atomic orbitals, with its electron density between the nuclei. Combining them out of phase is destructive interference and gives an antibonding orbital, higher in energy, with a node between the nuclei. Two atomic orbitals always give two molecular orbitals, one of each kind, and an asterisk marks the antibonding one.
concepts.evidence: Figure 8.28 shows constructive and destructive interference of waves, Figure 8.29 draws the σs and σs* orbitals from two s orbitals, and the exercises ask why a bonding orbital is lower in energy than its parent atomic orbitals and how many molecular orbitals five pairs of atomic orbitals give.

concepts.name: σ and π molecular orbitals
concepts.why: Molecular orbitals along the internuclear axis are σ orbitals, formed from s orbitals or from p orbitals overlapping end to end; those formed from p orbitals side by side, with electron density on opposite sides of the axis, are π orbitals. With the atoms on the x-axis, the six p orbitals of two atoms give σpx and σpx*, and two degenerate pairs of π and π* orbitals from the py and pz orbitals.
concepts.evidence: Figures 8.30 and 8.31 draw the σp, σp*, πp and πp* orbitals with their nodes, the text defines degenerate orbitals on the πpy and πpz pair, and Example 8.5 and its Check Your Learning ask the reader to name the orbital that a pair of overlapping lobes would give.

concepts.name: Filling a molecular orbital diagram
concepts.why: A molecular orbital diagram sets the atomic orbitals of the two atoms at the sides and the molecular orbitals they form in the center, each as a line at its energy. Electrons fill it as they fill an atom: lower-energy orbitals first by the Aufbau principle, singly across degenerate orbitals before pairing by Hund's rule, two to an orbital with opposite spins. The filled diagram gives the molecular electron configuration, written with superscripts and with degenerate orbitals in parentheses.
concepts.evidence: Figure 8.34 fills the diagram for Be2+ and writes its configuration, Figures 8.35 and 8.36 fill it for H2 and He2, and Example 8.6 draws it for O2; exercises ask for the valence configurations of a series of diatomic ions.

concepts.name: Bond order from a molecular orbital diagram
concepts.why: In molecular orbital theory the bond order is the number of bonding electrons minus the number of antibonding electrons, divided by two, since a bond consists of two electrons. It usually agrees with the count of bonds in a Lewis structure, it is a guide to the strength of a bond between two given atoms, and a bond order of zero means that no stable bond forms.
concepts.evidence: The section states the equation and applies it to H2 (bond order 1), He2 (0) and O2 (2), and Table 8.3 lists the bond orders of the period-two diatomic molecules; exercises ask for the bond orders of groups of ions and which member has the strongest bond.

concepts.name: s-p mixing and the order of the molecular orbitals
concepts.why: When the 2s and 2p orbitals of an atom are close in energy, the σs and σp wave functions combine, lowering the σs orbital and raising the σp orbital above the πp pair. The energy gap is small from lithium to nitrogen, so their diatomic molecules have the σp orbital above the π orbitals, and large for oxygen, fluorine and neon, whose diagrams keep the expected order. s-p mixing creates no new orbitals; it only shifts the energies of the existing ones.
concepts.evidence: Figure 8.37 draws the diagrams of every period-two diatomic molecule with the change of order between N2 and O2, and Figure 8.38 shows the orbitals shifting with and without mixing; exercises ask whether S2 shows s-p mixing and why N2 2+ is diamagnetic while O2 4+ is paramagnetic.

concepts.name: Predicting the configuration, bond order, and magnetism of a diatomic species
concepts.why: For a homonuclear diatomic molecule or ion of the first or second period, we choose the diagram with or without s-p mixing, add or remove electrons for the charge, fill it, and read off the configuration, the bond order and the number of unpaired electrons. The result predicts whether the species is stable and whether it is paramagnetic, and it explains the two unpaired electrons of O2 that the Lewis structure missed.
concepts.evidence: Table 8.3 gives the configurations and bond orders of Li2 to Ne2, Example 8.6 explains the paramagnetism of O2 and its Check Your Learning asks for N2, Example 8.7 predicts that C2 2− is stable with a bond order of 3, and a long run of exercises applies the procedure to ions.

concepts.name: The energy of a photon
concepts.why: Light is absorbed and emitted in discrete packets called photons, and the energy of one photon is set by the frequency of the radiation, E = hν, or equivalently by its wavelength, E = hc/λ. The Bohr model needs this before it can say anything at all, since the whole of its argument is that one photon carries away the difference between two orbital energies.
