concepts.evidence: The section states the relation as a key equation, Example 6.2 calculates the energy of a photon from a neon sign and its Check Your Learning that of a microwave photon, and several end-of-chapter exercises ask for the energy, frequency, or wavelength of a photon.

concepts.name: Line spectra
concepts.why: A gas excited by heat or by an electric current emits light at a few sharp wavelengths rather than over an unbroken band, and each element shows its own set of lines. Classical electromagnetic theory predicts a continuous spectrum and cannot account for this, which is the observation the Bohr model was built to explain.
concepts.evidence: The section contrasts continuous and line spectra in Figure 6.13, states the Balmer and Rydberg formulas, and the first end-of-chapter exercise asks the reader to describe the spectrum of a neon lamp.

concepts.name: Wavelength, frequency, and amplitude
concepts.why: Every wave, electromagnetic radiation included, is characterized by a wavelength, the distance between two consecutive peaks or troughs, a frequency, the number of cycles that pass a point per unit time, and an amplitude, one-half the height from peak to trough. The amplitude is related to the intensity of the wave, which for light is its brightness, and the wavelength and frequency are what the rest of the chapter measures light by.
concepts.evidence: The section defines the three quantities where it introduces waves, Figure 6.2 draws them on waves of three frequencies, and the glossary carries each of them.

concepts.name: The speed of a wave, $c=\lambda\nu$
concepts.why: The product of a wave's wavelength and its frequency is its speed, and for electromagnetic radiation in a vacuum that speed is the constant c. Wavelength and frequency are therefore inversely proportional: as one increases, the other decreases, and either one may be found from the other.
concepts.evidence: The section states the relation as a key equation, Example 6.1 finds the frequency of the yellow light of a sodium streetlight and its Check Your Learning the wavelength of a cellular signal, and several end-of-chapter exercises ask for a wavelength or a frequency.

concepts.name: The electromagnetic spectrum
concepts.why: Electromagnetic radiation spans an enormous range of wavelengths, from gamma rays and X-rays through ultraviolet, visible, and infrared light to microwaves and radio waves, and visible light makes up only a small portion of it. Across the spectrum the energy and frequency increase as the wavelength decreases, and each region is put to its own uses.
concepts.evidence: Figure 6.3 lays out the spectrum in order of decreasing frequency, the Chemistry in Everyday Life note places radio and cellular signals on it, and several exercises ask the reader to name the region or the color of a given radiation.

concepts.name: Standing waves and quantization
concepts.why: A standing wave is confined to a region of space, and a string held fixed at its two end points can form only those waves that have an integer number of half-wavelengths between them. This is an example of quantization, in which only discrete values of a property are observed, and the points between the ends that do not move are nodes, whose number grows with the energy of the wave.
concepts.evidence: The section works through the vibrating string of Figure 6.7 and the vibrating drumhead of Figure 6.8, and the glossary defines standing wave, node, and quantization.

concepts.name: Blackbody radiation and Planck's quantized energies
concepts.why: A heated object gives off a continuous spectrum whose distribution depends only on its temperature, and the peak of the curve moves to shorter wavelengths as the temperature rises. Classical theory predicted an intensity that grows without limit at short wavelengths, the ultraviolet catastrophe; Planck fitted the observed curves by restricting the vibrational energies to discrete values, E = nhν, which was the first appearance of energy quantization.
concepts.evidence: The section compares sunlight with a blackbody at 5250 °C in Figure 6.9, draws the blackbody curves for several temperatures in Figure 6.10, and states Planck's quantization and the value of his constant.

concepts.name: The photoelectric effect
concepts.why: Light ejects electrons from a clean metal surface only when its frequency is above a threshold, and the kinetic energy of the ejected electrons rises with the frequency and not with the brightness, while the number of electrons rises with the brightness. Einstein explained this by treating light as a stream of photons, each carrying the energy hν, so that only a photon with enough energy can free an electron.
concepts.evidence: Figure 6.11 draws light of three wavelengths striking a metal, Example 6.3 asks which statements about the effect are true and its Check Your Learning calculates a threshold energy, and an end-of-chapter exercise asks for the threshold frequency of sodium.

concepts.name: Wave-particle duality
concepts.why: Some phenomena of light, such as the interference fringes it makes after passing through two narrow slits, can be explained only by waves, while others, such as the photoelectric effect, can be explained only by particles. Light is both wavelike and particle-like, and this is called wave-particle duality; the next sections extend it to matter.
concepts.evidence: The section describes the interference patterns of Figure 6.6, contrasts them with the photoelectric effect, and names wave-particle duality in its summary and its glossary.

concepts.name: Why the planetary atom cannot be stable
concepts.why: In the planetary picture the electron moves about the nucleus as a planet moves about the sun, and the electrostatic attraction between the two depends only on the distance between them. An electron on such an orbit is always changing direction, and so is always accelerating, and classical electromagnetism says that an accelerating charge must continuously emit radiation. The orbit would then shrink until the electron spiralled into the nucleus, which would make every atom inherently unstable. The paradox is the reason a new postulate was needed.
concepts.evidence: The section opens by setting out the planetary model and the loss of orbital energy that follows from it, and an end-of-chapter exercise asks the reader to say how the Bohr and the Rutherford models are alike and how they differ, which turns on exactly this point.

concepts.name: Bohr's stationary states
concepts.why: Bohr resolved the paradox by setting aside the classical prediction: an electron on one of the allowed orbits does not radiate at all, and radiation is emitted or absorbed only when the electron moves from one allowed orbit to another. The energies of those orbits are quantized, which is to say that the electron may possess certain discrete energies and no value between them. This is the postulate the rest of the chapter is built on, and it is the one feature of the model that survived into quantum mechanics.
concepts.evidence: The section states the stationary state hypothesis and the quantization of the orbital energies in the paragraph that introduces the model, and an exercise asks the reader to say what it means for the energy of the electrons in an atom to be quantized, which the book answers in those words.

concepts.name: The allowed energies, $E_n=-kZ^2/n^2$
concepts.why: The energy of an electron on the orbit labelled n is the constant k, which gathers the electron mass and charge and Planck's constant together, divided by the square of n and multiplied by the square of the nuclear charge. The energies are negative because they are measured from the state in which the electron has been removed altogether, and they crowd toward zero as n grows, so that the rungs of the ladder are far apart at the bottom and close together at the top. Because they are measured that way, E = 0 is the ionization limit, the state in which the electron has been removed from the nucleus altogether, and the energy needed to take a ground-state hydrogen atom there is the constant k itself.
concepts.evidence: The section gives the expression twice, first for hydrogen and then for any one-electron atom, Figure 6.14 draws the lowest few levels with their energies, Example 6.4 calculates the energy of an electron with n = 3 in hydrogen, and four end-of-chapter exercises ask for the energy of an electron in a named orbit of hydrogen, He⁺ or Li²⁺. The section works the ionization limit out from the same expression.

concepts.name: Ground state and excited state
concepts.why: Matter is most stable with the lowest possible energy, so the electron in a hydrogen atom usually moves in the n = 1 orbit, and the atom is then said to be in its ground state. Energy from outside can move the electron to an orbit with a higher n, and the atom is then in an excited state. The two words name where the electron is on the ladder, and every transition the section describes runs between two such states.
concepts.evidence: The section defines both terms where it introduces the energy-level diagram, the glossary carries each of them, and Example 6.4 begins with a spark that promotes the electron of a hydrogen atom into the n = 3 orbit.

concepts.name: One transition, one photon: $|\Delta E|=h\nu=hc/\lambda$
concepts.why: When an electron moves between two allowed orbits the atom emits or absorbs a single photon whose energy is the whole of the difference between the two orbital energies. Falling to a lower orbit emits the photon, and absorbing one moves the electron up; because energy can be neither created nor destroyed, the energy needed to lift an electron from one level to another is exactly the energy liberated when it returns. The absolute value is used because a frequency and a wavelength are always positive.
concepts.evidence: The section states the relation as the first equation it writes and returns to it under the law of conservation of energy, Figure 6.15 draws the absorbed photons as upward arrows and the emitted ones as downward arrows, and Example 6.5 finds both the energy and the wavelength of the photon for a named transition.

concepts.name: Hydrogen-like atoms and ions
concepts.why: Because Bohr's model follows one electron only, it applies just as well to He⁺, Li²⁺, Be³⁺ and the rest of the one-electron ions, which differ from hydrogen only in their nuclear charge. Writing Z into the energy and the radius is the whole of the generalization, and it is also the boundary of the model: helium, with two electrons, is already beyond it, because the model says nothing about how two electrons act on each other.
concepts.evidence: The section introduces Z with the generalized energy expression and closes by saying that Bohr could not extend the theory to helium, and five end-of-chapter exercises ask for an energy or a photon in He⁺ or Li²⁺.

concepts.name: The radius of an allowed orbit, $r=n^2a_0/Z$
concepts.why: The allowed orbits grow as the square of the quantum number and shrink as the nuclear charge rises, measured in units of the Bohr radius, the radius of hydrogen's ground-state orbit. This is the other half of what n says: as the electron's energy increases it is found at greater distances from the nucleus, which is what the inverse dependence of the electrostatic attraction on distance implies, since an electron further out is held less tightly.
concepts.evidence: The section gives the expression with the value of the Bohr radius and explains what it means for the electron's distance from the nucleus, and two end-of-chapter exercises ask for the radius of a named orbit in angstroms or for the distance at which an electron has a given energy.

concepts.name: The Rydberg equation recovered, $R_{\infty}=k/hc$
concepts.why: Putting the quantized energies into the photon relation gives an expression for one over the wavelength that is identical in form to the Rydberg equation, with the Rydberg constant standing as the quotient of k by hc. When Bohr compared his theoretical value with the experimental one, which was among the most precisely measured constants of the day, the agreement was excellent, and that agreement is why a model resting on so many assumptions was taken seriously at all.
concepts.evidence: The section derives the expression in two steps and names the quotient as the Rydberg constant, and it closes by saying that the discrete lines in the spectra of the elements result from quantized electronic energies, which an end-of-chapter exercise asks the reader to explain for the spectra of hydrogen and of calcium.

concepts.name: Calculating the energy and wavelength of a transition
concepts.why: The second objective of the section is a calculation: given the two quantum numbers and the nuclear charge, find the energy difference from kZ²(1/n₁² − 1/n₂²), read its sign to say whether the photon is absorbed or emitted, and divide hc by its magnitude to get the wavelength. Doing it once with care is what turns the model from a picture into something that can be checked against a spectrum.
concepts.evidence: Example 6.5 works a transition from n = 4 to n = 6 in hydrogen through to a wavelength and names the part of the spectrum it falls in, its Check Your Learning repeats the work for He⁺, and four end-of-chapter exercises ask for the energy of a photon produced by a named transition in hydrogen, He⁺ or Li²⁺.

concepts.name: The de Broglie wavelength, $\lambda=h/mv$
concepts.why: De Broglie extended wave-particle duality to matter: a particle of mass m moving with velocity v behaves as a wave whose wavelength is Planck's constant divided by its momentum. The wavelength of an electron in an atom is about the size of the atom, so its wavelike behavior is noticeable there, while that of a softball is far too small to detect. Viewed as a circular standing wave, an electron fits an orbit only when a whole number of its wavelengths fits the circumference, which explains Bohr's quantization.
concepts.evidence: The section states the relation and de Broglie's orbit condition, Figure 6.17 draws the electron wave about the nucleus, Figure 6.18 shows the interference pattern that electrons build up one by one, and Example 6.6 calculates the wavelength of an electron while its Check Your Learning does the same for a softball.

concepts.name: The Heisenberg uncertainty principle
concepts.why: It is fundamentally impossible to determine simultaneously and exactly both the momentum and the position of a particle: the product of the two uncertainties is at least ħ/2. The limit is too small to notice for a baseball, but the mass of an electron is small enough that the uncertainty is large and significant, which is why an electron in an atom cannot be given a precise orbit.
concepts.evidence: The section states the principle and works the uncertainty in momentum for an electron located to within 1 pm, extends it to energy and time, and an end-of-chapter exercise asks the reader to state the principle and describe what it implies.

concepts.name: Wavefunctions and orbitals as probability
concepts.why: Schrödinger described electrons as three-dimensional stationary waves, or wavefunctions ψ, and Born interpreted them: the electron is still a particle, and the square of the magnitude of ψ gives the probability of finding it near a point in space. An atomic orbital is the region in which an electron is most probable to reside, so the quantum mechanical model describes where the electron is likely to be rather than a path it follows.
concepts.evidence: The section introduces the Schrödinger equation and Born's interpretation, Figure 6.20 graphs the probability density of the s orbitals against the distance from the nucleus, and the first end-of-chapter exercise asks how the Bohr and quantum mechanical models of hydrogen are alike and how they differ.

concepts.name: The principal quantum number and shells
concepts.why: The principal quantum number n = 1, 2, 3, … labels the energy levels of an electron in an atom and is essentially the n of the Bohr atom. Orbitals with the same n form a shell, and the greater n is, the farther the electron is from the nucleus and the greater its energy; a transition between levels absorbs or emits a photon that carries the energy difference.
concepts.evidence: Figure 6.19 numbers the shells about the nucleus, the section writes the energy change of a transition in hydrogen in terms of the initial and final values of n, and Table 6.1 gives the allowed values and physical meaning of n.

concepts.name: The secondary quantum number, subshells, and orbital shapes
concepts.why: The secondary (angular momentum) quantum number l takes the integer values 0 to n − 1 and specifies the shape of an orbital: l = 0, 1, 2, 3 are the s, p, d, and f orbitals, and orbitals with the same n and l form a subshell. An s orbital is spherical and a p orbital is dumbbell-shaped, and an orbital has n − l − 1 radial nodes, distances at which the probability of finding the electron is zero.
concepts.evidence: Figure 6.20 counts the radial nodes of the 1s, 2s, and 3s orbitals, Figure 6.21 draws the shapes of the s, p, d, and f orbitals, and Example 6.9 completes a table of orbitals, their quantum numbers, and their radial nodes.

concepts.name: The magnetic quantum number and degenerate orbitals
concepts.why: The magnetic quantum number m_l takes the values −l to +l and specifies the orientation of an orbital in space, so a subshell holds 2l + 1 orbitals: one s, three p, five d, and seven f. Orbitals of the same subshell have the same energy and are called degenerate; in hydrogen all orbitals of one shell are degenerate, but in atoms with more than one electron the subshells of a shell differ in energy.
concepts.evidence: The section counts the orbitals of each subshell, Figure 6.22 charts the energies of the subshells in a multi-electron atom, and two end-of-chapter exercises ask which subshells contain degenerate orbitals and how many.

concepts.name: The spin quantum number
concepts.why: Each electron has an intrinsic spin, a completely quantum property with no classical analogue, and it can be in only one of two states, m_s = +1/2 or −1/2. An electron acts as a tiny magnet, and in an external magnetic field the two spin states have slightly different energies, which is why some lines of the hydrogen spectrum are closely spaced pairs.
concepts.evidence: The section introduces spin through the fine structure of the hydrogen spectrum and Figure 6.23 draws the two spin states in a magnetic field.

concepts.name: The Pauli exclusion principle
concepts.why: No two electrons in the same atom can have the same set of all four quantum numbers. Since the spin quantum number has only two values, an orbital can hold no more than two electrons, and two electrons in the same orbital must have opposite spins; this is the last piece of information needed to understand how electrons fill the orbitals of an atom.
concepts.evidence: The section states the principle and summarizes the four quantum numbers in Table 6.1, Example 6.8 finds the maximum number of electrons in a shell, and an end-of-chapter exercise asks how many electrons the second shell could hold if the spin quantum number had three values.

concepts.name: Working with shells, subshells, and quantum numbers
concepts.why: Given a value of n, the reader lists the allowed values of l and m_l, names the subshells, counts the orbitals in each, and finds that a shell holds n² orbitals and at most 2n² electrons; given a set of quantum numbers, the reader names the subshell. This bookkeeping is what the next section uses to build the electron configurations of the atoms.
concepts.evidence: Examples 6.7, 6.8, and 6.9 and their Check Your Learning items all ask for it, and several end-of-chapter exercises ask the reader to identify a subshell from n and l or to write a set of quantum numbers for an electron.

concepts.name: The energy order of atomic orbitals
concepts.why: In an atom with two or more electrons, the energy of the orbitals increases with n and, within a shell, in the order s < p < d < f, because electrons with larger l penetrate less toward the nucleus and are more shielded by the inner electrons. For larger atoms the two trends overlap, so that the 4s orbital lies below the 3d and the filling order runs 1s, 2s, 2p, 3s, 3p, 4s, 3d, 4p, and so on.
concepts.evidence: Figure 6.24 charts the orbital energies of a multi-electron atom, Figure 6.26 gives the traditional way to remember the filling order, and the section explains why potassium adds its last electron to 4s rather than 3d.

concepts.name: The Aufbau principle
concepts.why: The electron configurations of the elements are built by adding one proton to the nucleus and one electron at a time, each electron entering the subshell of lowest energy available, subject to the Pauli exclusion principle. Electrons enter higher-energy subshells only after the lower ones have been filled to capacity, and reading the periodic table in order of increasing Z gives the same order.
concepts.evidence: The section builds the configurations from hydrogen through neon one electron at a time, Figure 6.27 shows how the periodic table gives the filling order, and Example 6.10 applies the principle to phosphorus.

concepts.name: Hund's rule
concepts.why: The lowest-energy configuration of electrons in a set of degenerate orbitals is the one with the maximum number of unpaired electrons: each orbital of a subshell is singly occupied, with all spins alike, before any is doubly occupied. So the two 2p electrons of carbon sit in different p orbitals with the same spin.
concepts.evidence: The section states the rule at carbon and applies it to nitrogen, oxygen, fluorine, and neon, the glossary defines it, and an end-of-chapter exercise asks which of several atoms has two unpaired electrons.

concepts.name: Writing electron configurations and orbital diagrams
concepts.why: An electron configuration lists each occupied subshell by its n, its letter, and a superscript that counts its electrons, as in 1s²2s²2p⁴, and an orbital diagram draws each orbital as a box and each electron as an arrow. The inner electrons may be abbreviated by the symbol of the noble gas whose configuration they match, as in [Ne]3s¹ for sodium, and the reader writes either form for any atom and identifies an atom from its configuration.
concepts.evidence: Figure 6.25 labels the parts of the notation, Figure 6.28 abbreviates the core of sodium, Example 6.10 writes the configuration and orbital diagram of phosphorus, and many end-of-chapter exercises ask for a configuration, an orbital diagram, or the atom a configuration belongs to.

concepts.name: Valence electrons and core electrons
concepts.why: The electrons in the outermost shell are the valence electrons and those in the inner shells are the core electrons. Valence electrons have the highest energy, are the most easily lost or shared, and play the most important role in chemical reactions, and elements with the same number of valence electrons have similar chemical properties.
concepts.evidence: The section defines both terms at sodium, Figure 6.28 marks the core and the valence electron of sodium, and an end-of-chapter exercise asks which of several atoms has only three valence electrons.

concepts.name: Exceptions to the predicted configurations
concepts.why: Some atoms do not follow the predicted filling order because the subshells involved are very close in energy. Half-filled and completely filled subshells represent conditions of preferred stability, so chromium and copper each move an electron from 4s into 3d, and in niobium the repulsion of pairing two 5s electrons outweighs the small gap between 5s and 4d; there is no simple method to predict such exceptions.
concepts.evidence: The section discusses chromium, copper, and niobium, and Figure 6.29 prints the observed configurations of every element.

concepts.name: Electron configurations and the periodic table
concepts.why: The periodic table puts elements whose atoms have the same number of valence electrons in the same group, which is why the chemical properties recur periodically. The subshell that receives the last electron divides the table into the main group elements (s and p), the transition elements (d), and the inner transition elements (f), and this classification decides which orbitals are counted in the valence shell.
concepts.evidence: Figure 6.29 shows the configuration of every element in periodic-table form, the section describes the three categories with the valence electrons of each, and end-of-chapter exercises ask which group has a given valence configuration and why aluminum is in group 13 rather than group 3.

concepts.name: Electron configurations of ions
concepts.why: A cation of a main group element loses the electrons that were added last, while a transition or inner transition metal loses its highest ns electrons before its (n − 1)d or (n − 2)f electrons; an anion adds electrons in the order the Aufbau principle predicts. The reader writes the configuration of an ion from that of its parent atom, and names an ion from a configuration and a charge.
concepts.evidence: Example 6.11 writes the configurations of five ions from Na⁺ to Sm³⁺ and its Check Your Learning names the ions of a given configuration, and several end-of-chapter exercises ask for the configuration of a named ion.

concepts.name: Effective nuclear charge, $Z_{\text{eff}}=Z-\text{shielding}$
concepts.why: The pull the nucleus exerts on one electron is its charge less the shielding of the other electrons. Core electrons shield well, while electrons in the same valence shell shield each other poorly, so each step to the right across a period raises Z by one but the shielding only slightly, and the effective nuclear charge increases across a period.
concepts.evidence: The section introduces the effective nuclear charge to explain why atoms get smaller across a period, and returns to it for the radii of ions and for electron affinities.

concepts.name: The trend in covalent radius
concepts.why: The covalent radius, one-half the distance between the nuclei of two identical atoms joined by a covalent bond, increases down a group because each step adds a shell farther from the nucleus, and decreases from left to right across a period because the rising effective nuclear charge draws the electrons closer.
concepts.evidence: Table 6.2 and Figure 6.30 give the radii of the halogens, Figure 6.31 graphs the radius against atomic number, Example 6.12 sorts four atoms by radius, and several end-of-chapter exercises ask which atom is largest or smallest or for an order of increasing radius.

concepts.name: The radii of ions and isoelectronic species
concepts.why: A cation is smaller than its parent atom, since the remaining electrons feel a greater effective nuclear charge, and a cation of higher charge is smaller still; an anion is larger than its parent, since the added electrons repel one another. Atoms and ions with the same electron configuration are isoelectronic, and among them the one with the greater nuclear charge is the smaller.
concepts.evidence: Figure 6.32 compares Al and S with Al³⁺ and S²⁻, the section lists two isoelectronic series, and several end-of-chapter exercises ask for an order of increasing ionic radius or for the species isoelectronic with a given ion.

concepts.name: The trend in first ionization energy
concepts.why: The first ionization energy, the energy required to remove the most loosely bound electron from a gaseous atom, is always positive and generally decreases down a group and increases across a period, the opposite of the trend in size. It dips each time a new subshell begins, as from beryllium to boron, and again where a p subshell becomes more than half-filled, as from nitrogen to oxygen.
concepts.evidence: Figure 6.33 graphs the first ionization energy against atomic number and Figure 6.34 gives its values in periodic-table form, the section explains the dips at boron and oxygen, and several end-of-chapter exercises ask for the largest or smallest first ionization energy or an order of increasing values.

concepts.name: Successive ionization energies
concepts.why: Removing an electron from a cation is harder than removing one from a neutral atom, so the successive ionization energies of an element always increase. There is a large jump when the core electrons begin to be removed, which falls after the last valence electron: after the third ionization for scandium and gallium, for example.
concepts.evidence: Table 6.3 lists the successive ionization energies of six elements, Example 6.13 ranks ionization processes that include a second and a third ionization, and an end-of-chapter exercise asks which main group atom has the lowest second ionization energy.

concepts.name: The trend in electron affinity
concepts.why: The electron affinity is the energy change when a gaseous atom accepts an electron, and it may be negative (energy released) or positive. Electron affinities tend to become more negative across a period as the effective nuclear charge increases, with exceptions in groups 2, 15, and 18 where a filled or half-filled subshell resists the added electron, and the second element of a group, such as chlorine, often has a more negative value than the first because the small n = 2 shell crowds its electrons.
concepts.evidence: Figure 6.35 gives electron affinities in periodic-table form, and the section explains the exceptions and why chlorine has the most negative value of any element.

concepts.name: Predicting sizes and energies from the periodic table
concepts.why: From the positions of elements in the periodic table the reader orders atoms and ions by radius, by ionization energy, or by electron affinity, putting the trend down a group together with the trend across a period and allowing for the exceptions the section explains. Because metallic character follows the same trend as size, the same reading tells which elements lose electrons most easily.
concepts.evidence: Examples 6.12 and 6.13 and their Check Your Learning items ask for such orders, and most of the end-of-chapter exercises of the section ask the reader to predict which atom is largest, smallest, or hardest to ionize, or to rank several atoms or ions.

concepts.name: Solutions and their defining traits
concepts.why: A solution is a homogeneous mixture in which the solute particles are individually dispersed among the solvent’s, so its composition is uniform, its state is usually the solvent’s, and its solute never settles out. Almost any gas, liquid or solid can act as a solvent, so air and brass are solutions just as saltwater is.
concepts.evidence: Figure 11.2 shows potassium dichromate dispersing into a uniform orange solution, Table 11.1 lists solutions of every phase, and the text sets out the five defining traits.

concepts.name: Ideal solutions and matter dispersal
concepts.why: When the attractions between unlike particles are no different from those between like particles, a solution forms with no change in energy, and it forms anyway, driven by the increased dispersal of matter alone.
concepts.evidence: Figure 11.3 lets helium and argon mix through an opened stopcock, and the text extends the same picture to methanol with ethanol and pentane with hexane.

concepts.name: Dissolution as three steps
concepts.why: The formation of a solution may be viewed as separating the solute particles and the solvent particles, both endothermic, and then letting solute and solvent attract one another (solvation), which is exothermic. The balance of the three steps decides whether dissolving releases or absorbs heat.
concepts.evidence: Figure 11.4 draws the stepwise path beside the direct formation of the solution, and the text applies it to an ionic compound dissolving in water.

concepts.name: Heat released or absorbed on dissolving
concepts.why: A solute whose solvation releases more energy than its separation costs dissolves exothermically, as sodium hydroxide does; one whose separation costs more dissolves endothermically, as ammonium nitrate does, and it can still dissolve because of the increase in dispersal.
concepts.evidence: Figure 11.5’s instant cold pack, and the contrast between calcium carbonate, lye and ammonium nitrate in the text; exercises on KNO<sub>3</sub> growing cold as it dissolves.

concepts.name: Predict whether two substances form a solution
concepts.why: Naming the strongest attractions within the solute, within the solvent and between the two lets us predict whether they will mix and which solvent suits a solute.
concepts.evidence: End-of-section exercises ask for the most important attractions in several solutions and whether oil, isopropyl alcohol and potassium bromide dissolve better in water or heptane.

concepts.name: Electrolytes and nonelectrolytes
concepts.why: An electrolyte yields ions when it dissolves, so its solution conducts electricity; a nonelectrolyte yields none. A strong electrolyte yields ions essentially completely, a weak electrolyte only in small part.
concepts.evidence: Figure 11.6 lights a bulb brightly through KCl solution, dimly through acetic acid and not at all through ethanol.

concepts.name: Ion-dipole attraction
concepts.why: The electrostatic attraction between an ion and a polar molecule turns the negative oxygen ends of water molecules toward a cation and the positive hydrogen ends toward an anion, and it is what lets water pull ions out of a solid.
concepts.evidence: Figure 11.7 draws water molecules oriented around K<sup>+</sup> and Cl<sup>−</sup> ions leaving the surface of solid KCl.

concepts.name: Ionic compounds dissociate
concepts.why: When an ionic compound dissolves, water surrounds and solvates its ions and they disperse through the solution, a physical change called dissociation. Ionic compounds dissociate nearly completely, so even a sparingly soluble one is a strong electrolyte.
concepts.evidence: The text follows solid KCl in water at the microscopic level, and an exercise asks which beaker best shows the ions of Fe(NO<sub>3</sub>)<sub>3</sub>(aq).

concepts.name: Covalent electrolytes react with water
concepts.why: Some covalent compounds conduct once dissolved because their molecules react chemically with water to form ions: a strong acid such as HCl ionizes completely and is a strong electrolyte, while weak acids and bases ionize partly and are weak electrolytes.
concepts.evidence: The ionization of water itself, and HCl transferring H<sup>+</sup> to water to form hydronium and chloride ions, drawn in Lewis structures in the text.

concepts.name: Classify a solute as a strong, weak or nonelectrolyte
concepts.why: Whether a solute is ionic, a strong acid, a weak acid or base, or an unreactive covalent compound tells us how well its solution will conduct.
concepts.evidence: An exercise asks for the expected conductivity of NaOH, HCl, glucose and NH<sub>3</sub> solutions; others contrast water and benzene or hexane as solvents for ions.

concepts.name: Solubility, saturated and unsaturated solutions
concepts.why: The solubility of a solute is the maximum concentration it can reach in a solvent under given conditions when dissolution is at equilibrium. A solution at that concentration is saturated, one below it is unsaturated.
concepts.evidence: The text adds sugar to water until some remains undissolved however long it is stirred.

concepts.name: Supersaturated solutions
concepts.why: A solution can hold more solute than its solubility, a nonequilibrium state that ends in precipitation or loss of gas when it is disturbed. Cooling a saturated solution of a solid, or warming or depressurizing a solution of a gas, can prepare one.
concepts.evidence: An opened carbonated beverage going flat (Figure 11.10), the Lake Nyos disaster (Figure 11.12) and the sodium acetate hand warmer (Figure 11.17).

concepts.name: Gases grow less soluble as temperature rises
concepts.why: Since a gaseous solute has no solute-solute attraction to overcome, only its attraction to the solvent sets its solubility, and that solubility typically decreases as the temperature increases, which is why thermal pollution starves natural waters of oxygen.
concepts.evidence: Figure 11.8 plots the solubilities of methane, oxygen, carbon monoxide, nitrogen and helium falling from 0 °C to 30 °C, and Figure 11.9 shows bubbles in warming water and a fish kill.

concepts.name: Henry’s law
concepts.why: The quantity of an ideal gas that dissolves in a definite volume of liquid is directly proportional to the pressure of the gas, $C_{\text{g}} = kP_{\text{g}}$, with k set by the gas, the solvent and the temperature. A gas that reacts with the solvent, as ammonia does with water, dissolves more than the law predicts.
concepts.evidence: The carbonated beverage of Figure 11.10 and the diver’s blood in the note on decompression sickness.

concepts.name: Calculate a gas solubility with Henry’s law
concepts.why: Finding k from one known solubility and pressure gives the solubility at any other pressure, and a constant read from a solubility graph answers whether a stream holds enough oxygen for its fish.
concepts.evidence: Examples 11.1 and 11.2 with their Check Your Learning, and the keyed exercises on O<sub>2</sub> and CO<sub>2</sub>.

concepts.name: Miscible, immiscible and partially miscible liquids
concepts.why: Liquids of similar polarity mix in all proportions because the attractions between unlike molecules are as strong as those between like ones, an illustration of “like dissolves like”; a nonpolar liquid and water form separate layers, and some pairs are only partially miscible.
concepts.evidence: Antifreeze and water (Figure 11.13), oil floating on water (Figure 11.14), and bromine and water forming two saturated layers (Figure 11.15).

concepts.name: Solubility curves of solids
concepts.why: The solubilities of most solids in water increase with temperature, though some, such as cerium sulfate, decrease, and a solubility curve reads off how much of a solid dissolves in 100 g of water at any temperature.
concepts.evidence: Figure 11.16 plots the solubility curves of sugar and seven salts from 0 °C to 100 °C, and an exercise reads KBr’s solubility at 10 °C from it.

concepts.name: Colligative properties
concepts.why: Vapor pressure lowering, boiling point elevation, freezing point depression and osmotic pressure depend only on the total concentration of solute particles, not on their identity, mass or size.
concepts.evidence: The text compares 1 m solutions of sucrose and ethylene glycol, which boil at the same temperature because each holds one mole of solute particles per kilogram of water.

concepts.name: Molality and mole fraction
concepts.why: Mole fraction is a component’s moles divided by the total moles, and molality is moles of solute per kilogram of solvent; both are built from masses and moles, so, unlike molarity, they do not change with temperature, and each can be converted into the others.
concepts.evidence: Examples 11.3 to 11.5 compute the mole fraction and molality of antifreeze, convert molality to mole fraction, and convert molarity to molality through a density.

concepts.name: Raoult’s law and vapor pressure lowering
concepts.why: The partial pressure of a component of an ideal solution is its mole fraction times the vapor pressure of the pure component, so a nonvolatile solute lowers the vapor pressure of the solvent in proportion to how much it dilutes the solvent.
concepts.evidence: Figure 11.18 contrasts evaporation from pure water and from a solution, and Example 11.6 computes the vapor pressure of glycerin in ethanol.

concepts.name: Distillation
concepts.why: The vapor above a mixture of two volatile liquids is richer in the more volatile one, so heating the mixture and condensing the vapor separates them; a fractionating column repeats the separation many times over.
concepts.evidence: The laboratory still of Figure 11.19 and the crude-oil column of Figure 11.20; Exercise 65 computes the enriched vapor of a methanol-ethanol solution.

concepts.name: Boiling point elevation
concepts.why: Because a nonvolatile solute lowers the vapor pressure, the solution must be hotter than the pure solvent before its vapor pressure reaches the atmosphere’s, and the elevation is proportional to the molality of all solute species, $\Delta T_{\text{b}} = K_{\text{b}}m$.
concepts.evidence: Table 11.2 lists K<sub>b</sub> for five solvents, Examples 11.7 and 11.8 compute boiling points, and Figure 11.23 shows the solution’s liquid-vapor curve lying beneath the solvent’s.

concepts.name: Freezing point depression
concepts.why: A solution freezes at a lower temperature than its pure solvent, by an amount proportional to the molality of all solute species, $\Delta T_{\text{f}} = K_{\text{f}}m$, because only the solvent freezes out; salted roads and antifreeze exploit it.
concepts.evidence: Example 11.9, the note on de-icing (Figures 11.21 and 11.22), and Figure 11.23’s solid-liquid curve displaced to the left.

concepts.name: Osmosis and osmotic pressure
concepts.why: Solvent diffuses through a semipermeable membrane into a solution faster than it returns, until the solution’s rising pressure equalizes the rates; that pressure is the osmotic pressure, $\Pi = MRT$. Applying more pressure reverses osmosis, and a cell swells or shrivels in a hypotonic or hypertonic solution.
concepts.evidence: The U-tubes of Figures 11.24 and 11.25, reverse osmosis in Figure 11.26, red blood cells in Figure 11.27, and Example 11.10’s glucose infusion.

concepts.name: Determine a molar mass from a colligative property
concepts.why: A measured freezing point depression, boiling point elevation or osmotic pressure gives the moles of solute in a known mass, and so the solute’s molar mass.
concepts.evidence: Example 11.11 from a freezing point in benzene and Example 11.12 from the osmotic pressure of hemoglobin, with their Check Your Learning.

concepts.name: Colligative properties of electrolytes and the van’t Hoff factor
concepts.why: An electrolyte yields more than one particle per formula unit, so its colligative effects are multiplied by the van’t Hoff factor i, the moles of particles per mole of formula units; residual attraction between ions, even ion pairs, makes the measured i smaller than predicted.
concepts.evidence: Table 11.3 sets predicted beside measured factors for 0.050 m solutions, Figure 11.28 draws ion pairs, and Example 11.13 finds the freezing point of a seawater-like NaCl solution.

concepts.name: Colloids between solutions and suspensions
concepts.why: A colloid’s particles are larger than most molecules yet small enough not to settle, so a colloid is intermediate between a solution, whose particles are molecules or ions, and a suspension, whose particles settle; colloidal particles scatter light, the Tyndall effect.
concepts.evidence: Figure 11.29 sets saltwater, milk and mud side by side, and Figure 11.30 shows searchlight beams made visible by fog and smoke.

concepts.name: Dispersed phase and dispersion medium
concepts.why: A colloid’s minor, particulate component is the dispersed phase and the substance it is spread through is the dispersion medium, and nearly every combination of states occurs: sols, aerosols, emulsions, foams and gels.
concepts.evidence: Table 11.4 names the colloidal systems by their phases, the gelatin dessert of Figure 11.37 is a gel, and an exercise asks for the phases of starch, smoke, fog, pearl and more.

concepts.name: Preparing colloids and emulsions
concepts.why: Colloidal particles are made by dispersion, grinding larger particles down, or by condensation, growing them from molecules or ions; an emulsion of two immiscible liquids is kept from separating by an emulsifying agent.
concepts.evidence: Paint pigments, clouds, the iron(III) hydroxide and gold sols, and milk and mayonnaise with their emulsifying agents, in the text.

concepts.name: How soaps and detergents clean
concepts.why: Soap and detergent molecules are amphiphilic, a nonpolar hydrocarbon end and an ionic end, so they gather at the boundary between grease and water and suspend the grease as colloidal particles that wash away.
concepts.evidence: Figures 11.31 and 11.32 draw soap and detergent molecules, Figure 11.33 an emulsified drop of oil, and the Deepwater Horizon note the dispersant sprayed on the spill.

concepts.name: Colloidal particles are charged
concepts.why: The particles of one colloid carry charges of the same sign, which keeps them dispersed by repulsion, and highly charged electrodes attract, neutralize and deposit them, as in the Cottrell precipitator that cleans smoke.
concepts.evidence: Iron(III) hydroxide particles bearing a positive charge, and Frederick Cottrell’s precipitator in Figures 11.35 and 11.36.

concepts.name: Gas pressure, $P = F/A$
concepts.why: A gas exerts a pressure on the walls of whatever confines it, because its molecules collide with those walls, and pressure is the force of those collisions divided by the area they act on. A small force on a small area can therefore give a larger pressure than a large force spread over a large one, and every law of the chapter is a statement about how this reading responds when something else about the gas is changed.
concepts.evidence: The section defines pressure as force per unit area with the elephant and the figure skater of Figure 9.3, draws the column of air pressing on a thumbnail in Figure 9.2, and sets end-of-chapter items on sharp knives, bridge weight limits and crawling across thin ice.

concepts.name: Converting among units of pressure
concepts.why: Pressures are reported in pascals, kilopascals, bar, pounds per square inch, atmospheres, torr and millimeters of mercury, depending on who measured them and why. Converting among these units with the relations of Table 9.1 is the first step of nearly every gas calculation, since the gas constant has to be used in units that match the pressure.
concepts.evidence: Table 9.1 lists the units and their relations, Example 9.1 converts 29.2 in. Hg into torr, atm, kPa and mbar, and end-of-chapter items convert the barometric pressures of Denver, Kansas City and Venus and the reading of a Canadian tire gauge.

concepts.name: Atmospheric pressure and the barometer
concepts.why: The weight of the column of air above an object presses on it, and at sea level this atmospheric pressure is about 1 atm. A barometer measures it by balancing it against a column of liquid in an inverted tube, and because mercury is about 13.6 times denser than water, a mercury column of about 760 mm does what a water column over 10 m tall would do.
concepts.evidence: Figure 9.2 draws the column of air above a thumbnail, Figure 9.4 compares the mercury and water barometers, and the text relates 1 atm to 760 mm of mercury; an exercise asks why a barometer must use a nonvolatile liquid.

concepts.name: Hydrostatic pressure, $p = h\rho g$
concepts.why: The pressure exerted by a column of fluid because of gravity is the product of its height, its density and the acceleration due to gravity. It is why the height of a liquid column can stand for a pressure at all, and it lets us check that 760 mm of mercury does correspond to 101,325 Pa.
concepts.evidence: The section states p = hρg, works Example 9.2 on the 760-mm mercury column, and its Check Your Learning asks for the height of a water column that normal atmospheric pressure supports.

concepts.name: Reading a gas pressure from a manometer
concepts.why: A manometer is a U-shaped tube of liquid connected to a gas. In a closed-end manometer the difference in liquid levels is the pressure of the gas itself; in an open-end manometer it is the difference between the gas pressure and the atmospheric pressure, added when the level is higher on the open side and subtracted when it is higher on the gas side.
concepts.evidence: Figure 9.5 draws the closed-end and both open-end cases with their equations, Examples 9.3 and 9.4 read a closed-end and an open-end manometer, and four end-of-chapter items read further manometers and ask how a volatile liquid would affect each kind.

concepts.name: Amontons’s law, $P_1/T_1 = P_2/T_2$
concepts.why: The pressure of a given amount of gas is directly proportional to its temperature on the kelvin scale when the volume is held constant. This is the first of the four relationships the section establishes, and it is the one that explains why a sealed can warns against heat: the gas inside cannot expand, so everything the heating does shows up on the gauge.
concepts.evidence: The section states the law under both of its names, draws the sealed sphere over a hot plate in Figure 9.10 and the measured pressure-temperature line for air in Figure 9.11, works Example 9.5 on the hair spray can left in a hot car, and sets end-of-chapter items on the spray can thrown into a fire and on what doubling the temperature at constant volume does to the pressure.

concepts.name: Charles’s law, $V_1/T_1 = V_2/T_2$
concepts.why: The volume of a given amount of gas is directly proportional to its temperature on the kelvin scale when the pressure is held constant. It is the law a balloon in a refrigerator demonstrates, and it is the one that makes a gas thermometer possible, since a volume read at a known pressure is a temperature.
concepts.evidence: The section states the law, graphs the volume of one mole of methane against temperature in Figure 9.12, works Example 9.6 on carbon dioxide warmed from 10 °C to 30 °C and Example 9.7 on a hydrogen gas thermometer in boiling ammonia, and sets items on hydrogen warmed from –196 °C and on reading a volume off the figure’s own line.

concepts.name: Boyle’s law, $P_1V_1 = P_2V_2$
concepts.why: The volume of a given amount of gas held at constant temperature is inversely proportional to the pressure under which it is measured. Unlike the two laws before it this one is not a direct proportionality, and the section uses it to make a second point as well: a curve is hard to read, so plotting the inverse of the pressure against the volume turns the same data into a straight line.
concepts.evidence: The section states the law, draws the syringe with its gauge and both graphs in Figure 9.13 and the two graphs alone in Figure 9.14, works Example 9.8 by reading a pressure off each graph and then computing it, keeps the Breathing and Boyle’s Law note with Figure 9.15, and sets items on a diver’s bubbles rising, on what tripling the volume does to the pressure, and on reading the syringe at 12.5 mL.

concepts.name: Avogadro’s law, $V_1/n_1 = V_2/n_2$
concepts.why: For a confined gas at constant pressure and temperature, the volume and the number of moles are directly proportional, which is another way of saying that equal volumes of all gases under the same conditions contain the same number of molecules. It is the law that makes the identity of the gas irrelevant, and it is what lets a volume stand in for a count in every gas calculation that follows.
concepts.evidence: The section states Avogadro’s hypothesis and the law it became, shows one mole each of helium, ammonia and oxygen filling the same volume in Figure 9.18, and sets items on a balloon inflated with more breaths of air, on what directly proportional means and what must be held equal, and on why a litre of methane holds more hydrogen atoms than a litre of hydrogen.

concepts.name: Absolute zero
concepts.why: Both of the section’s direct proportionalities hold only when the temperature is read on the kelvin scale, and the reason is visible on their graphs: extrapolated to lower temperatures, the pressure line and the volume line both reach zero at –273 °C. That temperature is zero on the kelvin scale and the lowest there is, and it is why a gas law calculation in Celsius gives the wrong answer.
concepts.evidence: The section defines absolute zero in the glossary and in the text, and the captions of Figure 9.11 and Figure 9.12 both follow the extrapolated line to the origin, noting that measurements stop where the gas condenses.

concepts.name: The ideal gas
concepts.why: An ideal gas is a hypothetical construct whose properties are described exactly by the gas laws, and no real gas is one. Saying so is not a technicality: it tells the reader when the equation may be trusted, which is at relatively low pressures and high temperatures, and the book is careful to point out where one of its own examples strains that assumption.
concepts.evidence: The section defines ideal behavior and the ideal gas, says that the assumption is reasonable only at low pressure and high temperature, and notes in Example 9.10 that a scuba tank at 153 atm is a case where the assumption is not very reasonable and the answer is a ballpark estimate.

concepts.name: The ideal gas law, $PV = nRT$
concepts.why: Combining the four separate laws yields one equation relating the pressure, volume, amount and temperature of a gas, with the gas constant R carrying the units. It contains five terms, so specifying any four of them gives the fifth, and this single relation replaces the four laws for every calculation the rest of the chapter makes.
concepts.evidence: The section lists the four laws as constant ratios, combines them into PV = nRT, names the two common values of R and explains that the units chosen decide which is used, and works Example 9.9 on the volume of 655 g of methane at 25 °C and 745 torr; a dozen end-of-chapter items solve for a volume, a pressure, an amount, a temperature or a mass from the other four terms.

concepts.name: The combined gas law, $P_1V_1/T_1 = P_2V_2/T_2$
concepts.why: When the amount of gas is the same under two different sets of conditions, both sides of the ideal gas law equal the same product of n and R, so the pressure, volume and temperature of the first condition may be set against those of the second directly. It is the form every two-state gas problem takes, and it contains Amontons’s, Charles’s and Boyle’s laws as the cases where one of the three quantities does not change.
concepts.evidence: The section derives the relation from the ideal gas law with the moles held constant and works Example 9.10 on a scuba tank emptied into a diver’s lungs at a different pressure and temperature, and items on a high altitude balloon, a cylinder of medical oxygen and a balloon clearing Mount Crumpit are solved the same way.

concepts.name: Standard temperature and pressure, and the standard molar volume
concepts.why: Because the volume of a gas depends on the conditions it is measured under, chemists agree on one set of conditions to report against: 273.15 K and 1 atm. At those conditions one mole of any ideal gas occupies about 22.4 L, which is a number worth carrying, since it turns a volume of gas straight into an amount without the equation.
concepts.evidence: The section defines standard conditions and the standard molar volume, footnotes the change of the IUPAC standard pressure to 1 bar and says which definition the text uses, draws the three one-mole balloons of Figure 9.18, and sets items on the volumes occupied by 10.0 g of two refrigerants at STP and on the hydrogen atoms in a litre of methane at STP.

concepts.name: The density of a gas, $d = \mathcal{M}P/RT$
concepts.why: Substituting the ideal gas law into the definition of density shows that the density of a gas is its molar mass times its pressure divided by RT. Unlike the ideal gas law itself, this relation depends on the identity of the gas, so a density measured at a known temperature and pressure can identify a gas, and a heavier gas is denser than a lighter one under the same conditions.
concepts.evidence: The section derives d = ℳP/RT, works Example 9.11 on the density of nitrogen at STP, and sets items on the densities of laughing gas and Freon 12 and on whether dry or humid air is denser.

concepts.name: Finding the molar mass of a gas from its mass, pressure, volume, and temperature
concepts.why: When a gas is unknown, measuring the mass, pressure, volume and temperature of a sample gives its molar mass through ℳ = mRT/PV. Compared with the mass of an empirical formula, that molar mass tells how many formula units make up a molecule, and the same measurement made on the vapor of a volatile liquid gives the liquid's molar mass.
concepts.evidence: Example 9.12 finds the molecular formula of cyclopropane, Example 9.13 finds the molar mass of chloroform with the flask of Figure 9.19, and end-of-chapter items find the molar masses and formulas of several gases, including a fluoride of phosphorus from its density at STP.

concepts.name: Dalton’s law of partial pressures
concepts.why: Unless they react, the gases in a mixture do not affect one another’s pressure: each exerts the pressure it would exert alone in the container, and the total pressure of the mixture is the sum of these partial pressures. The partial pressure of each gas can therefore be found from the ideal gas law using its own amount.
concepts.evidence: Figure 9.20 combines three cylinders at 300, 450 and 600 kPa into one at 1350 kPa, Example 9.14 finds the partial and total pressures of hydrogen, helium and neon in one vessel, and items ask for the pressure in a cylinder of calibration gas and whether a hydrogen and oxygen mixture is explosive.

concepts.name: Partial pressure from mole fraction, $P_A = X_A P_{Total}$
concepts.why: The mole fraction of a gas in a mixture is its number of moles divided by the total number of moles, and its partial pressure is that fraction of the total pressure. The relation lets us move between the composition of a mixture and the pressures of its components without computing each pressure from the ideal gas law.
concepts.evidence: The section defines the mole fraction, Example 9.15 finds the mole fractions and partial pressures of oxygen and nitrous oxide in an anesthetic mixture, and items find the partial pressures of the components of a petroleum gas from its percentages.

concepts.name: The pressure of a gas collected over water
concepts.why: A gas collected in an inverted bottle over water is saturated with water vapor, so the pressure it shows when the water levels are equal is the sum of its own partial pressure and the vapor pressure of water at that temperature. The pressure of the dry gas is the total pressure minus the vapor pressure of water, read from Table 9.2.
concepts.evidence: Figure 9.21 draws the collection apparatus and Figure 9.22 and Table 9.2 give the vapor pressure of water, Example 9.16 finds the partial pressure of argon collected at 26 °C, and an item finds the pressure of carbon monoxide collected at 18 °C.

concepts.name: Gases react in simple proportions by volume
concepts.why: Because equal volumes of ideal gases at the same temperature and pressure contain equal numbers of molecules, the volumes of gases that react or form are in the same ratio as the coefficients of the balanced equation. A volume of one gas can then be turned into the volume of another without passing through moles, provided both are measured under the same conditions.
concepts.evidence: Figure 9.23 shows one volume of nitrogen and three of hydrogen giving two of ammonia, Examples 9.17 and 9.18 find the volumes of oxygen for propane and of hydrogen for ammonia from the coefficients, and items find the oxygen needed to burn ethane and the volumes in the oxidation of NO.

concepts.name: Stoichiometry of reactions that produce or consume gases
concepts.why: When a reaction involves a gas, the ideal gas law turns a measured volume, pressure and temperature into moles, and moles of gas back into a volume under any conditions. With the mole ratios of the balanced equation, this links the mass of a solid or liquid reactant to the volume of a gas produced or consumed.
concepts.evidence: Example 9.19 finds the volume of hydrogen at 27 °C and 723 torr released by 8.88 g of gallium, its Check Your Learning the volume of sulfur dioxide from burning sulfur, and a run of items outline and answer such problems for Priestley’s oxygen, recycled chlorofluorocarbons and lime.

concepts.name: Mean free path
concepts.why: Gas molecules travel at hundreds of meters per second but collide billions of times a second, so each travels only a short average distance, the mean free path, between collisions. The mean free path grows as the pressure falls, and it is why a smell takes time to cross a room although the molecules carrying it move so fast.
concepts.evidence: The section opens with the aroma of a pizza spreading through a room, defines the mean free path in the text and the glossary, and says it is generally hundreds of times the diameter of a molecule.

concepts.name: Diffusion and effusion
concepts.why: Diffusion is the dispersal of molecules through space from regions of higher concentration to regions of lower concentration, which happens because the molecules move randomly and there are more of them to move away from a crowded region. Effusion is the escape of gas molecules through a tiny hole into a vacuum. The rates of the two processes differ, but for two gases the ratio of their rates is the same.
concepts.evidence: Figure 9.27 opens a stopcock between hydrogen and oxygen, Figure 9.28 contrasts diffusion with effusion, and an item asks why the two bulbs hold different numbers of molecules just after the stopcock is opened.

concepts.name: Graham’s law of effusion
concepts.why: The rate of effusion of a gas is inversely proportional to the square root of its molar mass, so for two gases at the same temperature and pressure the ratio of their rates is the inverse ratio of the square roots of their molar masses. Lighter gases escape faster, which is why a helium balloon goes flat before an argon balloon does.
concepts.evidence: The section states Graham’s law, shows the helium and argon balloons of Figure 9.29, works Example 9.20 on hydrogen effusing four times as fast as oxygen, and keeps the note on enriching uranium by diffusion with Figure 9.30.

concepts.name: Using Graham’s law for effusion times and molar masses
concepts.why: Since the time for a given amount of gas to effuse is inversely proportional to its rate, the effusion times of two gases are in the direct ratio of the square roots of their molar masses. Graham’s law can then give an unknown effusion time, or a molar mass from a measured ratio of rates, which is a way of identifying a gas.
concepts.evidence: Example 9.21 finds the effusion time of neon from that of xenon, Example 9.22 finds a molar mass of 16.0 g/mol for a gas effusing 1.66 times as fast as CO2, and items find the time for a hydrogen balloon to deflate and where the ring of ammonium chloride forms in a glass tube.

concepts.name: The postulates of the kinetic-molecular theory
concepts.why: The kinetic-molecular theory explains the empirical gas laws with a microscopic model of five postulates: gas molecules move continuously in straight lines, they are negligibly small compared with the distances between them, their collisions with the walls cause the pressure, they exert no forces on one another so that their collisions are elastic, and their average kinetic energy is proportional to the kelvin temperature.
concepts.evidence: The section lists the five postulates, and items ask how they explain why a gas fills a container of any shape and whether the speed of one molecule can double at constant temperature.

concepts.name: How the kinetic-molecular theory explains the gas laws
concepts.why: Each gas law follows from the theory when pressure is read as the frequency and force of molecular collisions with the walls. Heating a gas at constant volume makes the collisions faster and more forceful, so the pressure rises; compressing it makes collisions with the smaller wall area more frequent; and adding molecules at constant pressure requires a larger volume to keep the collisions per unit area the same.
concepts.evidence: The section explains Amontons’s, Charles’s, Boyle’s, Avogadro’s and Dalton’s laws in turn, draws three of them in Figure 9.31, and an item asks what happens to the average kinetic energy when the pressure is raised by compression or by heating.

concepts.name: The distribution of molecular speeds
concepts.why: The molecules of a gas move at widely varying speeds, but because there are so many of them the distribution of speeds is constant at a given temperature. It rises to a most probable speed and then falls off, shifts to higher speeds and flattens as the temperature rises, and lies at higher speeds for lighter molecules than for heavier ones at the same temperature.
concepts.evidence: Figure 9.32 draws the distribution for oxygen at 300 K with its most probable and root mean square speeds, Figure 9.33 draws nitrogen at four temperatures, Figure 9.34 draws four noble gases, and an item asks whether cooled helium would look more like H2 or H2O.

concepts.name: Average kinetic energy and temperature, $\text{KE}_{\text{avg}} = \tfrac{3}{2}RT$
concepts.why: The average kinetic energy of a mole of gas molecules is directly proportional to the kelvin temperature and does not depend on what the gas is. At a given temperature, then, all gases have the same average kinetic energy, and heavier molecules must move more slowly on average to have it.
concepts.evidence: The section states KE_avg = 3/2 RT with R = 8.314 J/mol·K, and items ask for the effect of heating CO from STP to 546 K on the average kinetic energy and for the ratio of the average kinetic energies of SO2 and O2 in a mixture.

concepts.name: The root mean square speed, $u_{\text{rms}} = \sqrt{3RT/\mathcal{M}}$
concepts.why: The root mean square speed is the square root of the average of the squared speeds of the molecules. Setting the two expressions for the average kinetic energy equal shows that it grows with the square root of the kelvin temperature and falls with the square root of the molar mass, which must be written in kilograms per mole.
concepts.evidence: The section defines u_rms and derives u_rms = √(3RT/ℳ), Example 9.23 finds 519 m/s for nitrogen at 30 °C, and items find the effect of doubling the temperature and the speed of nitrogen from that of hydrogen.

concepts.name: Graham’s law derived from the kinetic-molecular theory
concepts.why: The rate of effusion of a gas depends directly on the average speed of its molecules, and the root mean square speed is inversely proportional to the square root of the molar mass. The ratio of the effusion rates of two gases is therefore the inverse ratio of the square roots of their molar masses, which is Graham’s law obtained from the theory rather than from experiment.
concepts.evidence: The section’s last part derives the ratio of effusion rates from u_rms = √(3RT/ℳ), and items ask for this derivation and for a proof that the ratio of two rates of diffusion is the same at 0 °C and 100 °C.

concepts.name: The compressibility factor, Z
concepts.why: The compressibility factor is the ratio of the measured molar volume of a gas to the molar volume of an ideal gas at the same temperature and pressure, (PV_m/RT) measured. It equals 1 for an ideal gas, so its departure from 1 measures how far a real gas departs from the ideal gas law.
concepts.evidence: The section defines Z, Figure 9.35 plots it against pressure up to 1000 atm for several gases, and an item asks what the graph of Z against pressure would look like for an ideal gas.

concepts.name: Why real gases depart from ideal behavior
concepts.why: Real gas molecules occupy some volume and attract one another. At high pressures the volume of the molecules themselves becomes an appreciable part of the whole, so the gas is less compressible than an ideal gas; at moderate pressures and low temperatures the attractions pull the molecules together, lowering the pressure at constant volume or the volume at constant pressure.
concepts.evidence: The section explains both effects, Figure 9.36 compares ideal and real gases at constant pressure and at constant volume, the dips and rises of Figure 9.35 are read in these terms, and items ask which gas needs the largest volume correction and what factors cause the deviations.

concepts.name: When a gas behaves ideally
concepts.why: The ideal gas law describes a gas well when intermolecular attractions are negligible and the molecules occupy a negligible part of the volume, which is the case at low pressure and high temperature. It is this, and not a property of any particular gas, that justifies treating gases as ideal in most of the chapter’s calculations.
concepts.evidence: The section states the conditions of low pressure and high temperature, and items ask which of three sets of conditions gives the most ideal behavior and whether treating gases as ideal was justified.

concepts.name: The van der Waals equation
concepts.why: The van der Waals equation corrects the ideal gas law with two constants of each gas: a, for the attraction between molecules, adds n²a/V² to the pressure, and b, for the size of the molecules, subtracts nb from the volume. When the volume is large and the amount small, both corrections vanish and the equation reduces to PV = nRT.
concepts.evidence: The section introduces the equation with its two corrections, Table 9.3 lists a and b for six gases, and Example 9.24 compares the pressure of CO2 in a 4.25-L flask from the ideal gas law, 33.5 atm, and from the van der Waals equation, 32.4 atm.

concepts.name: The rate of a reaction
concepts.why: The rate of a reaction is the change in the amount or concentration of a reactant or product per unit time. Since a reactant’s concentration falls as the reaction proceeds, its change is multiplied by −1 so that the rate is, by convention, a positive quantity.
concepts.evidence: The decomposition of hydrogen peroxide in Figure 12.2, followed every 6 hours at 40 °C, gives a rate that falls from 0.0833 to 0.010 mol L⁻¹ h⁻¹ over a day.

concepts.name: Average, instantaneous, and initial rates
concepts.why: A rate computed over a time interval is an average rate; the rate at one instant is the instantaneous rate, the slope of the tangent to the concentration curve at that time, and the instantaneous rate at time zero is the initial rate. Like a car slowing toward a stop sign, a reaction’s average rate falls between its initial and final rates.
concepts.evidence: Figure 12.3 draws tangents to the hydrogen peroxide curve at t = 0 h and at t = 12 h.

concepts.name: Calculating an average rate from concentration and time data
concepts.why: Dividing the change in concentration by the time interval over which it occurred, and changing the sign for a reactant, gives the average rate over that interval.
concepts.evidence: The text computes 0.0833 mol L⁻¹ h⁻¹ for the first 6-hour period of Figure 12.2 and 0.010 mol L⁻¹ h⁻¹ for the last.

concepts.name: Rates of change are related by the stoichiometry
concepts.why: For aA ⟶ bB, the rate may be written from either species, and the two expressions agree once each change is divided by its coefficient: $\text{rate}=-\frac{1}{a}\frac{\Delta[\text{A}]}{\Delta t}=\frac{1}{b}\frac{\Delta[\text{B}]}{\Delta t}$.
concepts.evidence: Figure 12.5 shows the tangents at 500 s for the decomposition of ammonia, where hydrogen forms three times as fast as nitrogen.

concepts.name: Writing the related rate expressions for a reaction
concepts.why: From a balanced equation, the rates of consumption of reactants and formation of products may be written as equal once each is divided by its coefficient, so a rate measured for one species gives the rate for every other.
concepts.evidence: Example 12.1 writes the expressions for the combustion of ammonia, and Example 12.2 finds the rates of production of water and oxygen from the rate of decomposition of hydrogen peroxide.

concepts.name: The nature of the reactants affects the rate
concepts.why: Reactions that appear similar may proceed at very different rates under the same conditions, depending on the identity of the reactants.
concepts.evidence: Sodium reacts completely with air overnight while iron is barely affected, and sodium reacts almost explosively with water while calcium reacts at a moderate rate.

concepts.name: Subdivision and the physical state of the reactants
concepts.why: A reaction between reactants in different phases takes place only at the interface between them, so a finely divided solid, with its greater surface area, reacts faster than one large piece.
concepts.evidence: Figure 12.6 compares iron powder and an iron nail in dilute hydrochloric acid; wood smolders, burns rapidly or burns explosively as it is divided more finely.

concepts.name: Higher temperatures speed reactions
concepts.why: Chemical reactions typically occur faster at higher temperatures, and for many processes the rate roughly doubles when the temperature is raised by 10 °C.
concepts.evidence: Food spoils on the kitchen counter but keeps for days in a refrigerator.

concepts.name: Higher concentrations usually speed reactions
concepts.why: The rates of many reactions increase when the concentration of one or more reactants increases.
concepts.evidence: Figure 12.7 shows a limestone statue weathered by sulfur dioxide, which attacks it faster in polluted air, and phosphorus burns faster in pure oxygen than in air.

concepts.name: A catalyst increases the rate of a reaction
concepts.why: A catalyst is a substance that increases the rate of a reaction without itself being consumed by it.
concepts.evidence: Hydrogen peroxide decomposes slowly on the shelf but foams on an open wound, where substances in the tissue accelerate its decomposition.

concepts.name: The rate law, $\text{rate}=k[\text{A}]^{m}[\text{B}]^{n}$
concepts.why: A rate law relates the rate of a reaction to the concentrations of its reactants, each raised to a power called its order, multiplied by a rate constant. The concentration of a reactant whose order is zero does not appear, since any number raised to the zero power is 1.
concepts.evidence: Example 12.3 writes the rate law for NO₂ with CO, second order in NO₂ and zero order in CO.

concepts.name: Reaction orders and the overall order
concepts.why: The exponent of a reactant’s concentration in the rate law is the order with respect to that reactant, and the overall order is the sum of these orders. Orders are usually 0, 1 or 2, but they may be fractional or negative.
concepts.evidence: rate = k[H₂O₂] is first order overall, rate = k[C₄H₆]² second order, and rate = k[H⁺][OH⁻] first order in each ion and second order overall.

concepts.name: The rate constant
concepts.why: The rate constant k is specific to a particular reaction at a particular temperature; it does not depend on the reactant concentrations, but it does vary with temperature.
concepts.evidence: Example 12.4 finds k = 2.20 × 10⁷ L mol⁻¹ s⁻¹ for the reaction of nitric oxide with ozone at 25 °C.

concepts.name: Rate laws come from experiment, not from the equation
concepts.why: The orders in a rate law must be found by observing how the rate changes with concentration; they sometimes match the coefficients of the balanced equation, but only by coincidence.
concepts.evidence: The rate laws listed in the section, among them rate = k[NO₂]² for NO₂ + CO and rate = k[N₂O₅] for the decomposition of 2N₂O₅, do not follow their coefficients.

concepts.name: Finding a rate law by the method of initial rates
concepts.why: Comparing initial rates from trials in which one reactant’s concentration changes while the others are held fixed gives each order, from the ratio of rates or by logarithms; one trial’s data then give the rate constant.
concepts.evidence: Examples 12.4 and 12.5 derive the rate laws for nitric oxide with ozone and for nitric oxide with chlorine.

concepts.name: The units of a rate constant
concepts.why: The unit of k is whatever makes the rate come out in mol L⁻¹ s⁻¹, so it depends on the overall order x as L^(x−1) mol^(1−x) s⁻¹.
concepts.evidence: Table 12.1 lists the units for zero-, first-, second- and third-order reactions.

concepts.name: Using a rate law to predict a rate
concepts.why: With a rate law and its rate constant, the rate at any set of concentrations may be calculated, and the effect of changing one concentration follows from its order.
concepts.evidence: The end-of-section exercises predict how the rate of CO with NO₂ changes when the concentration of NO₂ is halved and when that of CO is tripled.

concepts.name: Integrated rate laws relate concentration to time
concepts.why: Integrating a differential rate law gives an equation relating the concentration of a reactant to the elapsed time, which tells how much reactant remains after a period or how long a reaction takes to reach a given extent.
concepts.evidence: The text uses one to find how long a radioactive material must be stored before its radioactivity decays to a safe level.

concepts.name: The first-order integrated rate law
concepts.why: For rate = k[A], the concentration falls exponentially, $[\text{A}]_{t}=[\text{A}]_{0}e^{-kt}$, so $\ln[\text{A}]_{t}=-kt+\ln[\text{A}]_{0}$ and a plot of ln[A] against t is a straight line of slope −k.
concepts.evidence: Example 12.7 plots ln[H₂O₂] against time in Figure 12.9, a straight line whose slope gives k = 0.116 h⁻¹.

concepts.name: The second-order integrated rate law
concepts.why: For rate = k[A]², $\frac{1}{[\text{A}]_{t}}=kt+\frac{1}{[\text{A}]_{0}}$, so a plot of 1/[A] against t is a straight line of slope k.
concepts.evidence: Figure 12.10 plots the dimerization of butadiene both ways; only the plot of 1/[C₄H₆] is linear.

concepts.name: The zero-order integrated rate law
concepts.why: For rate = k, the concentration falls linearly, $[\text{A}]_{t}=-kt+[\text{A}]_{0}$, and a plot of [A] against t is a straight line of slope −k. Zero-order behavior is seen only under certain conditions.
concepts.evidence: Figure 12.11 shows ammonia decomposing linearly on tungsten but exponentially on quartz.

concepts.name: Finding the order and rate constant from a linear plot
concepts.why: Plotting [A], ln[A] and 1/[A] against time shows which is a straight line, which gives the order; the rate constant is then the slope or its negative.
concepts.evidence: Examples 12.7, 12.9 and 12.10 find the orders and rate constants for hydrogen peroxide, butadiene and ammonia on tungsten.

concepts.name: The half-life of a reaction
concepts.why: The half-life is the time required for one-half of a given amount of reactant to be consumed; in each succeeding half-life, half of the remaining reactant is consumed.
concepts.evidence: Figure 12.12 follows hydrogen peroxide as its concentration halves every 2.16 × 10⁴ s.

concepts.name: Half-lives for zero-, first-, and second-order reactions
concepts.why: The half-life of a first-order reaction, $t_{1/2}=0.693/k$, is independent of concentration; that of a second-order reaction, $1/k[\text{A}]_{0}$, grows as the reactant is used up, and that of a zero-order reaction, $[\text{A}]_{0}/2k$, shrinks.
concepts.evidence: Table 12.2 sets the three side by side, and Examples 12.11 and 12.12 use them for hydrogen peroxide and butadiene.

concepts.name: Calculating concentrations, times, and half-lives
concepts.why: Choosing the integrated rate law of the reaction’s order and solving it for the unknown gives the concentration remaining after a time, the time to reach a concentration, or the half-life.
concepts.evidence: Example 12.6 finds how long 80.0% of cyclobutane takes to decompose, and Example 12.8 the butadiene remaining after 10.0 min.

concepts.name: Collision theory
