concepts.why: Reactant species must collide in order to react, so the rate of a reaction is proportional to the rate of collisions, and a collision leads to reaction only when it has a suitable orientation and enough energy. More molecules per unit volume mean more collisions, which is why rates rise with concentration.
concepts.evidence: The section sets out the three postulates and applies them to carbon monoxide and oxygen.

concepts.name: The orientation of a collision
concepts.why: The colliding species must meet in an orientation that brings together the atoms that will bond in the product.
concepts.evidence: Figure 12.13 shows carbon monoxide striking oxygen with its oxygen end and with its carbon end; only the second can form O=C=O.

concepts.name: Activation energy and the transition state
concepts.why: The activation energy is the minimum energy a collision needs to form products; a collision with enough energy and the proper orientation forms an unstable, short-lived activated complex, or transition state. A reaction is slow when its activation energy is much larger than the average kinetic energy of the molecules.
concepts.evidence: Figure 12.14 draws the activation energy as the rise from the reactants to the transition state.

concepts.name: Reading a reaction diagram
concepts.why: A reaction diagram traces the energy of a system from reactants through the transition state to products; the activation energy is the height of the peak above the reactants, and ΔH is the difference between products and reactants.
concepts.evidence: Figure 12.14 is the diagram for an exothermic reaction A + B ⟶ C + D.

concepts.name: The fraction of molecules with enough energy
concepts.why: Of the molecules’ distribution of energies, only those above the activation energy can react; a lower activation energy or a higher temperature increases that fraction and so the rate.
concepts.evidence: Figure 12.15 shades the molecules above two activation energies at one temperature, and above one activation energy at two temperatures.

concepts.name: The Arrhenius equation, $k=Ae^{-E_{\text{a}}/RT}$
concepts.why: The rate constant depends on the frequency factor A, which reflects how often molecules collide in a favorable orientation, and on the exponential term, which is the effect of the activation energy and the temperature.
concepts.evidence: The section reads each factor of the equation against the postulates of collision theory.

concepts.name: Finding an activation energy from rate constants at different temperatures
concepts.why: A plot of ln k against 1/T is a straight line of slope −E_a/R, and rate constants at just two temperatures give E_a through the two-point form of the Arrhenius equation.
concepts.evidence: Example 12.13 finds 180 kJ/mol for the decomposition of hydrogen iodide both ways, from the plot of Figure 12.16 and from two data pairs.

concepts.name: Reaction mechanisms, elementary reactions, and intermediates
concepts.why: A reaction mechanism is the step-by-step sequence of elementary reactions by which a reaction occurs; the steps sum to the overall equation, and an intermediate is produced in one step and consumed in a later one.
concepts.evidence: Ozone decomposes in two steps whose oxygen atom is an intermediate, so no two ozone molecules ever collide directly.

concepts.name: Molecularity: unimolecular, bimolecular, and termolecular reactions
concepts.why: The molecularity of an elementary reaction is the number of reactant entities in it; termolecular steps are uncommon because three particles rarely collide at once.
concepts.evidence: The decomposition of cyclobutane is unimolecular, NO₂ with CO in Figure 12.17 is bimolecular, and 2NO + O₂ appears to be termolecular.

concepts.name: The rate law of an elementary reaction follows from its equation
concepts.why: Since an elementary reaction occurs exactly as written, its rate law may be written from its equation: first order for a unimolecular step, rate = k[A][B] or k[A]² for a bimolecular one.
concepts.evidence: The first-order rate law predicted for the decomposition of cyclobutane agrees with the one measured.

concepts.name: The rate-determining step
concepts.why: A reaction cannot proceed faster than its slowest step, so that step limits the overall rate; when it is the first step, the overall rate law is its rate law.
concepts.evidence: Figure 12.18’s cattle chute, and the two-step mechanism for NO₂ with CO below 225 °C, whose slow first step gives rate = k[NO₂]².

concepts.name: Testing a mechanism against the measured rate law
concepts.why: A rate law is determined by experiment and a mechanism deduced from it; a mechanism whose predicted rate law disagrees with the measured one is incorrect, and one that agrees is plausible.
concepts.evidence: NO₂ with CO follows a single bimolecular step above 225 °C but not below it, where the rate law changes.

concepts.name: Deriving a rate law from a mechanism
concepts.why: The rate law of the rate-determining step is the overall rate law; when it contains an intermediate, a fast, reversible earlier step at equilibrium expresses the intermediate’s concentration in terms of the reactants.
concepts.evidence: Example 12.14 derives rate = (k₂k₁/k₋₁)[NO]²[Cl₂] for nitrogen monoxide and chlorine.

concepts.name: A catalyst provides a path of lower activation energy
concepts.why: A catalyst speeds a reaction by providing a different mechanism whose rate-determining step has a lower activation energy; it takes part in the reaction but is regenerated, so the overall reaction and the energies of reactants and products are unchanged.
concepts.evidence: Figure 12.19 draws the uncatalyzed one-step path and the catalyzed two-step path for one endothermic reaction; in the NO-catalyzed decomposition of ozone, NO is consumed in the first step and returned in the last.

concepts.name: Identifying the catalyzed path on reaction diagrams
concepts.why: Of two reaction diagrams for the same reaction, the one with the lower activation energy for its rate-determining step is the catalyzed one.
concepts.evidence: Example 12.15 finds 26 kJ and 14 kJ for its two diagrams and names the second as catalyzed.

concepts.name: Homogeneous catalysts
concepts.why: A homogeneous catalyst is in the same phase as the reactants; it forms an intermediate that reacts further to give product and regenerate the catalyst.
concepts.evidence: Nitric oxide and chlorine atoms catalyze the decomposition of ozone in the upper atmosphere, the work for which Mario Molina shared the 1995 Nobel Prize.

concepts.name: Heterogeneous catalysts
concepts.why: A heterogeneous catalyst is in a different phase, usually a solid, and furnishes a surface on which reactants are adsorbed, activated and react before the products desorb.
concepts.evidence: Figure 12.23 follows ethylene and hydrogen on nickel, and the automobile catalytic converter of Figure 12.24 uses platinum and rhodium.

concepts.name: Enzymes as biological catalysts
concepts.why: Enzymes are usually proteins that catalyze specific reactions of cellular metabolism by binding a substrate at an active site, in the lock-and-key or the induced fit model.
concepts.evidence: Table 12.3 lists the classes of enzymes, Figure 12.25 draws the two models, and G6PD deficiency shows what the lack of one enzyme costs.

concepts.name: Reversible reactions
concepts.why: A reversible reaction may proceed in both the forward (left to right) and reverse (right to left) directions, and a special double arrow is used in its equation to emphasize this.
concepts.evidence: Colorless dinitrogen tetroxide decomposes to brown nitrogen dioxide, and nitrogen dioxide combines to form dinitrogen tetroxide, in the sealed tube of Figure 13.2: N2O4(g) ⇌ 2NO2(g).

concepts.name: Equilibrium is reached when the forward and reverse rates are equal
concepts.why: As a reversible reaction proceeds, the falling reactant concentration slows the forward reaction and the rising product concentration speeds the reverse reaction. When the two rates become equal, the concentrations of reactants and products remain constant and the system is at equilibrium.
concepts.evidence: Figure 13.2 plots the concentrations and the two rates, $\text{rate}_{f}=k_{f}[\text{N}_{2}\text{O}_{4}]$ and $\text{rate}_{r}=k_{r}[\text{NO}_{2}]^{2}$, against time until they level off.

concepts.name: Equilibria are dynamic
concepts.why: A reaction at equilibrium has not stopped; it is proceeding in the forward and reverse directions at the same rate. Physical changes such as phase transitions establish such equilibria too, and the concentrations at equilibrium need not be equal, only constant.
concepts.evidence: The two jugglers of Figure 13.3 throw and catch clubs at the same rate, and the sealed tube of Figure 13.4 holds liquid and gaseous bromine vaporizing and condensing at equal rates.

concepts.name: The reaction quotient, $Q$
concepts.why: The reaction quotient is derived directly from the stoichiometry of the balanced equation: product concentrations raised to their coefficients, divided by reactant concentrations raised to theirs. Its value changes as the reaction proceeds, so it serves as an indicator of the reaction’s status.
concepts.evidence: For 2SO<sub>2</sub> + O<sub>2</sub> ⇌ 2SO<sub>3</sub>, Figure 13.5 shows $Q_{c}$ rising from zero when the reaction starts from reactants and falling from an undefined value when it starts from product.

concepts.name: Writing reaction quotient expressions
concepts.why: From a balanced equation we can write $Q_{c}$ using molar concentrations or, for gases, $Q_{P}$ using partial pressures, including terms only for gaseous and solute species.
concepts.evidence: Example 13.1 writes the concentration-based reaction quotients for the formation of ozone, the synthesis of ammonia and the oxidation of ammonia.

concepts.name: The equilibrium constant and the law of mass action
concepts.why: The constant value of $Q$ exhibited by a system at equilibrium is the equilibrium constant, $K$. At a given temperature it has the same value whichever way the equilibrium is approached, which is the law of mass action.
concepts.evidence: Both scenarios of Figure 13.5 end at the same $K_{c}$, and Example 13.2 evaluates $K_{c}=0.042/0.016^{2}=1.6\times10^{2}$ for the dimerization of NO<sub>2</sub>.

concepts.name: What the magnitude of $K$ tells us
concepts.why: A reaction with a large $K$ reaches equilibrium when most of the reactant has been converted to product, whereas a small $K$ means very little has been converted. The magnitude of $K$ does not indicate how rapidly equilibrium is reached.
concepts.evidence: The text notes that some equilibria are established nearly instantaneously and others so slowly that no change is observed over days or years, whatever their $K$.

concepts.name: Predicting the direction of reaction by comparing $Q$ with $K$
concepts.why: A reaction proceeds in whatever direction is necessary to achieve equilibrium: forward when $Q < K$, in reverse when $Q > K$, and not at all when $Q = K$.
concepts.evidence: Figure 13.6 shows three mixtures of CO, H<sub>2</sub>O, CO<sub>2</sub> and H<sub>2</sub> at 800 °C with $K_{c}=0.640$, and Example 13.3 finds $Q_{c}$ = 0.040, 140 and 0.48 for three experiments.

concepts.name: Relating $K_{P}$ and $K_{c}$, $K_{P}=K_{c}(RT)^{\Delta n}$
concepts.why: Since the partial pressure of an ideal gas is $P = MRT$, each pressure in $K_{P}$ is a concentration times $RT$, and the factors collect into $(RT)^{\Delta n}$, where $\Delta n$ is the difference in the molar amounts of product and reactant gases.
concepts.evidence: Example 13.4 finds $K_{P}=K_{c}$ when $\Delta n = 0$, and $K_{P}=3.0\times10^{-5}$ from $K_{c}=0.28$ at 900 °C for CS<sub>2</sub> + 4H<sub>2</sub> ⇌ CH<sub>4</sub> + 2H<sub>2</sub>S.

concepts.name: Homogeneous and heterogeneous equilibria
concepts.why: In a homogeneous equilibrium all reactants and products are in the same phase; in a heterogeneous equilibrium they occupy two or more phases. Because the relative concentrations of pure liquids and solids equal 1, they do not appear in $Q$ or $K$.
concepts.evidence: For PbCl2(s) ⇌ Pb2+(aq) + 2Cl−(aq), $K_{c}=[\text{Pb}^{2+}][\text{Cl}^{-}]^{2}$, and water as a solvent is left out of the expressions for HF and NH3 in water.

concepts.name: Equilibrium constants of coupled equilibria
concepts.why: Reversing an equation inverts its $K$, multiplying its coefficients by $x$ raises $K$ to the power $x$, and adding equations multiplies their $K$ values, so the $K$ of a net reaction follows from the $K$ values of the reactions that sum to it.
concepts.evidence: Example 13.5 reverses the ammonia synthesis and triples the formation of HI to find $K_{c}=(2.0)(1.2\times10^{5})=2.4\times10^{5}$ for 2NH<sub>3</sub> + 3I<sub>2</sub> ⇌ N<sub>2</sub> + 6HI at 400 °C.

concepts.name: Le Châtelier’s principle
concepts.why: A change in conditions that affects the forward and reverse rates differently (a stress) leaves the rates unequal, and the system experiences a net reaction in the direction of greater rate (a shift) that re-establishes equilibrium.
concepts.evidence: Changes in concentration and temperature are the two stresses that can shift an equilibrium, since they are what the rate law and the Arrhenius equation say affect rates.

concepts.name: A change in concentration shifts an equilibrium without changing $K$
concepts.why: Adding reactant or removing product makes $Q_{c} < K_{c}$ and the equilibrium shifts right; removing reactant or adding product makes $Q_{c} > K_{c}$ and it shifts left. The new composition differs, but the value of the equilibrium constant is the same after the stress as before.
concepts.evidence: For H<sub>2</sub> + I<sub>2</sub> ⇌ 2HI with $K_{c}=50.0$ at 400 °C, adding H<sub>2</sub> consumes I<sub>2</sub> and produces HI as equilibrium is re-established.

concepts.name: A change in volume shifts a gas equilibrium toward fewer or more moles of gas
concepts.why: Changing the volume changes every partial pressure by the same factor. If the reactant and product gases have equal total molar amounts, $Q_{P}$ is unchanged and there is no shift; otherwise decreasing the volume shifts the equilibrium toward the side with fewer moles of gas.
concepts.evidence: Compressing by a factor of 3 leaves $Q_{P}$ unchanged for H<sub>2</sub> + I<sub>2</sub> ⇌ 2HI but makes $Q_{P}{}'=3Q_{P}>K_{P}$ for 2NO<sub>2</sub> ⇌ 2NO + O<sub>2</sub>, which shifts left.

concepts.name: A change in temperature changes $K$
concepts.why: For an elementary reaction $K_{c}=k_{f}/k_{r}$, and the rate constants vary with temperature, so $K$ varies too. Treating heat as a reactant of an endothermic reaction and a product of an exothermic one predicts the shift: heating shifts an endothermic equilibrium right and an exothermic one left.
concepts.evidence: For N2O4 ⇌ 2NO2 with ΔH = +57.20 kJ, raising the temperature shifts the equilibrium to the right.

concepts.name: A catalyst does not change the equilibrium constant
concepts.why: A catalyst lowers the activation energies of both the forward and the reverse reactions, so both are accelerated and equilibrium is reached more quickly, but without a change in the equilibrium constant.
concepts.evidence: The reaction diagrams of Figure 13.8 show the lowered transition state of the catalyzed path above unchanged reactant and product energies.

concepts.name: Predicting the shift of a stressed equilibrium
concepts.why: Given a stress (a species added or removed, a change in volume or temperature, a catalyst), Le Châtelier’s principle predicts the direction of the shift and how each concentration changes as equilibrium is re-established.
concepts.evidence: The Haber-Bosch process of Figure 13.9 uses high pressures, continual removal of ammonia and a catalyst at 400–500 °C to favor the exothermic formation of NH<sub>3</sub>.

concepts.name: Relating the changes in concentration by the stoichiometry
concepts.why: Whatever the initial composition, the changes in the concentrations of the species in an equilibrium are related by the reaction stoichiometry, so all of them can be written as multiples of one unknown, $x$.
concepts.evidence: For 2NH<sub>3</sub> ⇌ N<sub>2</sub> + 3H<sub>2</sub>, if [N<sub>2</sub>] increases by $x$, then [H<sub>2</sub>] increases by $3x$ and [NH<sub>3</sub>] decreases by $2x$; Example 13.6 completes the change terms for three reactions.

concepts.name: Calculating an equilibrium constant with an ICE table
concepts.why: Collecting the initial concentrations, their changes and the equilibrium concentrations in an ICE table derives every equilibrium concentration from the data given, and substituting them into the $K$ expression gives the equilibrium constant.
concepts.evidence: Example 13.7 finds $x = 3.39\times10^{-4}$ M from the equilibrium concentration of I<sub>2</sub> and $K_{c}=776$ for I<sub>2</sub> + I<sup>−</sup> ⇌ I<sub>3</sub><sup>−</sup>.

concepts.name: Calculating a missing equilibrium concentration
concepts.why: When the equilibrium constant and all but one equilibrium concentration are known, the $K$ expression can be rearranged and solved for the missing concentration.
concepts.evidence: Example 13.8 finds [NO] = 3.6 × 10<sup>−4</sup> M in air at 2000 °C from $K_{c}=4.1\times10^{-4}$, [N<sub>2</sub>] = 0.036 M and [O<sub>2</sub>] = 0.0089 M.

concepts.name: Calculating equilibrium concentrations from initial concentrations
concepts.why: Four steps find the equilibrium composition from initial concentrations and $K$: identify the direction of reaction, develop an ICE table, solve for the change (by the quadratic formula where needed, keeping the physically meaningful root), and confirm the result by recalculating $K$.
concepts.evidence: Example 13.9 solves $x^{2}+0.0211x-0.0211=0$ for PCl<sub>5</sub> ⇌ PCl<sub>3</sub> + Cl<sub>2</sub> starting from 1.00 M PCl<sub>5</sub>, giving $x$ = 0.135 M.

concepts.name: Simplifying the algebra when the change is small
concepts.why: When $K$ is small, the change in concentration may be much less than the initial concentration, so the initial concentration minus $x$ can be approximated by the initial concentration. The result must be checked, and the calculation repeated without the approximation if $x$ is not negligible.
concepts.evidence: Example 13.10 finds $x = 8.6\times10^{-6}$ M for 0.15 M HCN with $K_{c}=4.9\times10^{-10}$, which is indeed much less than 0.15 M.

concepts.name: Brønsted-Lowry acids and bases
concepts.why: Brønsted and Lowry defined acids and bases in terms of the transfer of hydrogen ions: a compound that donates a proton is a Brønsted-Lowry acid, and a compound that accepts a proton is a Brønsted-Lowry base. An acid-base reaction is, thus, the transfer of a proton from a donor to an acceptor.
concepts.evidence: When hydrogen fluoride dissolves in water, protons are transferred from HF molecules to water molecules, yielding hydronium ions and fluoride ions.

concepts.name: Conjugate acid-base pairs
concepts.why: When an acid donates H<sup>+</sup>, the species that remains is its conjugate base, because it reacts as a proton acceptor in the reverse reaction; when a base accepts H<sup>+</sup>, it is converted to its conjugate acid. Every Brønsted-Lowry reaction therefore involves two conjugate pairs.
concepts.evidence: In the reaction of water with ammonia, water donates a proton and becomes OH<sup>−</sup>, its conjugate base, while ammonia accepts it and becomes NH<sub>4</sub><sup>+</sup>, its conjugate acid.

concepts.name: Writing acid and base ionization equations
concepts.why: Acid ionization is the reaction of an acid with water to give hydronium ion and the acid’s conjugate base; base ionization is the reaction of a base with water to give hydroxide ion and the base’s conjugate acid. Writing these equations requires identifying which species donates and which accepts the proton.
concepts.evidence: Pyridine, C<sub>5</sub>NH<sub>5</sub>, undergoes base ionization in water, yielding hydroxide and pyridinium ions, C<sub>5</sub>NH<sub>6</sub><sup>+</sup>.

concepts.name: Amphiprotic species
concepts.why: Species capable of either donating or accepting protons are called amphiprotic. When such a species is added to water, both its acid and its base equilibria are established at the same time.
concepts.evidence: Bicarbonate ion reacts with water as an acid to give CO<sub>3</sub><sup>2−</sup> and as a base to give H<sub>2</sub>CO<sub>3</sub>, and Example 14.3 writes HSO<sub>3</sub><sup>−</sup> reacting as an acid with OH<sup>−</sup> and as a base with HI.

concepts.name: The autoionization of water and $K_{\text{w}}$
concepts.why: Liquid water undergoes autoionization to a very slight extent, and the equilibrium constant for this reaction is the ion-product constant for water, $K_{\text{w}}$. The process is endothermic, so the extent of ionization, and with it $K_{\text{w}}$, increases with temperature.
concepts.evidence: At 25 °C, $K_{\text{w}}=1.0\times10^{-14}$, and approximately two out of every billion water molecules are ionized; at 100 °C, $K_{\text{w}}$ is about $5.6\times10^{-13}$, roughly 50 times larger.

concepts.name: Calculating [H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup>] and [OH<sup>−</sup>] from $K_{\text{w}}$
concepts.why: Because the product of the hydronium and hydroxide ion concentrations is fixed by $K_{\text{w}}$, the two are inversely proportional: knowing one gives the other, and in pure water each is the square root of $K_{\text{w}}$.
concepts.evidence: Example 14.1 finds [H3O+] = [OH−] = 1.0 × 10−7 M in pure water at 25 °C, and Example 14.2 finds [OH−] = 5.0 × 10−9 M when [H3O+] = 2.0 × 10−6 M.

concepts.name: Acidic, basic, and neutral solutions
concepts.why: A solution is neutral if it contains equal concentrations of hydronium and hydroxide ions, acidic if it contains a greater concentration of hydronium ions than hydroxide ions, and basic if it contains a lesser one. Since $K_{\text{w}}$ depends on temperature, the pH of a neutral solution does too.
concepts.evidence: At 25 °C a neutral solution has pH = 7.00, whereas at 80 °C neutral solutions exhibit pH = pOH = 6.31 (Table 14.1).

concepts.name: The pH and pOH scales
concepts.why: Hydronium and hydroxide ion concentrations span many orders of magnitude, so they are expressed with the p-function, the negative base-10 logarithm: pH = −log[H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup>] and pOH = −log[OH<sup>−</sup>]. Each unit of pH is a tenfold change in hydronium ion concentration.
concepts.evidence: Figure 14.2 shows the pH and pOH scales for common substances, from 1 M HCl near pH 0 to 1 M NaOH near pH 14.

concepts.name: pH + pOH = p$K_{\text{w}}$
concepts.why: Taking the negative logarithm of the $K_{\text{w}}$ expression shows that the pH and pOH of any aqueous solution sum to p$K_{\text{w}}$, which is 14.00 at 25 °C.
concepts.evidence: Example 14.6 finds the pOH of 0.0125 M KOH to be 1.903 and then its pH as 14.00 − 1.903 = 12.10.

concepts.name: Converting between concentrations, pH, and pOH
concepts.why: The definitions of pH and pOH and their sum let us move among [H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup>], [OH<sup>−</sup>], pH, and pOH; when taking the log of a value, we keep as many decimal places in the result as there are significant figures in the value.
concepts.evidence: Example 14.4 finds pH 2.92 for stomach acid with [H3O+] = 1.2 × 10−3 M, and Example 14.5 finds [H3O+] = 5 × 10−8 M for blood at pH 7.3.

concepts.name: Measuring pH with meters and indicators
concepts.why: The acidity of a solution is typically assessed by measuring its pH, directly with a pH meter or visually with colored indicators; the pOH is not usually measured, as it is easily calculated from the pH.
concepts.evidence: Figure 14.4 compares a research-grade pH meter with a portable one, and Figure 14.5 shows universal indicator and pH paper taking on different colors at different pH values.

concepts.name: Acid and base ionization constants, $K_{\text{a}}$ and $K_{\text{b}}$
concepts.why: The relative strength of an acid or base is the extent to which it ionizes in water, and it is quantified by the equilibrium constant of its ionization, $K_{\text{a}}$ or $K_{\text{b}}$, in which water, being the solvent, does not appear. The larger the constant, the stronger the acid or base.
concepts.evidence: The six common strong acids and six strong bases of Figure 14.6 ionize essentially completely, whereas the ionization constants of weak acids such as HSO<sub>4</sub><sup>−</sup>, HNO<sub>2</sub> and CH<sub>3</sub>CO<sub>2</sub>H span several powers of ten.

concepts.name: Percent ionization
concepts.why: Another measure of the strength of an acid is its percent ionization, the equilibrium hydronium ion concentration divided by the initial acid concentration, times 100. Unlike $K_{\text{a}}$, the percent ionization of a weak acid varies with its initial concentration, decreasing as the concentration increases.
concepts.evidence: Example 14.7 finds the percent ionization of 0.125 M nitrous acid at pH 2.09 to be 6.5%.

concepts.name: $K_{\text{a}}\times K_{\text{b}}=K_{\text{w}}$ for a conjugate pair
concepts.why: Adding the acid ionization of HA to the base ionization of A<sup>−</sup> gives the autoionization of water, so the product of their constants is $K_{\text{w}}$. The stronger an acid or base, the weaker its conjugate partner, and the conjugate of a strong acid or base has negligible strength.
concepts.evidence: Example 14.8 uses $K_{\text{b}}=2.17\times10^{-11}$ for the nitrite ion to find $K_{\text{a}}=4.6\times10^{-4}$ for HNO<sub>2</sub>; Figure 14.7 and Figure 14.8 rank several conjugate pairs against water.

concepts.name: The leveling effect of water
concepts.why: Acids stronger than H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup> react completely with water to give H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup>, and bases stronger than OH<sup>−</sup> react completely to give OH<sup>−</sup>, so in water all such acids and bases appear equally strong. Their differences show up only in a solvent that is a weaker base or acid than water.
concepts.evidence: Perchloric, hydrochloric and nitric acids are all completely ionized in water, yet Figure 14.8 lists them in order of strength measured in solvents such as acetic acid.

concepts.name: Determining $K_{\text{a}}$ or $K_{\text{b}}$ from equilibrium concentrations or pH
concepts.why: Substituting equilibrium concentrations into the ionization constant expression gives $K_{\text{a}}$ or $K_{\text{b}}$ directly; when only the formal concentration and the pH are known, the pH gives the equilibrium [H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup>] and an ICE table gives the rest.
concepts.evidence: Example 14.9 calculates $K_{\text{a}}=1.8\times10^{-5}$ for acetic acid from its equilibrium concentrations, and Example 14.11 calculates $K_{\text{a}}$ for nitrous acid from a 0.0516-M solution at pH 2.34.

concepts.name: Calculating equilibrium concentrations and pH in a weak acid or base solution
concepts.why: An ICE table built from the initial concentration and the ionization constant gives the equilibrium concentrations. When the constant is small and the initial concentration large, the change $x$ may be neglected against it, provided $x$ is less than 5% of the initial concentration; otherwise the quadratic equation is solved.
concepts.evidence: Example 14.12 finds pH 2.01 for 0.534 M formic acid with the assumption, and Example 14.14 solves the quadratic for 0.50 M HSO4−, where $x$ is about 15% of the initial concentration.

concepts.name: Strengths of binary acids across a period and down a group
concepts.why: Across a row of the periodic table, the acid strength of binary hydrogen compounds increases with the electronegativity of the nonmetal, because the polarity of the H–A bond increases; down a group, it increases as the H–A bond strength decreases.
concepts.evidence: Figure 14.11 shows acid strength increasing in the order CH<sub>4</sub> < NH<sub>3</sub> < H<sub>2</sub>O < HF across a period and HF < HCl < HBr < HI down a group.

concepts.name: Strengths of oxyacids and hydroxy compounds
concepts.why: In a ternary compound E–O–H, a central atom of low electronegativity makes the E–O bond ionic and the compound a base; a central atom of high electronegativity or high oxidation number draws electron density from the O–H bond and makes the compound an acid. Elements of intermediate electronegativity give amphoteric hydroxides.
concepts.evidence: Figure 14.12 shows nitric acid stronger than nitrous acid and sulfuric acid stronger than sulfurous acid, as the oxidation number of the central atom increases, and H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> is a stronger acid than H<sub>2</sub>SeO<sub>4</sub> because sulfur is more electronegative than selenium.

concepts.name: Acidic and basic ions in salts
concepts.why: The ions of a dissolved salt may undergo acid or base ionization with water. Acidic cations are typically the conjugate acids of weak bases, basic anions are the conjugate bases of weak acids, and the conjugates of strong acids and bases, like the group 1 and 2 cations, are inert.
concepts.evidence: Dissolving ammonium chloride gives weak acid cations (NH<sub>4</sub><sup>+</sup>) and inert anions (Cl<sup>−</sup>), an acidic solution; dissolving sodium acetate gives inert cations and weak base anions (CH<sub>3</sub>CO<sub>2</sub><sup>−</sup>), a basic solution.

concepts.name: Predicting whether a salt solution is acidic, basic, or neutral
concepts.why: We consider each ion separately; where a salt contains both an acidic and a basic ion, or a single amphiprotic ion, the solution is acidic or basic according to whether $K_{\text{a}}$ or $K_{\text{b}}$ is the larger.
concepts.evidence: Example 14.17 finds KBr neutral, NaHCO<sub>3</sub> and Na<sub>2</sub>HPO<sub>4</sub> basic because $K_{\text{b}}\gg K_{\text{a}}$ for their anions, and NH<sub>4</sub>F acidic because $K_{\text{a}}$ for NH<sub>4</sub><sup>+</sup> exceeds $K_{\text{b}}$ for F<sup>−</sup>.

concepts.name: Calculating the pH of a salt solution
concepts.why: The ionization constant of a salt’s acidic or basic ion is found from that of its conjugate partner through $K_{\text{a}}\times K_{\text{b}}=K_{\text{w}}$, and the usual ICE approach then gives the equilibrium concentrations and the pH.
concepts.evidence: Example 14.15 derives $K_{\text{a}}$ for anilinium ion from $K_{\text{b}}$ for aniline and finds the pH of a 0.233-M anilinium chloride solution to be 2.64.

concepts.name: Hydrated metal ions as acids
concepts.why: Many metal ions bond to water molecules to form complex ions such as [Al(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>6</sub>]<sup>3+</sup>; the metal draws electron density from the bonded water molecules, weakening their O–H bonds so that they can donate protons. Aside from the group 1 and some group 2 ions, most metal ions undergo acid ionization to some extent.
concepts.evidence: Figure 14.13 shows a hydrated aluminum ion donating a proton to water, and Example 14.18 finds the pH of 0.10 M aluminum chloride to be 2.92.

concepts.name: Polyprotic acids ionize stepwise
concepts.why: Acids are classified by the number of protons per molecule they can give up: monoprotic, diprotic, triprotic. A polyprotic acid ionizes in steps, one proton at a time, and each successive ionization is less extensive than the one before, so $K_{\text{a1}}>K_{\text{a2}}>K_{\text{a3}}$.
concepts.evidence: For carbonic acid, the first ionization constant is larger than the second by a factor of 10<sup>4</sup>, and phosphoric acid’s three stepwise constants decrease in turn.

concepts.name: Calculating concentrations in a solution of a polyprotic acid
concepts.why: If the first ionization constant of a weak diprotic acid is larger than the second by a factor of at least 20, each step may be treated separately: the first gives [H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup>] and the monoanion, and those concentrations feed the second.
concepts.evidence: Example 14.19 finds [H3O+] = [HCO3−] = 1.2 × 10−4 M and [CO32−] = 4.7 × 10−11 M in carbonated water that is 0.033 M in H2CO3.

concepts.name: Polyprotic bases
concepts.why: Polyprotic bases accept more than one proton, in steps, and, as for polyprotic acids, each successive base ionization constant is smaller than the one before.
concepts.evidence: The carbonate ion is a diprotic base, accepting one proton to form HCO<sub>3</sub><sup>−</sup> and a second to form H<sub>2</sub>CO<sub>3</sub>.

concepts.name: What a buffer is
concepts.why: A solution containing appreciable amounts of a weak conjugate acid-base pair is a buffer, and it resists a change in pH when small amounts of a strong acid or a strong base are added.
concepts.evidence: In Figure 14.14, 1 mL of 0.01-M HCl turns an unbuffered solution at pH 8 acidic but leaves a pH 8.0 buffer unchanged; acetic acid with sodium acetate and ammonia with ammonium chloride are the book’s two examples.

concepts.name: How a buffer neutralizes added acid or base
concepts.why: The weak acid of the pair neutralizes added hydroxide, converting it to the conjugate base, and the conjugate base neutralizes added hydronium, converting it to the weak acid. The ratio of the two changes only a little, and so does the pH.
concepts.evidence: Figure 14.15 shows added NaOH converting some acetic acid to acetate and added HCl converting some acetate to acetic acid, with the pH barely moving.

concepts.name: Calculating the pH of a buffer before and after adding acid or base
concepts.why: We first let the added strong acid or base react completely with the buffer component that neutralizes it, find the new concentrations of the two components, and then solve the equilibrium as before.
concepts.evidence: Example 14.20 finds pH 4.74 for an acetate buffer with 0.10 M of each component and pH 4.75 after 1.0 mL of 0.10 M NaOH is added to 100 mL of it, whereas the same addition takes an unbuffered solution from pH 4.74 to 10.99.

concepts.name: Buffer capacity and the choice of buffer
concepts.why: A buffer can neutralize only as much acid or base as it has of the conjugate partner that consumes it, so its capacity depends on the amounts of both components. A good buffer has about equal concentrations of the two, and weak acids and their salts suit pHs below 7 while weak bases and their salts suit pHs above 7.
concepts.evidence: Figure 14.16 shows a large amount of acid exhausting a buffer, and Figure 14.17 shows the pH of an acetate buffer changing slowly with added NaOH until one component falls below about 10% of the other.

concepts.name: The Henderson-Hasselbalch equation
concepts.why: Rearranging the acid ionization constant expression and taking the negative logarithm gives pH = p$K_{\text{a}}$ + log([A<sup>−</sup>]/[HA]), which relates the pH of a buffer to the $K_{\text{a}}$ of its weak acid and the ratio of the concentrations of the pair; when the two are equal, pH = p$K_{\text{a}}$.
concepts.evidence: The book uses it for the carbonate buffer of blood, where [HCO3−] ≈ 0.024 M and [H2CO3] ≈ 0.0012 M give a pH near 7.4.

concepts.name: Titration curves and their stages
concepts.why: A titration curve plots the pH of the sample against the volume of added titrant. Its initial point is set by the acid, the pre-equivalence region by the unreacted acid and its conjugate base, the equivalence point by the products alone, with a drastic rise in pH, and the postequivalence region by the excess titrant.
concepts.evidence: Table 14.2 and Figure 14.18 give the pH of 25.00 mL of 0.100 M HCl and of 0.100 M CH3CO2H against the volume of 0.100 M NaOH added.

concepts.name: Calculating pH in a strong acid-strong base titration
concepts.why: Before the equivalence point the pH is set by the excess strong acid, at the equivalence point only water and a neutral salt remain, so the pH is 7.00 at 25 °C, and beyond it the pH is set by the excess strong base.
concepts.evidence: Example 14.21 finds pH 1.000, 1.477, 7.00 and 12.30 after 0.00, 12.50, 25.00 and 37.50 mL of 0.100 M NaOH are added to 25.00 mL of 0.100 M HCl.

concepts.name: Calculating pH in a weak acid-strong base titration
concepts.why: Before any base is added the pH is that of the weak acid; halfway to equivalence the acid and its conjugate base are equal, so pH = p$K_{\text{a}}$; at equivalence the conjugate base alone makes the solution basic; beyond it the excess strong base sets the pH.
concepts.evidence: Example 14.22 finds pH 2.87 initially, 4.74 at the half-equivalence point and 8.72 at the equivalence point in the titration of 0.100 M acetic acid with 0.100 M NaOH.

concepts.name: How an acid-base indicator works
concepts.why: An indicator is a weak acid or base whose conjugate forms have different colors, and the perceived color is set by the ratio [In<sup>−</sup>]/[HIn], which the solution pH fixes. The color change is therefore spread over a color-change interval of about two pH units centered near its p$K_{\text{a}}$.
concepts.evidence: Methyl orange is red as HIn and yellow as In<sup>−</sup>, and Figure 14.19 charts the color-change intervals of several indicators.

concepts.name: Choosing an indicator for a titration
concepts.why: A suitable indicator has a color-change interval that falls within the steep, nearly vertical part of the titration curve at the equivalence point, so that its color changes sharply as the equivalence point is passed.
concepts.evidence: Figure 14.20 shows methyl orange, bromthymol blue and phenolphthalein all suiting the strong acid titration, but only phenolphthalein suiting the weak acid titration, whose equivalence point lies above pH 8.

concepts.name: The solubility product constant, $K_{\text{sp}}$
concepts.why: A saturated solution of a sparingly soluble ionic solid is an equilibrium in which the solid dissolves and its ions precipitate at equal rates. Its equilibrium constant is the solubility product, which, because only gases and solutes appear in an equilibrium constant expression, includes no term for the undissolved solid.
concepts.evidence: For silver chloride, AgCl(s) ⇌ Ag+(aq) + Cl–(aq) and Ksp = [Ag+][Cl–].

concepts.name: Writing dissolution equations and solubility product expressions
concepts.why: The dissolution equation shows the ions a compound yields and their coefficients, and each coefficient becomes the exponent of that ion's concentration in the solubility product expression.
concepts.evidence: Magnesium hydroxide dissolves as Mg(OH)2(s) ⇌ Mg2+(aq) + 2OH–(aq), so Ksp = [Mg2+][OH–]2 (Example 15.1).

concepts.name: Calculating $K_{\text{sp}}$ from a measured solubility
concepts.why: When dissolution involves only dissociation and solvation, a measured solubility, converted to molar solubility where it is given in grams per liter, fixes every ion concentration through the dissolution stoichiometry, and the solubility product follows.
concepts.evidence: A saturated fluorite solution has [Ca2+] = 2.15 × 10–4 M and so [F–] = 4.30 × 10–4 M, giving Ksp = 3.98 × 10–11 (Example 15.2).

concepts.name: Calculating a molar solubility from $K_{\text{sp}}$
concepts.why: Writing the equilibrium concentrations of an ICE table in terms of the molar solubility x and substituting them into the solubility product expression gives an equation in x alone, whose root is the molar solubility.
concepts.evidence: For Ca(OH)2, 1.3 × 10–6 = (x)(2x)2 = 4x3, so the molar solubility is 6.9 × 10–3 M (Example 15.4).

concepts.name: Predicting precipitation by comparing $Q_{\text{sp}}$ with $K_{\text{sp}}$
concepts.why: The dissolution equilibrium is established in any solution containing the ions, whatever their source. If the ion concentrations give a reaction quotient greater than the solubility product, the solution is supersaturated and precipitation occurs until the quotient equals the solubility product; if the quotient is smaller, no precipitate forms.
concepts.evidence: Mixing equal volumes of 2.0 × 10–4 M AgNO3 and NaCl gives Q = 1.0 × 10–8, greater than Ksp = 1.6 × 10–10, so AgCl precipitates (Example 15.8).

concepts.name: Calculating the ion concentration at which precipitation begins
concepts.why: Setting the reaction quotient equal to the solubility product and substituting the known ion concentration gives the concentration of the counter ion at which a precipitate first forms, or the concentration needed to lower a dissolved ion to a chosen level.
concepts.evidence: With [Ca2+] = 2.2 × 10–3 M in blood serum, CaC2O4 begins to precipitate when the oxalate concentration reaches 8.9 × 10–7 M (Example 15.9).

concepts.name: Selective precipitation
concepts.why: When two ions form insoluble compounds with the same counter ion, raising the counter ion concentration slowly precipitates first the ion whose compound reaches its solubility product at the lower counter ion concentration, which depends on both the solubility products and the ion concentrations.
concepts.evidence: In a solution 0.00010 M in Br– and 0.10 M in Cl–, AgCl begins to precipitate at [Ag+] = 1.6 × 10–9 M, before AgBr, despite its larger Ksp (Example 15.11).

concepts.name: The common ion effect on solubility
concepts.why: Because the product of the ion concentrations is constant at equilibrium regardless of the source of the ions, adding one of the ions shifts the dissolution equilibrium to the left, and an ionic compound is less soluble in a solution that already contains a common ion than in pure water.
concepts.evidence: The molar solubility of CdS is only 1.0 × 10–26 M in a 0.010-M solution of CdBr2 (Example 15.13).

concepts.name: Coordinate covalent bonds
concepts.why: A coordinate covalent bond, or dative bond, occurs when one of the atoms in the bond provides both bonding electrons.
concepts.evidence: When a water molecule combines with a hydrogen ion to form a hydronium ion, the oxygen atom provides both electrons of the new O–H bond.

concepts.name: Lewis acids, Lewis bases, and adducts
concepts.why: In Lewis's definition, a base donates an electron pair and an acid accepts one, forming a coordinate covalent bond in a product called an adduct. Brønsted-Lowry acid-base reactions are the subcategory in which the acid is H<sup>+</sup>.
concepts.evidence: Boron trifluoride, with only six valence electrons on boron, accepts a lone pair from fluoride ion to form the adduct BF<sub>4</sub><sup>–</sup>.

concepts.name: Complex ions and ligands
concepts.why: A complex ion comprises a central atom, typically a transition metal cation acting as a Lewis acid, surrounded by ligands, molecules or ions that each donate an electron pair as Lewis bases.
concepts.evidence: Each of two ammonia molecules donates a pair of electrons to a silver ion to form Ag(NH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub><sup>+</sup>.

concepts.name: Formation and dissociation constants of complex ions
concepts.why: The equilibrium constant for the reaction of a metal ion with ligands to form a complex ion is its formation constant, and the constant for the reverse reaction is the dissociation constant, its reciprocal. A large formation constant lowers the free metal ion concentration enough to dissolve a sparingly soluble salt of the metal.
concepts.evidence: With Kf = 1.7 × 107 for Ag(NH3)2+, ammonia lowers [Ag+] until [Ag+][Cl–] falls below the Ksp of AgCl, and more silver chloride dissolves.

concepts.name: Calculating concentrations in a complex ion equilibrium
concepts.why: An ICE table for the dissociation of a complex ion, with the small-x assumption that a very large formation constant justifies, gives the concentrations of the free metal ion and ligand.
concepts.evidence: A solution initially 0.10 M in Ag(NH3)2+ contains 1.1 × 10–3 M free silver ion (Example 15.14).

concepts.name: Salts of basic anions are more soluble in acid
concepts.why: When a salt's anion is a base, its dissolution is coupled with the anion's reaction with hydronium ion, which removes the anion and shifts the dissolution equilibrium to the right. The net reaction's constant is the solubility product divided by the conjugate acid's ionization constant.
concepts.evidence: For calcium carbonate in acid, K = Ksp/Ka2 = 180, much greater than Ksp, which is why ocean acidification threatens coral reefs.

concepts.name: Complex formation increases solubility
concepts.why: When dissolution is coupled with the formation of a complex ion of the dissolved metal, the constant for the net reaction is the product of the solubility product and the formation constant, and it can be large even when the solubility product is tiny.
concepts.evidence: Aluminum hydroxide dissolves in strong base as Al(OH)4–, with K = KspKf = (2 × 10–32)(1.1 × 1033) = 22.

concepts.name: Calculating solubilities in coupled equilibria
concepts.why: The concentrations in a coupled system follow from one equilibrium at a time, such as the hydroxide ion concentration of a buffer and then the solubility product, or from the constant of the combined net reaction.
concepts.evidence: In a buffer of 0.100 M acetic acid and 0.100 M sodium acetate, [OH–] = 5.5 × 10–10 M and the molar solubility of Al(OH)3 is 1.2 × 10–4 M, about ten million times that in pure water (Example 15.15).
